en: The Scripture on the Collection of Right Practices for the Covering of Blessings, Volume One.
Compiled by Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master of the Western Heaven, Chao San Dafu [and other titles].
I prostrate in homage to all Buddhas and the assembly of noble Bodhisattvas, who, with the eye of pure wisdom, universally guide all living beings.
Śakra possesses a thousand eyes; Maheśvara has three eyes.
Even the light of the sun and moon cannot illuminate it all.
With his two eyes, Nārāyaṇa manifests various forms and subdues the asuras who rely on arrogance and wrath.
Only the Buddha possesses the light of wisdom, extinguishing evil and dispelling accumulated darkness;
it is as if using a peacock’s tail to brush away all defilements and poisons.
The Tathāgata, the Great Man, extends the mark of the white tuft from his crown.
Circled seven times to the right in a clockwise spiral, it was lustrous and most lovely;
the light of the sun and moon, the lamps of the world, were all eclipsed and did not appear.
All the devas and the people of the world made offerings to it and praised it.
Having heard this teaching, what should one do?
One should respect and cherish the words of the Buddha.
That light of wisdom shines afar like a lamp, capable of destroying the darkness of the cataracts of ignorance; therefore, it has been revealed.

The Buddha’s eye of wisdom is like a great cloud capable of pouring down sweet rain; it is like the full moon of autumn capable of removing the heat of affliction. It ultimately upholds the true Dharma of all Buddhas and increases the wisdom of all Buddhas. It definitively accomplishes the faculties, powers, and factors of enlightenment; it calms and eliminates the two kinds of wind and waves—karma and delusion—and is not submerged by the river of craving. Riding the ship of the True Dharma, one reaches the other shore.

One should skillfully cultivate practices such as giving; by using precious treasures for the purpose of almsgiving, one destroys the fault of greed and increases meaningful benefit. One should delight in upholding the pure precepts and reciting the sūtras.
Having acted in this way, you bhikṣus will swiftly attain the perfection of that canopy of merit.
As the Buddha has taught, why do you not practice the ten wholesome courses of action?

Your mind is driven by craving like a servant; though your body is clothed in pleasure, you do not realize impermanence. You pursue objects again and again without rest, and out of ignorance you give rise to pride. You are stingy and protective of your own wealth and treasures, turning away with a scowl when any beggars approach. You have never for even a moment practiced pure precepts or cultivated meditative concentrations in a secluded and quiet place. Regarding the conduct for benefiting sentient beings as taught by the Buddha, you have gained nothing therein.

Furthermore, this wealth increases arrogance, restlessness, and distraction; it gives rise to much sorrow and affliction, produces various fears, and obstructs the path to wholesome states. It is a phenomenon that disintegrates, a phenomenon that leads to downfall, and a phenomenon that is impermanent. It has no master and no place of refuge; it cannot be found in either the past or the future. Its present pleasure lasts but a moment and does not abide, being like a dream, a magical illusion, a mirage, a city of the Gandharvas, or a whirling firebrand. Like the core of a plantain tree, it has no substance; like a bubble on the water, it disperses and perishes in an instant.
Fools do not understand this; they grasp at various things with longing, and for this reason, they experience much suffering and little joy, accumulating the very root of all afflictions.
Therefore, one should cultivate the perception of non-solidity and the perception of impermanence.

By means of such remedies, one will not be harmed or diminished by thieves, water, fire, government officials, or kinsmen; nor will one be devoured by King Yama, but shall certainly achieve the blissful rewards of merit in future lives.

By gathering sentient beings through the gift of material wealth, such a person is like the *kumuda* flower, which blooms in full splendor and is joyfully beheld by all; all accumulated sins and obscurations are extinguished in an instant, just as a blazing fire consumes dry wood without remainder. Like the Ganges washing away all impurities until they are entirely purified, or like a mani-jewel that fulfills the desires of all who come to beg, such a person is universally praised and becomes a refuge for all.
One shall accomplish supreme, auspicious, and true merit; one’s fine reputation will spread far and wide, one will be free from all faults and afflictions, and one’s lifespan will be long.

By extensively cultivating the holy life (*brahmacarya*), one can destroy the poisons of greed, hatred, and delusion, as well as the faults of false views; mounting the vehicle of merit, one will never again fall.
If one’s defiled mind becomes attached to sensual objects and creates black karma, one will swiftly pass away and transmigrate, just like the celestial son Gamanasara.
One should know that women are loathsome with impurities, yet deluded sentient beings vie with one another to crave and cling to them.

Those who are attached to desire are like a thirsty person drinking salt water, whose heart knows no satisfaction; they are like a tree whose roots are severed, soon to wither away; like a mountain torrent, impossible to dam; like dwelling in a snake's den, subject to its bites and stings; like touching a red-hot iron ball, producing only suffering and distress; like eating a poisonous fruit, which will surely cause harm later; like dew on the grass, unable to remain for long; like floating clouds in the sky, suddenly dispersing and vanishing; like a castle built of sand, destined for swift destruction; like a vessel made of unbaked clay, its substance not firm; like Indra’s bow, soon to fade away; like riding a broken cart, which overturns as soon as it moves; and like a net, which binds as soon as one touches it. They take all manner of calamities as their companions; therefore, a true gentleman should abandon them.
Furthermore, the World-Honored One said:

"If one does not give rise to greedy attachment toward the five desires, one will obtain immeasurable rewards of happiness in the present life; such a person can cut off the torrential flood of afflictions and, by boarding the ship of the True Dharma, reach the other shore."
Having accumulated meritorious conduct for three great asaṃkhyeya kalpas, I have finally attained this eloquence of abundant meaning and flavor, which I now impartially reveal to all sentient beings.
"You all should go to secluded and quiet places, investigate and discern what I have taught, just as one seeks butter, curd, and clarified butter from within milk."
Having understood this, one accumulates the wealth of the Dharma and pure substances to employ in giving.

Furthermore, all Tathāgatas have emerged from the mire of the afflictions of the three realms and have accomplished pure, untainted, and supreme virtues; they skillfully reveal and teach the Dharma of contentment.
Like a supreme grove, those who dwell therein find coolness and are free from all feverish afflictions.
By skillfully cultivating this practice, one attains birth in the Brahma Heaven.
In that place, no afflictions can disturb or unsettle me, and all fears are entirely eliminated.
For this reason, one destroys saṃsāra and attains perfect enlightenment.

Furthermore, all Tathāgatas are endowed with great compassion and are well able to subdue all non-Buddhists; through pure wisdom they observe and discern, and through gentle speech they gather and instruct. Bestowing fearlessness, they preach the True Dharma, causing beings to give rise to faith and understanding, to destroy the net of Māra, and to attain abiding peace within the Buddha-dharma.

This great man is able to roar the lion’s roar; like a great dragon-elephant, his majestic virtue is exceptionally sublime. He raises great clouds and thunder, pouring down the rain of ambrosia; he cultivates the wondrous fragrance of untainted precepts and meditative concentration, such that all his actions are never in vain.

He proclaims the essential teachings of the Dharma for all sentient beings, causing them to be free from all harshness and affliction and bringing them joy; like a kalpavṛkṣa tree blooming with soft flowers, the supreme medicinal Dharma removes the defilements of the mind.
As the World-Honored One has said:

"Those who uphold the pure precepts possess wholesome dharmas; they are free from all sorrow and fear, attain peace and happiness, are able to cross the ocean of suffering to reach the other shore, and skillfully destroy the four māras—namely, the celestial māra, the aggregate māra, the death māra, and the affliction māra."

Such a person is able to blow the great Dharma conch, beat the great Dharma drum, and light the great Dharma torch; with a pure and joyful mind, they benefit all beings and perform the work of a Buddha by teaching and transforming devas and humans.

Furthermore, throughout immeasurable kalpas, all Tathāgatas have accumulated merit and virtue and cultivated wisdom, thereby achieving unimpeded eloquence, the four fearlessnesses, and the ten powers of knowledge; they have skillfully mastered the factors of enlightenment and are able to shatter all demonic adversaries with the arrows of wisdom.
Having directly realized such qualities, he becomes the foremost in the three realms and acts as a great compassionate father to all sentient beings.

Furthermore, by virtue of possessing ten kinds of superior powers of knowledge (*jñānabala*), the Tathāgatas convert non-Buddhists to become their disciples, causing them to develop a profound aspiration for the Buddha’s wisdom and ethical discipline.
The first to realize the state of an Arya was Kauṇḍinya;
he was able to dispel the cataracts of ignorance, dullness, and stupidity, and was thus most distinguished among those of the True Dharma. These were Mahākāśyapa and Uruvilvākāśyapa.
Among the brahmins, he was the foremost; having taken the medicine of the Buddha’s Dharma to cure the disease of afflictions, he is called the Venerable Śāriputra.
Capable of restraining the wild elephant of the mind with the hook of wisdom and possessing great supernormal powers, he is called Mahāmaudgalyāyana.

Those who have fully cultivated sublime practices and ascended the ladder of the True Dharma, dwelling securely in the pavilion of pure liberation—namely, Anuruddha, Piṇḍola, Pāṭaliputra, Mahākauṣṭhila, Ānanda, and others.

Furthermore, they were able to transform and deliver King Bimbisāra, causing him to give rise to profound faith and understanding within the Buddha-dharma, so that he honored and revered them as disciples of the Buddha.

All these noble ones used the axe of wisdom to fell the tree of dependent origination; free from all deluded thoughts and aspiring to omniscience, they abandoned the views of non-Buddhists, subdued and eliminated their pride, and were fully able to accomplish all meritorious virtues.
If one falsely assumes mastery over the four great poisonous snakes and the empty heap of the five aggregates, there will be no liberation; one must therefore sever them with the sword of wisdom.
Furthermore, with the eye of wisdom, one views the objects of the six sense bases as enemies and bandits, and the twelve bases and so forth as thickets of thorns.
One who skillfully enters into this understanding is not scorched or oppressed by the blazing flames of internal and external afflictions; such a person is one who well maintains pure precepts.

Abiding on the ground of patience and attaining the factors of mindfulness, they possess the radiance of wisdom to shatter the darkness of ignorance; such persons can then drink the water of the Eightfold Noble Path and further cause the flowers of the factors of enlightenment to bloom.

This is the ability to transcend the pavilions of the three periods of time, sever the fetters of existence, and enter the ocean of wisdom; to sit cross-legged at the site of enlightenment, dwelling skillfully in the four dhyānas and the supreme untainted samādhis, and to enjoy all unsurpassed dharmic bliss.

Furthermore, those foolish worldlings who destroy their share of wholesome dharmas and take pleasure in attachment to the objects of the five worldly desires are like dew touched by the wind, unable to endure for long; drifting in the ocean of suffering, they fail to attain liberation, seeing the bridge of the Dharma yet abandoning it and departing from afar.
As it is said in a sutra:
Long ago, there was a certain elder among the brahmins who intended to harm a woman with a sharp sword.
Suddenly beholding the Tathāgata, he cried out in a loud voice:
"May the Buddha rescue us," they prayed,
and immediately attained liberation.
It is also like Aṅgulimāla, who intended to harm his mother and others.

Furthermore, he was able to subdue the Brahma-ascetic Dīrghanakha, who had given rise to great arrogance, causing him to enter the Buddha-dharma and partake of the flavor of the True Dharma; likewise, he caused all foolish people, upon hearing this teaching, to abandon their pride and conceit.
It is also like a malevolent dragon that, harboring burning affliction in its heart, exhales fierce poisonous breath to damage the crops.
Or again, it is like a yakṣa who, with an evil eye, gazes upon hundreds of thousands of sentient beings to cause them harm.
Just as a multitude of merchants have sunk into the great ocean and are about to be swallowed by a timi fish,
so too are they beset by such terrifying evils and perils that only the Tathāgata can rescue and deliver them.

Furthermore, just as the sun and moon are feared by the asuras, Śakra, Lord of Devas, fears falling into the evil realms, and Brahmā holds the heterodox view of conceiving a self as eternal—through such unreal views, one wanders through saṃsāra and undergoes all manner of oppression. May all who hear the True Dharma attain awakening and understanding, drink the flavor of liberation, and shatter the shell of ignorance.

The light of that wisdom is as pure as the moon; therefore, one should engender deep respect for the Tathāgata’s teachings, draw near to Dharma masters, delight in hearing the True Dharma, investigate its true meaning, and practice in accordance with the instructions.
The teachings of those non-Buddhist paths are the dharmas of saṃsāra; all who possess wisdom should reflect upon this well.

Furthermore, the Honored Muni taught the Dharma of the Deathless (amṛta) as the light of wisdom to shatter the darkness of ignorance, like one standing on a high peak looking down upon the multitude of things below.
The accumulation of unrighteousness is like a heap of excrement and soil; one should use the spade of wisdom to clear it away.

By crushing all demonic adversaries and destroying all heterodox arguments, one causes others to enter into understanding and give rise to the mind of wisdom. Thus, the feverish afflictions of body and mind are entirely dispelled, and all evils are utterly extinguished.
The Sage has said that it is like a broad parasol providing shade from the sun of afflictions, thereby attaining coolness.
If one can paint or fashion images of the Buddha and make offerings of incense, flowers, and garlands according to one's means, this constitutes a gradual step toward rebirth in heaven.
By virtue of relying on the Buddha’s words, all karmic obstructions are purified in an instant, and meditative concentrations and liberations are all brought before one;
this is not like the outsiders who waste their lives in vain, performing no cultivation yet giving rise to false and deluded views, seeking liberation by washing in the waters of the Ganges.

Having understood this, you should courageously transcend the realm of Māra; wielding the sword of wisdom, destroy the thieves of affliction, shatter the wheel of birth and death, and tear asunder the net of entanglements and hindrances. Equip yourself with the eye of pure knowledge to extinguish all darkness of ignorance, stifle the heart of craving and attachment, subdue the venomous snake of anger, sever all false views, and demolish the mountain of self-conceit.
One should feel love, joy, and reverence for the place where the Buddha was born, scattering *śāla* flowers as an offering; then all that one seeks will be accomplished.

Free from all slander and liberated from all fears, one should abide in the true principle of all Buddhas, depart from the marks of arising and ceasing, attain the bliss of tranquility, and with a single mind, aspire to hear the Dharma.
Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, there were two non-Buddhist practitioners in the assembly, namely the great seers Kapila and Ulūka. Having abandoned their original false views and entered into an understanding of the Buddha’s wisdom, they skillfully eliminated the darkness of ignorance and were able to cross the ocean of suffering. They then reflected thus:

"How is it that the Tathāgata has achieved such pure and vast merit as a canopy, with such exquisite physical marks as molten pure gold; so majestic and preeminent like Mount Sumeru; possessing the thirty-two marks of a Great Man and the eighty minor marks of excellence, appearing with such clarity and peerless dignity, untainted by any dust or defilement?"
He manifests a body sixteen feet tall, its radiance dazzling and pervasive throughout the entirety of space, illuminating everything whether hidden or manifest.

His eyes are like the broad petals of a great blue lotus; the tuft of white hair between his brows is like the full moon in autumn. His face is lustrous, subtle, and lovely; his hair is a deep azure, like the tail feathers of a peacock. The crown of his head is level and full like the canopy of Indra, and his pure *uṣṇīṣa* is like a *maṇi* jewel. His entire body is resplendent with golden light that shines upon one another, a sight that all sentient beings delight to behold.
"Just as a swarm of bees gathers the exquisite fragrance of flowers, one never tires of beholding each of my marks and signs of excellence; they are like *kusuma* flowers blooming in spring.

At that time, the Tathāgata, in accordance with the thoughts in the minds of those non-Buddhists, surveyed all sentient beings throughout immeasurable and boundless worlds with the eye of pure wisdom. Feeling great compassion, he addressed them, saying:
"O sons of good family!..."

For three great asaṃkhyeya kalpas, I have cultivated immeasurable pure and correct practices and accumulated vast, boundless merit and wisdom; it is not through minor causes that one can obtain abiding in this inexhaustible treasure-store of merit. With a heart of great compassion, I have resolutely rescued immeasurable hundreds of thousands of beings in the hells, causing them all to cease their suffering by eliminating the notions of enemy and kin.

Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, the Court Scattered Official, Acting Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial, the Great Master of Xuanfan, the Purple-Robed Śramaṇa Subject Rìchēng, and others, by imperial decree. At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, wearing a most exquisite jeweled crown of *maṇi* gems upon his head, came from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to the place where the Buddha was.

Beholding the Buddha’s physical marks and the manifold virtues with which he was adorned, his heart was filled with great joy; having attained what he had never experienced before, he prostrated himself at the feet of the World-Honored Buddha and, with a sublime and wondrous voice, extolled the Buddha’s virtues:

“If sentient beings behold the Buddha’s marks and signs and give rise to a sense of rare wonder, making offerings, showing reverence, honoring, and praising him, they shall be able to destroy the four types of demonic activities, accomplish their aims and benefits, and attain great auspiciousness.”
"You gods, humans, māras, and brahmās, all should come here to behold the Unsurpassed Honored One."

At that time, there were various vidyādhara maharṣis, the sun and moon devaputras, as well as the lunar mansions and planets, Varuṇa, Agni, Vaiśravaṇa, Yāma, Mahābrahmā, Baladharman, Nārāyaṇa, Prajāpati, and others; along with nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, piśācas, and śṛgālas—all such classes of beings united their minds to make offerings, prostrate, and praise the Buddha’s merit. This is the supreme supramundane wisdom, whose vast renown is heard and known by all, yet which the great śrāvakas such as Śāriputra and others cannot fathom within its sphere of knowledge.

From the summit of Mount Sumeru up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, all sentient beings together gaze intently upon the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān. The Dharma he teaches is free from falsehood; it is excellent in its beginning, middle, and end. His words are skillful and his meaning is profound and vast, capable of shattering the ignorance, delusion, and dullness of sentient beings who have heard little and lack wisdom.

Having caused them to hear this, may they give rise to great awakening, delight in practicing right conduct, and increase their life of wisdom; may they certainly escape the terrors of the evil realms, open wide the gates of the vast city of Nirvana, and enter the inconceivable realm of liberation.
This sūtra explains the prior causes for the "Canopy of Merit" (*Puṇyāvatamsaka*).
How is this to be understood?

Having heard this teaching, one extensively practices pure giving and firmly upholds the prohibitive precepts; one does not give rise to craving or delight in worldly sensual pleasures, and develops faith and compliance toward all wholesome benefits. By practicing in this manner, one will swiftly achieve accomplishment.

It is like a person who, at night in the darkness, carries a great torch and enters a large house; in every direction within that place, they are able to see clearly all the treasuries of precious jewels and various articles, whether fine or coarse, each appearing distinctly, so that they can fully utilize them and obtain peaceful happiness.

Furthermore, if there should be a person who, within this sutra, upholds, recites, and reads it; delights in hearing its profound meaning; draws near to the Dharma Master; reflects according to the principle; and gives rise to awakening in their mind—know that such a person is able, amidst the long night of birth and death, to hold aloft the great torch of wisdom and enter the city of Nirvana. Regarding the profound Dharma, whether in principle or in phenomena, they will be able to understand it all and attain complete penetration. Free from all doubt and having shattered the darkness of ignorance, they will transcend saṃsāra and achieve liberation of mind, thereby enjoying inexhaustible Dharma-joy.
As the Blessed One has said:
"Defiled worldly states do not give rise to superior wisdom; only the lamp of right knowledge can dispel the darkness of delusion.
Therefore, the wise should seek the supramundane, untainted True Dharma and should skillfully examine the teachings corresponding to the sūtras and treatises spoken by the Buddha.
Just as all sentient beings create merit or non-merit and each receives their respective retribution without fail, one should know that the world arises entirely from causes and conditions:
if there were no sentient beings, there would be no afflictions; and if there were no afflictions, there would be no hells.

Therefore, I now teach the Dharma of causes and conditions; it is not like the false attachments and divergent views of the non-Buddhists, who claim that all phenomena arise without cause or condition.
They speculate:
"Who sharpened the sharp points of thorns?"
The feathers and fur of birds and beasts—who paints them?
This matter is evident; why rely on karma as the cause?
From this, one understands that everything in the world arises spontaneously and does not require cultivation or effort.

The Tathāgata, having known this, gave rise to great compassion and, out of pity, taught and transformed them; with the light of wisdom, he extinguished their darkness of delusion and gradually led them to awaken to and enter the knowledge of all-knowledge (sarvajñajñāna), causing them to abandon their original false views and attain liberation of mind within the Buddha-dharma.
This sutra states that the teachings of the Buddha regarding the dharma of giving and other practices enable one to transcend saṃsāra and attain all forms of happiness.
We observe in the world that sentient beings create meritorious or non-meritorious karma and receive the retributions of suffering or pleasure accordingly.

For example, when the householder Anāthapiṇḍada gave rise to pure faith, he offered thirty koṭis of gold, silver, and precious jewels to the Tathāgata and his disciples, such as the great arhat Ānanda; he constructed a vihāra and performed great offerings. In this very life, he obtained immeasurable karmic rewards, possessed great renown, and lived in peace, security, and abundance. His various treasuries were all overflowing, and his relatives, friends, slaves, and servants became numerous and flourishing; they all attained perfect enjoyment of inexhaustible and sublime happiness.
It is because of such giving that such a retribution is experienced.

Furthermore, all Tathāgatas, out of great compassion, take pity on all sentient beings; they are like the King of Physicians in the world who can skillfully treat the various ailments of the world—such as wind, bile, and phlegm—with excellent medicines, causing them to be healed and cured.
The Tathāgata is likewise; he skillfully expounds the medicine of the Dharma, able to remove the root and secondary afflictions of sentient beings and cause them to attain liberation.
Yet those sentient beings lack the seeds of goodness and possess no provisions; they fail to exert diligence and do not seek liberation, being bound by the chronic malady of the three poisons.

Such persons are difficult to transform and deliver; therefore, the Tathāgata, with impartial great compassion and without thoughts of enemy or friend, bestows the medicine of the Dharma upon them to be taken and practiced. For their sake, he teaches the practices of giving, upholding the precepts, and so forth, and instructs them that they should always receive and uphold the profound sutras.
Furthermore, a human body is extremely difficult to obtain, like a blind turtle encountering the hole of a floating log.

One must diligently cultivate the ten wholesome paths of action to seek liberation from the limits of suffering. Even if one obtains a human body, it may not be born in a central land; or one’s faculties may be incomplete; or one may lack affection for the Buddha-dharma; or one may be born in a world where no Buddha resides; or, due to evil karma, one may suffer the retribution of being mute and unable to proclaim the true Dharma of the Buddhas, thus failing to understand the merits of the Buddhas.

Furthermore, all sentient beings, shrouded by ignorance and with minds deluded by false views, turn their backs on spiritual friends, destroy the ship of the True Dharma, topple the mountain of Dharma-jewels, and fell the forest of wisdom. They flee the city of liberation and open wide the three evil realms; unable to enter the rope of faith that purifies the mind, they cannot raise the true banner of the Dharma, and thus they burn down the palaces within the heavens.

Having accumulated vast wealth and treasures in this world, they rely on their own opulence and give rise to great pride. Lacking wisdom and being foolish, they fail to examine things properly; they neither practice generosity nor enjoy their possessions. Held fast by the planet of avarice, they do not realize that this body is constantly pursued by the sufferings of old age, sickness, and death, and thus they commit various evil deeds without confessing them.
In his prime, his physical strength and vitality were full and robust, his body radiant and lustrous; he washed away all impurities and constantly experienced joy.

Yet, upon reaching old age, his limbs trembled, his skin became slack and wrinkled with many dark spots, his lips and mouth grew parched, his breath became labored and gasping, his hair turned white and thin, his teeth fell out and became sparse, his body broke out in sores and scabs, and his flesh wasted away. His faculties became dull and obstructed, his sinews grew taut and pulled him about; his head and feet drew near to one another as his gait became slow and faltering.

All his limbs are as if bound; wherever he wishes to go, he must rely on support from others. He no longer thinks of singing, dancing, or playful amusements; he can no longer eat even the most exquisite delicacies, and should he wish to drink, his throat cannot swallow.

His eyes gaze at written characters yet cannot discern them; his mind finds the words he intends to speak unclear; his inhalations and exhalations are faint and do not continue in succession; saliva and mucus flow out, and excrement soils his body; his abdomen swells with a constricting pain, and his moans resound far and wide.
Possessing nothing but skin and bone, he lay prostrate upon his bed; his face presented a hideous appearance that inspired great terror.
At that time, when the wind touched the joints of his limbs, it was like the piercing sting of needles, unbearable to endure, so that all physicians abandoned him and departed.

Scorched and boiled by immeasurable grief and affliction, all that was once cherished is now possessed by others; having utterly abandoned all precious wealth, like a thunderbolt fire that destroys everything without remainder, one passes away suddenly in a state of total unconsciousness.

This instantaneous transformation strikes terror into the heart; parents, wives, children, and all kinsmen—both internal and external—are choked with sobs and tears as their hearts tear apart in agony, crying out to one another:
"Leaving us behind, where are you going?"

In that other world, one goes alone, like a young merchant without a companion, entering great darkness, proceeding toward great peril, falling into a deep abyss, and sinking into a vast ocean of suffering—without refuge, without rescue, and without any place of reliance.

The messengers of Yama and the goddesses of the Black Night, with wrathful eyes, sharp fangs, and fearsome, hideous forms, rebuked them in fury, bound them, and departed; they went to the abode of Yama as swiftly as the wind.

Having failed to honor the good while alive, they return to a place of suffering after death. Immeasurable blades descend from the sky, hacking and piercing their bodies, severing and destroying their limbs and joints; hearts are split open and tongues cut out, with flesh and blood mingling and flowing away; the fingers and joints of hands and feet are sliced off and cast aside, until only the sinews and bones remain connected and do not scatter.
Experiencing great anguish, they immediately faint; blown by the winds of karma, they suddenly return to life and suffer for a long time until, when their karma is exhausted, they attain liberation.

If sentient beings have faith and compliance with the Buddha’s words, delight in performing meritorious deeds, and bring benefit and peace to all sentient beings—providing whatever they require and giving warmth to those who are cold and frozen—[they shall not undergo such suffering].
To those afflicted by feverish distress, he provides cooling relief; to those parched with thirst, he draws from clear springs;
to those famished, he bestows food and drink; to those drowning in rivers, he rescues them with boats and rafts;
to those without shelter, he grants them dwellings; to the destitute, he bestows wealth and silk; and to those engaged in disputes, he exhorts them toward reconciliation.

May they bring harmony and accord; may they act as companions for those who wander alone; may they show the excellent medicine to those suffering from illness and administer it so that they find relief;
may they use mantra-empowerment to eliminate the venom of those bitten by snakes;
and may they bestow the sword of wisdom upon those who rely on pride, causing them to subdue themselves, so that all may attain peace, security, and happiness.

If one can thus bring benefit and happiness to sentient beings, one will immediately obtain the desired rewards of merit in the present life; in future lives as well, only this meritorious karma will serve as one's companion, refuge, protection, and basis of reliance.

If there are sentient beings who are habituated to the karma of stinginess and are unable to practice generosity toward superior fields of merit, even if a disciple of the Buddha such as Upāli were to come to transform them, their minds would not rejoice;

they would have no faith that the merit of giving can summon pleasant retributions, and they would continue to accumulate evil deeds to undergo saṃsāra thereafter. Even if they obtain human birth, they will be born into inferior lineages—such as butcher families, scavenger families, cartwrights, cotton-weavers, fishermen, potters, plowmen, weavers, barbers, or dyers and washers—in various unwholesome stations. Their food and clothing will be meager and insufficient; they will be employed by others, their hands and feet will be cracked and chapped, and they will experience much suffering and constant toil, having no leisure for even a moment each day.

Furthermore, they were bound and oppressed by various diseases: scabies, leprosy, sores, ringworm, hemorrhoids, fistulas, carbuncles, coughs, malaria, dysentery, epilepsy, and fevers. Such ailments as these afflicted their bodies, leaving them emaciated and haggard; their hands and feet were cramped and withered, their lips and mouths were crooked and askew, their hair was disheveled and matted, and tears flowed from both eyes.
Seeking out people of inferior appearance, he puts on tattered and worn-out rags; he drags himself forward or even casts them aside without noticing.
Blown by the wind, his body is left naked; sitting or lying in filth and mire, he still finds it a source of amusement, plucking out his own hair without the slightest sense of shame.
He addressed those who passed by, saying, "Look at me; what am I doing?
Sometimes he would carry a broken vessel through the streets and alleys, gathering a little leftover food to sustain his life.
Hundreds of thousands of flies and insects vied with one another to swarm and suck at them; filthy both inside and out, they were loathed and despised by all.
Having been drawn together by unwholesome causes—having committed evil deeds themselves and further incited others to do so—such people become a treasury of suffering and affliction.

Therefore, the World-Honored One constantly regards all beings with great compassion, causing them to resolve their minds toward awakening and decisively repent, so that they may swiftly be liberated from all evils and afflictions.
This sutra states that only by personally practicing right conduct and performing meritorious deeds can one attract the superior retribution of wealth and happiness among gods and humans.
Therefore, if a bhikṣu upholds this sutra, explains it to others, and practices according to its teachings, he will cause the canopy of merit for both himself and others to be perfected.
At that time, the World-Honored One was staying at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove in Rājagṛha.

Then Devadatta, being utterly ignorant and foolish, sought to harm the Buddha-dharma with a malicious and poisonous mind, creating hundreds of thousands of obstacles and hindrances; yet he could not disturb even a single hair-tip of the Buddha.
He immediately said to King Ajātaśatru:
"You must issue a strict decree to proclaim throughout the city that not a single person is permitted to go to the Buddha's location, nor is anyone allowed to provide offerings of food and drink."
"You should know that Gautama will gain nothing here; he will surely abandon this place and travel far to another kingdom.
When the king heard these words, he believed them and followed their advice.
At that time, the upāsakas within the city, having learned of this matter, all said:
“Alas! Now the city of Rājagṛha has no sovereign.
The appearance of a Tathāgata in the world is difficult to encounter, like the udumbara flower.”
"How is it, Great King, that you have placed your faith in false teachers, refusing to allow us to go and make offerings, and not permitting the Tathāgata to accept us?
When the Venerable Ānanda heard these words, he immediately went to inform the Buddha.
The Buddha said to him:
"I have already foreseen this; why must you be so distressed?
Within my Dharma, there has never been a single disciple who lacked anything, much less I myself."

At that time, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, emitted a great radiance that illuminated the city of Rājagṛha, making it entirely pure; those touched by this light found their bodies and minds to be at ease.

Then Śakra, beholding the Buddha’s radiance, observed with his divine eye and understood its cause. He aroused great valor and manifested great majestic power, acting as a great donor to offer grand offerings.

Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, Chao-san Dafu, Acting Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial, Great Master of Xuanfan, the Imperially Enfeoffed Purple-Robed Śramaṇa, Subject Rìchēng, and others, by imperial decree. At that time, Śakra-devānām-indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"I only pray that you will dwell peacefully in this city of Rājagṛha; I shall provide you with food, drink, clothing, bedding, and medicine, so that you lack for nothing.
The Buddha said, "Lord of Devas!"
"Let us set this matter aside.
There are many people who, with pure hearts, all desire to cultivate meritorious deeds for my sake.
At that time, Śakra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“I only pray that you will accept my offerings during these five summer retreats.
Having said this, the Buddha again declined him.
Śakra spoke once more:
"I now invite the Buddha to accept my offerings for five days; I only pray that, out of great compassion, you will accept my sincere invitation.
At that time, the World-Honored One, out of pity for the Heavenly Lord and to cause his roots of merit to continue into the future, silently granted his consent.
At that time, Śakra, knowing that the Buddha had accepted his invitation, was filled with great joy.
He immediately returned to his celestial palace, summoned the devaputra Viśvakarman, the master of crafts, and said to him:
"You should know this: I now wish to construct a great vihāra in the Bamboo Grove of Kalanda at Rājagṛha, and to provide the four types of offerings to the Tathāgata and his disciples."

"You should take the most excellent mani-jewels, gold, silver, lapis lazuli, coral, crystal, sapphire, and other such gems, and go there to construct a magnificent, pure, and vast palace, exactly like those in the heavens and no different."

These devaputras exerted their utmost skill and artistry to construct the palaces; the corridors, eaves, pillars, beams, windows, and railings were all adorned with various jewels interspersed together, shining upon one another like a thousand suns.

Furthermore, various exquisite and rare birds were carved and adorned, interspersed and arrayed with pearl flower-garlands; subtle incense was burned and myriad famous flowers were scattered, their fragrant vapors billowing and pervading everywhere without exception.
Furthermore, they constructed heavy gates and multi-storied pavilions that rose high and were magnificent and beautiful, likewise adorned with a hundred jewels.

Exquisite *maṇi* gems served as their doors, and each of those jeweled pillars was composed of a combination of *vajra* and various rare treasures. Countless jewel mirrors, pure and free from blemish, were suspended in the air like hundreds of thousands of moons.
Furthermore, he fashioned a three-legged pedestal out of molten gold and spread exquisite celestial garments upon it.

He also had various exquisite celestial maidens carved, their deportment so upright and elegant that they appeared as if they could move about; holding lotus flowers in their hands, they made offerings.
Its ground was paved with exquisite crystal jewels.
There were wonderful ponds adorned with lotuses, which had golden petals and stalks of emerald; countless celestial maidens stood within them, performing various musical performances as an offering.
The spire of the stupa rose high and prominent, with various silk banners and streamers suspended, swirling in mid-air so that they were visible from both far and near.
Various *rishi* (powerful beings) guarded the gates and courtyards, standing in rows to the left and right, holding staffs of blue precious gems.

Everywhere mandārava flowers and nāgeśvara flowers were planted; fragrant and in full bloom, they carpeted the ground in profusion, their verdant leaves reflecting one another as a fragrant breeze drifted through them from time to time.
There were sons of gods, their bodies radiant and pure, their countenances joyful and serene, strolling and resting beneath it.
Furthermore, there were goddesses of incomparable beauty, walking slowly with tinkling ornaments, their voices harmonious and elegant.
Various yakṣī women frolic within the grove, casting sidelong glances with their beautiful eyes as they drop flowers and shed fragrances.
There are also nāga-elephants moving slowly through the woods, lifting their trunks to nibble at the branches and playing about in graceful movements.
There were also various birds with feathers of five colors, flapping their wings at ease as they pecked at the flower blossoms.
Furthermore, a marvelous parrot was placed in a golden cage; its voice was beautiful, clear, and skillful, its tongue sounding like a reed organ.
Furthermore, there is a river source, clear and cool, lovely to behold; its flowing springs resound with splashing sounds, causing frogs and tadpoles to startle and flee.

There is also a vast, pure pond, with steps and banks interspersed with the seven treasures. Its waters are full to the brim, limpid and stainless. *Utpala* flowers and *Kumuda* flowers are arranged in rows and in full bloom, their various colors blending together, while kingfishers and waterfowls soar and gather amidst them.
There were various fish darting to and fro, swimming and leaping, tossing up the waves, which caused the gulls and egrets to take flight in alarm.
Furthermore, there were water birds—storks, cranes, and wild geese—their cries resounded with a piercing clarity, a sound that people delighted to hear.
On the four banks of the pond stand *kalpavṛkṣa* trees; their supple branches brush against the water, generating a refreshing breeze.
Various flowers grow in dense clusters, and long creepers spread luxuriantly; the branches and leaves are thick and flourishing, and their fragrance is perceived from afar.
There were various wandering bees vying to gather its pollen, emitting a subtle sound like that of chanting songs.
Furthermore, golden rivers surrounded it on all sides, flowing through the groves in continuous, winding currents.
At that time, the people called out to one another, and their kinsmen and friends all went together to witness the spectacle.

There were members of noble families, rich and prosperous, adorned with finery, accompanied by a retinue of dignified attendants, carrying canopies and parasols, performing various musical entertainments, and providing a full array of delicacies; they traveled about and surveyed everything, their hearts never wearying of it.
The ground there is as soft as *tūla* cotton; as one wanders back and forth, the feet feel no fatigue or weariness.
Such a most excellent and vast garden, with its pure ponds and pools, is unsurpassed by anything except those found within the heavens.
At that time, the various devaputras skilled in craftsmanship, having completed their tasks, went before the celestial palace and addressed Śakra.

Upon hearing these words, his heart was filled with joy and he experienced what he had never known before; immediately surrounded by hundreds of thousands of immeasurable devaputras, they performed various musical entertainments—flutes, pipes, lutes, harps, zithers, drums, and trumpets all played together—and descended from the sky.
At that time, the body of the Lord of Devas emitted a brilliant light that illuminated all mountains and rivers, making them glow intensely.
He wore a crown of *maṇi* jewels, adorned with various precious gems; its radiance shone forth as brilliantly as the full splendor of the sun.

His countenance was dignified and majestic, with a broad and level forehead; his eyes were deep blue and long, his nose was refined, high, and straight, and his chin and cheeks were exceptionally fair, white, and lustrous.

His ears were adorned with jeweled pendants, and his neck hung with necklaces and garlands; his finger rings and armlets were composed of various precious gems that radiated light in succession, like the brilliance of a white jade moon.
His physical appearance was exceptionally distinguished, always as if in the prime of youth; his height and proportions were full and well-proportioned, each attaining its proper measure.
He anointed his body with kunkuma, tagara, and candana sandalwood incense, so that it became soft and radiant.
His fingers were slender and rounded, and his nails were like copper leaves.
His speech was skillful and eloquent; its clarity resonated far and wide like the voice of the kalaviṅka bird, such that those who heard it never grew weary.
Furthermore, he provided him with garments made of exquisite, wondrous, and rare fine cotton cloth, adorned by grinding gold into patterns;

he fashioned for him a girdle of various wonderful and precious gems, in which diverse jewels were interspersed to form a mass of radiance; and he further embellished his body with various exquisite celestial flower garlands.
Surrounded by a trailing canopy, his gait was level and upright; like a king of elephants, he moved with graceful ease, requiring no assistance from attendants.

At that time, all the people were able to behold and revere him: those harboring anger immediately felt joy; those who had given rise to resentment and malice immediately conceived a mind of loving-kindness; and those indulging in sleep immediately attained awakening.

At that time, having arrived at that grove, the Lord of Devas observed that everything created was exactly as he had intended; leaping for joy beyond measure, he changed its former name, Kalanda, to the Grove of Joy (Nandana).

He immediately covered the ground everywhere with exquisite carpets of various colors. Furthermore, he prepared high and broad seats made of gold, silver, pearls, *maṇi* jewels, sapphire, lapis lazuli, and *mūlaka* gems, and invited the Buddha, the World-Honored One, to be seated upon them; he provided pedestals of various jewels to support His feet.
He arranged seating for the assembly using five-colored silk threads and commanded the bhikṣus to each take their respective places.

At that time, the Lord of Devas joined his palms in reverence, paid homage with respect and praise, and prostrated at the Buddha’s feet. He prepared the finest delicacies and exquisite flavors found among the gods.

Then the Tathāgata extended his golden arm like the trunk of an elephant king and accepted the food; having eaten, he set aside the bowl, washed his hands, rinsed his mouth, and remained established in majestic deportment, serene and pure.
At that time, the Lord of Devas and his retinue were struck with wonder; desiring to hear the Dharma, they took low seats and remained focused and solemn.

Then, the World-Honored One, through great skillful means, expounded the essentials of the Dharma for them, praising such practices as giving, instructing, benefiting, and gladdening them so that they might give rise to faith and understanding.
Thus they made offerings for four days.

When King Ajātaśatru heard of these matters, he ascended the highest pavilion in his palace and looked down with careful observation; there he saw the Buddha, the World-Honored One, and his disciples in the Bamboo Grove Monastery, peaceful and at ease, having prepared solemn offerings and performing great Buddhist rites.
At that time, the king’s mind was awakened, and he repented and reproached himself:
"I have been greatly foolish and ignorant; through my errors and delusions, I have committed sins as heavy as Mount Sumeru."
Now the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has appeared in the world, fully endowed with vast and pure merit.
Yet I am unable to believe and accept his teachings; by reason of this karmic cause, I shall surely fall into a place of suffering.
"Even those sons of the gods have abandoned the most sublime sensual pleasures of the heavens to come to the presence of the Buddha; how is it that we do not give rise to wholesome benefit?
Having spoken these words, they immediately prepared their precious carriages and proceeded to the place where the Buddha was.
Prostrating with his head at [the Buddha’s] feet, his heart filled with sorrow and distress, he wept and lamented, repenting for his former transgressions.
At that time, the laymen and laywomen of Rājagṛha cried out in a loud voice:
“Excellent, O King!
"We have attained great awakening within the Buddha-dharma;
we have now all obtained excellent benefit.
At that time, the king struck the bell to proclaim a decree, summoning all his ministers, the people, and his kinsmen, and addressed them, saying:
“The appearance of our Buddha in the world is difficult to encounter.
Having now obtained the opportunity to behold him, you should give rise to a pure mind to offer worship and respect, and take delight in hearing the True Dharma.”
Thereupon, he made offerings with exquisite incense, flowers, lamps, ointments, powdered incense, various flower garlands, rare treasures, garments, and all manner of ornaments.
Having performed these deeds, his heart was filled with great joy.
At that time, the Tathāgata, with a Brahma-like voice, revealed and expounded for the assembled congregation the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths: suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.
Immeasurable humans and devas heard the Dharma and understood it, attaining the vision of reality.
Then the Buddha, the World-Honored One, asked the bhikṣus:
"Do you see these devas and people who have now made vast offerings before me?"
Then the bhikṣus joined their palms above their heads and marveled at this unprecedented event,
saying, "Indeed, we have seen it.
The Buddha said:

“Within my teaching, if there is a person who, with a pure mind, gives rise to sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*) toward the meritorious deeds of others, you should know that this person has attained indestructible faith and possesses the eye of pure wisdom.”
"O Bhikṣus!

I recall that in the past, during immeasurable lifetimes, there was a Buddha who appeared in the world named Ratnagiri Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān. He dwelt in the world, preaching the Dharma for the benefit of sentient beings."

At that time, there was a king who invited that Tathāgata and his disciples to spend the three-month summer retreat within the royal palace, where he reverently provided them with various kinds of food, drink, and clothing as offerings.

After this period had passed, all those people went to where the Buddha was and requested him for five years, providing various offerings so that everything required was fully provided without exception.
"O bhikṣus! What do you think?
The king who made offerings to that Buddha in the past was none other than myself."
Due to causes planted in the past, they have now reached maturity, whereby they receive extensive offerings from humans and devas.
The relationship between past causes and present fruits does not deviate by even a hair’s breadth; because fruit is induced by cause, the fruit corresponds exactly to its cause.
Through this correct knowledge, one eliminates all webs of doubt: that the retribution of good and evil karma is invariably unfailing, like a torrential stream whose momentum cannot be restrained.

By the power of such karma, each [being] draws forth its own retribution—the earth element, water element, fire element, wind element, as well as the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and so forth. Having oneself created the causes of merit, one then experiences the fruits of happiness.
Then the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Even after passing through hundreds of thousands of kalpas, that karma cannot be destroyed;
when causes and conditions converge, its retribution will certainly be experienced."

“O bhikṣus! This is called the Right Practice of the Canopy of Merit; you should receive and uphold it. Diligently cultivate generosity, ethical discipline, and all meditative concentrations, so that by enjoying the canopy of merit, you may be freed from feverish affliction.”
This meaning briefly clarifies the manner in which the Buddhas of the past taught and the manner of the compilation of the sūtras and their dependent originations (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
At the very beginning of each sūtra, the phrase "Thus have I heard" (*evam mayā śrutam*) is set forth.
For what reason is it called thus?
Because it is not different from what the Buddha has taught.
In what sense is it named "self"?
This refers to the present body, as it accords with worldly convention.
In what sense is there "hearing"?
It means that when the ear gives rise to consciousness, one directly and clearly understands both the words and their meaning, free from the faults of exaggeration, diminution, or inversion.
The first council was that of the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*.

At that time, the assembly gathered consisted of four hundred and ninety-nine great Arhats; the only exception was Ānanda, who alone remained at the stage of a learner (*śaikṣa*), along with all other devas, nāgas, ghosts, and spirits.
Upon first hearing the proclamation "Thus have I heard," we raised our voices in grief, unable to restrain ourselves.

In the past, we personally beheld the World-Honored One, endowed with the ten powers and the four fearlessnesses, expounding the Dharma for the assembly with a Brahma-like voice; how is it that now one merely says "I have heard"?
One will come to know that the power of impermanence cannot be escaped.
At that time, the entire assembly attained awakening, was freed from the defilements of the three poisons, and dwelt securely in right mindfulness, maintaining it without forgetfulness.
In what sense is he called "One"?
It is because he is the beginning of all numbering.

This refers to the fact that he is uniquely the one born as a Sage, the one who has emerged through the Dharma of renunciation, the one who dwells in the place of peace, the one whose holy life is pure, and the one whose voice is liberation—all of which are identical.
In what sense is it called "time"?
It is established according to worldly convention.
Once the discourse on the events of the sutra has been delivered and the great assembly is filled with joy and satisfaction, it is termed "at one time."
The Tathāgata’s preaching of the Dharma is like the sun illuminating the world, for it shatters the darkness of the three realms of existence and causes beings to attain liberation.
As various Māras and non-Buddhists slander the True Dharma, the Buddha now manifests this profound, rare, and difficult-to-attain teaching in order to subdue them.
In what sense is he called Bhagavān?
Because he is endowed with supreme and vast renown, such that none in the mundane or supramundane realms can equal him;
because he has ultimately transcended the cycle of rebirth within the realms and destinies; and because he is worthy of receiving the sublime offerings of gods and humans.
What is meant by Śrāvastī?
It is so called because it abounds in all manner of exquisite things, as well as in men of letters and conduct, male and female lay devotees, and wealthy elders, owing to its superior enjoyments.
In what sense is it called "abiding"?
It is the basis for wandering and transforming others, free from all conceptual constructions, because one arrives at whatever is distant or near according to one's will.
