Translated by the Imperial Preceptor Xuanfan, the Purple-Robed Śramaṇa and Subject Nichiren, and others, by imperial decree. For what reason is it called the Jeta Grove? In the language of the Han, it means "Victory over Battle" (Zhenshenglin); following ancient usage, it is not translated [into Chinese].

In the past, King Jayasena fought a battle with a neighboring kingdom and achieved victory; at that very time, a crown prince was born, and he was named "Victory" (Jayasena) in commemoration of that triumph.
Because the grove belonged to him, it was called Jeta’s Grove. With its boundless magnificence and infinite adornments, all the people were filled with joy at the sight of it.
Within this grove, he extensively provided human wealth and resources to maintain and protect it, making it a place for recreation and pleasure.

The grove was dense, its branches and foliage luxuriant; a cool shade spread far and wide, shielding it from the scorching rays of the sun. It was refreshingly cool in summer, free from harsh winds in winter, and devoid of muddy mire during the rains. Exquisite flowers, fragrant and in full bloom, were scattered everywhere, while the drooping branches bent low like parasols.
It is well-guarded by many sentries, and there is no report of thieves or bandits; its ground is pure and excellent, comparable to the Nandana Grove.
For what reason is it named Anāthapiṇḍada?
Because he bestowed food and drink upon those who were without kin and provided for them all around; this matter is explained in detail within the Vinaya Piṭaka.

By the power of the roots of goodness cultivated by that elder in previous lives, desiring to invite the World-Honored One for offerings and veneration, he first constructed a vihāra for the Tathāgata.
He then traded the land with the Crown Prince at a price of hundreds of thousands of koṭis of gold.

Having fulfilled his ambition, he summoned all manner of masters of extraordinary skill from every quarter to construct a supreme palace and pavilions, complete with doors, porches, windows, and shutters, as well as flowing springs and bathing pools; all varieties of adornments were fully provided, and it was surrounded on all sides by lofty and steep ramparts.
Thereupon, the elder went to Rājagṛha, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and spoke these words:

“I now invite the Buddha to visit Śrāvastī; I only pray that the Tathāgata, out of great compassion, will grant his consent. There is a monastery there, vast and pure, where he and his disciples may go together to observe the rains retreat.”
At that time, having finished his address, the elder returned.
Then, there was an elder in the city of Rājagṛha named Śānta, who said to the World-Honored One:
"There is no need to go there."
"I shall build a vihāra for the Buddha.
The Buddha immediately stopped him.
When the Buddha had arrived at that city of Śrāvastī, the elder then offered the monastery he had built to the Tathāgata.
Out of compassion for them, the Buddha accepted it and further praised it, saying:
"That place is most supremely auspicious and foremost in peace; past Buddhas as well have benefited and brought happiness to all sentient beings in this very location."
"You have long planted the roots of virtue under previous Buddhas; by the power of your past vows, you are now likewise so.

At that time, there was a non-Buddhist practitioner named Mataṅgiñjina who lived in a grass hut practicing austerities. He was thoroughly proficient in the speech and wisdom of all sentient beings in the world, and he said:
"The Jeta Grove is most supreme, exquisite, and exceedingly magnificent; how can the World-Honored One and his bhikṣus enjoy such a place?"
The Buddha, having known this, out of great skillful means and compassion for such beings, spoke to them, saying:
"My disciples have reached the end of suffering; they have thoroughly mastered the worldly and supramundane collections of Sūtra, Vinaya, and Abhidharma, because they have severed the afflictions."
Thereupon, the World-Honored One spoke these verses for that non-Buddhist:
"Though you may be like a great dragon, You are still defiled by craving;
Regarding the two—praise and blame— You are moved by them."
"If the body has many sores, flies will swarm around it;
circling through the three realms of existence is like a worm dwelling in filth.
When those non-Buddhists heard the Buddha’s words, they attained realization in their hearts and praised the Buddha with this verse:
“The Tathāgata has appeared in the world; the sun of wisdom shatters all darkness.
How much more so for one of my meager and inferior intellect—by what means could I attain awakening?
Even were I to spend many eons, using a hundred thousand tongues,”
To praise the Buddha’s virtues, one could not exhaust even a small fraction of them.
The Buddha is the seer among gods; knowing the various conducts of sentient beings, amidst the four modes of deportment, he acts solely for the benefit and happiness of all conscious creatures.

At that time, there were many non-Buddhists and brahmins in Śrāvastī who were clever and wise; hearing that the Buddha had arrived there, they vied with one another to come and pose difficult challenges.

The Tathāgata, employing skillful means appropriate to each, taught them accordingly—just as a lion’s roar terrifies the various beasts—causing them all to attain full realization and depart from the darkness of ignorance.
At that time, there was a wise man named Rāhula who, having heard the praise of the Buddha’s virtues, spoke these verses:
“The Greatly Compassionate, Unsurpassed Honored One, Dedicates himself solely to the practice of benefiting others;
He seeks neither worldly fame nor renown, Nor the increase of wealth and profit.”
"When first descending into the royal palace, he surveyed the four quarters, manifested a smile,
and entered into contemplation— all for the sake of delivering all living beings.
At that time, there was also the youth Subāhu, who likewise spoke a verse in praise of the Buddha:
“The Honored Muni, the Great Seer, has skillfully expounded the essentials of all dharmas;
free from fault and devoid of desire, those who hear him all receive benefit.
Both devas and worldly people alike offer him worship and reverence.”
"I take refuge in the Honored One of Ten Powers; may you deign to accept me.
This Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, inspires love and joy for five reasons:

first, it is vast and situated in the center of the city; second, it is not far from where bhikṣus go for alms; third, it is secluded and free from all clamor; fourth, it is clean and devoid of mosquitoes and gadflies; fifth, many virtuous people frequent its midst.
For this reason, the World-Honored One frequently delights in dwelling here.

Abiding in the wisdom of reality and free from conduct lacking shame, all merits are manifested as his support; endowed with the ten powers and adorned with merit and wisdom, he serves as the supreme guide for that world. Thus, he is able to bring the roots of goodness in sentient beings to maturity, just as a lotus emerges from the mud; because both self-benefit and the benefit of others are fully perfected.

At that time, King Jayasena, together with all the people, as well as the various non-Buddhists and brahmins, all proceeded to the Jeta Grove Monastery; with palms joined and minds focused, they prostrated themselves at the feet of the Buddha.

At that time, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, out of compassion and to gather in all sentient beings, shattered their various heterodox views so that they might give rise to faith and understanding; for those who wander through the five destinies due to unwholesome causes, he taught that they should rely upon the True Dharma to seek liberation.
He proclaimed for them the Dharma of the Six Recollections: "Good son!
To faithfully accept and follow my instructions within my Dharma, and to possess right view—this is called recollecting the Buddha."
If one delights in hearing the sublime Dharma extensively and reflects upon it according to principle, this is called mindfulness of the Dharma.
To always conceive of all bhikṣus as venerable spiritual friends is called mindfulness of the Saṃgha.
To cherish and embrace all wholesome dharmas, and to be fully endowed with dignified deportment—this is called mindfulness of precepts (*śīlānusmṛti*).
To constantly give food and drink to the Buddha and the Saṅgha, abiding by such causes—this is called mindfulness of giving (*tyāgānusmṛti*).
Constantly delighting in paying homage to all great bodhisattvas and following the Buddha’s instructions is called "mindfulness of the noble ones.
If sentient beings rely on what the Buddha has taught and abide in right reflection, they will eliminate doubt; by relying on right mindfulness, they will be free from distraction.
These are the six recollections, which cause all wholesome qualities to grow.
For what reason is one called a bhikṣu?
It is because they are able to eternally sever all afflictions.

Because all such sufferings as the suffering of birth in the world, the suffering of aging, the suffering of illness, the suffering of death, the suffering of grief, lamentation, pain, and despair, the suffering of the five aggregates of clinging, the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks, the suffering of separation from the beloved, and the suffering of encountering the hated have been completely exhausted.
This clarifies that the five aggregates of clinging in the world are suffering, as it is stated thus:
In what sense is there "birth"?
As the Blessed One said:

Those various sentient beings perform diverse karmic actions that induce the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*). Through this, the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*) continue in succession, and the five sense faculties (*pañcendriya*) arise. Because the five sense faculties arise, the homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*) arises; by means of this, physical form increases and becomes complete.
This is called birth.
In what sense is it called old age?
As the Blessed One said:

The aggregate of formations undergoes transformation and decay: the sense faculties wither and decline, the body becomes hunched and bent, the muscles become parched and emaciated, the skin becomes slack and wrinkled and covered with many dark spots; one’s movements become heavy and sluggish such that one must rely on a staff, becoming so exhausted and frail as to be incapable of self-sufficiency, requiring the protection of others.
Such is the characteristic of old age.
It is of two kinds: first, the need for others to provide service; second, the absence of anyone to rely upon.
This is called old age.
In what sense is it called "sickness"?
As the Blessed One has said:
when the four great elements increase or decrease and the constituent elements become unbalanced, they are like venomous snakes, giving rise to all manner of suffering and affliction.
This is of two kinds: first, that which is internally originated; second, that which is caused by external conditions. Furthermore, there are three kinds:
first, that which is summoned by karmic retribution; second, that which is inflicted by sudden calamities; and third, that which results from the incantations of others.

When analyzed in detail, there are countless varieties, namely: wind, bile, phlegm, and mucus; scabies, leprosy, carbuncles, and abscesses; coughing, diarrhea, and toxic fevers; emaciation, wasting, and aches and pains, and so forth.
This is what is called "sickness.
In what sense is it called "death"?
As the Blessed One has said:

This refers to when those sentient beings relinquish their homogeneous character (*nikāyasabhāga*), the aggregates (*skandha*) disperse, the sensation of warmth gradually fades, and the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is severed.
This occurs in two ways: first, natural exhaustion; second, passing away.

Furthermore, there are three initial cases: namely, when the life-faculty has ended but its merit has not yet ended; or when the merit has ended but the life-faculty has not yet ended; or when both the life-faculty and the merit end simultaneously.

Second, there are also three types of going forth: first, going oneself to capture fierce beasts and the like; second, being approached by others who have been plundered and so forth; third, meeting with others in such encounters as battle.
Furthermore, there are three categories: first, those who are negligent; second, those who violate the precepts; and third, those whose retribution has exhausted.

Because of negligence, they sever the life-force of their wisdom; because of violating the precepts, they destroy all dignified deportment; and because their retribution has exhausted, they are surrounded by internal and external kinsmen who, out of grief and attachment, cannot bear to leave them.
This is called death.
What is called sorrow?
It is the distress and grief within the inner mind, as urgent as fire and as scorching as the sun heating water until it becomes like boiling broth.
This is called sorrow (*daurmanasya*).
What is called lamentation (*parideva*)?

It is the shedding of tears and weeping, with a choked voice that makes speech difficult; it is like a filial son grieving for his compassionate father or other relatives—all such states are alike—and the mind is not at peace.
This is called compassion (*karuṇā*).
What is suffering (*duḥkha*)?
It is harsh, acrid, and poisonous, contrary to pleasure, and is experienced through association with the five groups of sensory consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna-kāya*).
This is called suffering.
What is affliction?

It is like a piece of withered wood being burned by fire, causing those sentient beings to experience distress, vexation, and agitation, which they receive through association with the mental consciousness-body.
This is called vexation (*upāyāsa*).
What is meant by the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks?
It refers to when one does not obtain as desired the various things sought after; the mind becomes exhausted and revolves like a potter’s wheel—this mind follows along with that [frustration].
What is called the suffering of separation from the beloved?
It is the moment-to-moment transformation of the physical forms and characteristics of those objects of affection and one’s corresponding kinsmen.
What is called the suffering of encountering the hated and the loathed?
This refers to encountering those with whom one has mutual animosity despite having no prior connection.

The sequence of birth and so forth described herein, when investigated through successive stages, results only in burning affliction; it is like a deer in the wilderness surrounded by fire, unable to escape and certain to be consumed by the flames.

Except for when the Tathāgata first descends into birth—increasing wholesome dharmas, tranquil and secure, his essential nature being spontaneous and free from all feverish afflictions—as a sūtra verse says:
"The appearance of the Buddhas in the world is bliss; The proclamation of the True Dharma is bliss."
The harmony of the Saṃgha is blissful, enabling the cultivation of all virtuous deeds.
If the Buddha did not appear in the world, how could there be any happiness within the three realms?
Because the Buddha has appeared, we have obtained peace and joy.

"Because all sentient beings take the seeds of unwholesomeness as their cause, they are able to grow within the realm of the tree of suffering, constantly being burned by the fires of suffering of the three poisons."
Regarding matters such as worldly wealth and pleasure in that world, one can only hear of them from others; by what means could one truly know them?
One must traverse vast wildernesses and perilous, evil paths, enduring all manner of hardships amidst sand, gravel, and thorns, seeking a livelihood through begging with nowhere to turn for refuge.
Thus, these sentient beings, lacking the roots of virtue from their past lives, sink into the evil realms and transmigrate without end, like an actor changing his appearance and form.
Even if they should obtain a human birth, they are born into a poor family and undergo various sufferings within the mother’s womb.
How do sentient beings undergo various sufferings while dwelling within the womb?
As the Blessed One has said:

at the moment of initial conception, they take as their conditions the impurities of the father’s semen and the mother’s blood; gradually growing, they form their physical body, residing between the receptacle for raw food (āmāśaya) below and the receptacle for digested food (pakvāśaya) above, in that place of extreme foulness and impurity.
Whether the mother has eaten to satiety or suffers from hunger and thirst, she experiences suffering through the movements of her limbs and the act of sexual desire.
Furthermore, at the time of birth, she no longer finds pleasure in dwelling within the mother’s womb; conceiving thoughts of impurity, she turns toward the birth canal.
When the two hands first touch the body of the infant, it experiences great agony and most intense burning distress.
That newborn child, driven by hunger and thirst, utters cries of weeping and seeks milk from the mother.
Furthermore, that milk is produced from the transformation of blood; or, when food is insufficient, they suffer the torment of heat.
Gradually becoming infants, they lie in excrement and urine, or at times, while playing, they fall into ditches and pits.
This is called the heat and affliction experienced after birth;
all other worldly beings are likewise the same.

Furthermore, as those sentient beings gradually grow older, their physical strength and vitality reach full maturity, yet they become arrogant, indulgent, and heedless, pursuing the objects of the five sensory desires at every thought-moment.
Due to defiled wisdom, one clings with attachment and refuses to let go, yielding to one's own impulses until swiftly meeting one’s end.
What are the various sufferings of old age and decay? One’s physical form becomes emaciated; the cheeks become sunken and distorted;

the teeth fall out, becoming sparse and missing; the hair and body hair grow thin and white; the neck, arms, chest, and ribs all stand bare as bone; the digestive fire gradually weakens so that food and drink are taken in meager amounts; like a bird placed within a cage, one grows increasingly gaunt until nothing remains but a bundle of skin and hair; what was undertaken in the morning is forgotten by evening; one desires to act at first but later falters and withdraws; one’s speech is like that of a small child, lacking all measure or restraint.

At times, he would not wish to speak for the entire day, devoting himself solely to sleep throughout the day and night; even when asleep, he could not rest, coughing incessantly, and his speech was indistinct as he attempted to describe his suffering.

Just as a traveler does not delight in staying long and finds it difficult for all his undertakings to go according to his wishes, so too, when even a slight thing does not accord with his heart, he gives rise to sorrow and affliction; his friends and kin should console him, urging him to settle his mind in peace.

He could no longer enjoy the objects before his eyes; all matters of pleasure were merely heard of by the ear. When he wished to travel about, his feet would not move, and he was forced to rely on a chair and staff as his only companions, becoming an object of derision for women.

Reflecting on how his faculties were once healthy and he enjoyed various sensual pleasures, which have now been transformed and ruined in an instant, he feels deep remorse and distress, wondering, "What is the use of living for long?
This is called the characteristic of the feverish affliction of aging.
What is the feverish affliction of the suffering of illness?

It refers to those foolish people who, in the prime of their youth and vigor, become heedless and attached to sensual desires; they gradually grow weak, are ensnared by chronic diseases, and are confronted with manifold sufferings.
When virtuous people see him, they feel deep compassion and instruct him with kind words to bring forth his confession.
Having heard this, he becomes sorrowful and fearful, dreading that he will fall into the evil realms.
Though his physical appearance was once upright, it has been ravaged by disease; he cannot consume even the most exquisite foods, and though he dwells in luxury and wealth, he is like a pauper.

In this world, the wise person constantly examines themselves and should know that the suffering of illness is not to be cherished or delighted in; it is like hail damaging young seedlings, suddenly destroying their flourishing growth; like a land tortoise constantly longing for water; like the moon during the day, lacking its radiant brilliance; like a parched person falling into a dry well; like a lamp with exhausted oil that cannot remain long; like a decaying wall that possesses no solidity; like a foolish, ignorant child who is held in contempt by others; or like a mad elephant destroying a lotus pond.
This is called the feverish affliction of the suffering of illness.

How can foolish people repeatedly become attached to it, thereby diminishing their lifespan, incinerating their roots of goodness, being shrouded by ignorance, and seeking through wrong livelihoods? Craving the food, drink, and clothing of that worldly life, with outflows from body and mind, they destroy right wisdom; they take no pleasure in relying upon the tranquility of mountain forests to uphold and recite Mahāyāna sūtras, and they cannot steadfastly maintain pure precepts. By what means, then, could they proceed to the other shore of Bodhi?

If the mind is tranquil and turns its back on the objects of desire, or if one feels weary of and no longer dwells upon all former acts of negligence—viewing them as one would a deep-seated enemy with whom one has no desire to meet, like the dregs of sugarcane that can no longer be tasted, or like a withered stump consumed by fire until nothing remains.
One who realizes this in such a way will not be oppressed by King Yama. Furthermore, women are generally full of greed and cruelty;

their hearts harbor resentment and jealousy, and they delight in exercising dominion. They are like a leaking jar filled with impurities; like a mare’s womb, deeply loathsome; like delicious food mixed with poison; like an enemy brandishing a sword, whom one should not approach; and like a mass of fire, which produces burning affliction upon contact.

If the mind is distracted by attachment to sensual objects, it destroys all pure conduct as if one were without precepts; it cuts off the causes of happiness and forfeits the life of wisdom. When the army of death appears before one, one must go alone toward that perilous difficulty, with no one able to save them.
All arise from defiled desire giving birth to various deluded thoughts; lacking shame and remorse, they abandon the practice of contentment and become subject to all manner of worldly slander.
What is meant by "death"?
As a verse says:
"Wisdom is the supreme eye; Ignorance is the most grievous darkness.
Illness inevitably arises from its enemy; Death is called the foremost terror."
"When one takes delight in the True Dharma and practices it well with wisdom,
then at the time of death, one will certainly be free from perilous difficulties.
This is called the feverish distress associated with death.

Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, the Court Scattered Official, Acting Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial, the Great Master of Xuanfan, the Imperially Enfeoffed Purple-Robed Śramaṇa, the Subject Rìchēng, and others, by imperial decree. Furthermore, for what reason is it designated as "sorrow" (*daurmanasya*)?

It means that all sentient beings, due to their craving and desire, are submerged in sorrow and fear, like wild beasts surrounded by fire, like fish from a deep abyss cast onto dry land, or like those who have entered the great ocean and damaged their ship or raft; they are deeply distressed in heart, fearing for their very lives, like a few drops of water falling upon a glowing iron ball.
As one enters the gateway of death, life will not endure for long; it is like beans boiling and bubbling over in a cauldron when dry firewood is added.

When people of the world dwell within their homes, they are oppressed by anxiety; their faculties wither and their minds find no moment of peace. It is as if a jar of ghee were placed near a blazing fire—one should know that before long it will be consumed and destroyed.
Furthermore, for what reason is it called "compassion" (*karuṇā*)?

It refers to those sentient beings who, previously possessing precious wealth, were unable to maintain it; their bodies became indolent, leading to poverty and suffering. Their forms were exposed, their complexions withered, their throats parched, and their speech and thoughts were full of sorrow, as they remembered their former abundance which could no longer be obtained.
Furthermore, for what reason is it called suffering?

It is because sentient beings who engage in unrighteous conduct encounter the net of the law, swords, staves, and poisons; or they are hacked, pierced, and mangled by non-human beings, even to the point of losing their lives and undergoing all manner of agonizing torments.
Furthermore, for what reason is it called "affliction" (*upāyāsa*)?
It refers to when sentient beings are subjected to harsh speech, like being struck by a poisoned arrow; their faculties become agitated and they lose their perception of pleasure.
Furthermore, what is called the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks?

It refers to when sentient beings, desiring to practice the True Dharma, are unable to enter into its understanding and thus experience physical and mental exhaustion; or, due to negligence, their many pursuits fail to be fulfilled, giving rise to burning affliction.
When there is no desire and no seeking, the mind is peaceful and secure.
Furthermore, what is meant by the suffering of separation from the beloved?

It refers to the sudden dispersal of one's cherished kin and friends with whom one has been in harmonious and joyful companionship; the mind then harbors longing and attachment, giving rise to feverish distress.
Furthermore, what is meant by the suffering of association with the hated?

It refers to those sentient beings who, being attached to sensual desires and seeking much wealth and profit, engage in mutual aggression and competition, thereby forming deep-seated enmity; or who, bound by the affection for wives and children as if by shackles and fetters, are unable to attain freedom.

You should know that the color of women causes delusion and confusion; their speech is as soft as the *kumuda* flower, and fools relish it, whereby their youthful vigor is consumed and they soon wither away, like the seer Gautama.
Even the gods are deeply attached to sensual pleasures; like firewood near a flame, they are inevitably consumed by them.
Therefore, a bhikṣu should always remain far removed from them;
for if he draws near to those desires, he will experience the foremost suffering.

All the devas and humans in every world are universally oppressed by the fire of desire; they currently encounter manifold sufferings and, at death, fall into the evil destinies, being scorched as they are surrounded by those thirteen vast masses of fire.
The Buddha is the compassionate father of all sentient beings in the world;

out of pity for them, he has preached this sutra. These are the thirteen kinds of hells: first, Saṃjīva (Reviving); second, Kālasūtra (Black Rope); third, Saṃghāta (Crushing); fourth, Raurava (Crying Out); fifth, Mahāraurava (Great Crying Out); sixth, Tapana (Heating); seventh, Pratāpana (Great Heating); eighth, Avīci (Uninterrupted); ninth, Kukūla (Hot Embers); tenth, Kuṇapa (Putrid Excrement); eleventh, Kṣuramārga (Razor-Blade Path); twelfth, Asipatravana (Sword-Leaf Forest); and thirteenth, Kṣāranadī (Ash River).
In such hells, all manner of evils, perils, and immeasurable sufferings are gathered together.

Countless sentient beings, having committed various evil karmas, enter them at the end of their lives and undergo manifold torments. They are punished by the hell-wardens in various ways; with wrathful intent, the wardens strike them with glowing iron hammers until their bodies are crushed and mangled, bleeding profusely everywhere, and every joint of their bones blazes with fire.
Again, they seize their feet and hurl them into the fire pit; their hands flail in agitation as they wail and cry out in distress.
Those executioners of Yama are extremely cruel and terrifying; as soon as the sinners see them, they are struck with panic and fear.

Or again, they may fall into the Hell of Hot Ashes (*Kukūla*), where their skin, flesh, sinews, and bones are consumed and dissolved as soon as they set foot there; yet, due to their evil karma, they are reborn instantly upon lifting their feet.

Furthermore, there is a deep and vast pit of extremely hot human excrement, its stench unbearable to hear, where iron-beaked insects called *Kuṇapa* move back and forth, biting the feet of the offenders, piercing through the flesh and bone to consume the marrow.
Furthermore, they arrange countless sharp-edged blades in succession to form a path; they compel those sinners to tread upon it with their feet, while fierce winds blow them along its surface.
Seeking to escape that suffering, they enter the Forest of Sword-leaves; countless sword-blades descend from the sky, hacking and piercing their bodies until they are severed and destroyed.
Furthermore, there is a great river filled with caustic lye, its waves surging and boiling, which cooks those sinners.
On both banks there are various hell-wardens who, wielding three-pronged spears, come and go piercing [the beings] with them, causing them to undergo extreme suffering or occasionally fainting away.

There are also those who hide and flee like fish sinking into the mud; they are immediately pulled out by the lips with iron hooks and cast onto hot ground with great iron nets, where they are scorched and seared by the fierce, overturning flames of a great fire.

Furthermore, they pry open their mouths with iron tongs and force molten copper down their throats; or they compel them to swallow glowing iron balls, which scorch and rot their gums, jaws, throats, and tongues, burning everything from the gullet all the way down.
Furthermore, there are two stones used to clamp his body; from head to foot, they saw it asunder.

The hell-wardens are violent and cruel like drunken elephants; their hair bristles upward in rage and sparks fly in all directions. They drive the sinner onto an iron bed, stretching him with lines, or hacking and boring him, as flames erupt on all sides, and nothing but wailing is heard.
Furthermore, mountain peaks fall from the sky, striking the bodies of those sinners so that their limbs are shattered to pieces; they fall to the ground in a swoon and only recover after a long time.

There are various hell-wardens of hideous appearance, some wielding sharp axes, mallets, clubs, wheels of blades, bows and arrows, pestles, cannons, and heated iron weapons; with these various instruments of torture, they interrogate and lash the sinners.
Furthermore, hundreds of thousands of fierce flaming fire-spikes come from the four directions and converge upon his body, completely scorching and rotting it like burning logs.
Then, with sharp knives, they take his tongue and either hack or mince it into hundreds of thousands of pieces; even all his bodily limbs are suddenly dispersed like floating clouds.

Furthermore, the sinner is placed within a cauldron of glowing iron; fierce fires surround it on all sides as the boiling liquid overflows. They float and sink up and down like beans being cooked, their bodies swelling and bursting until the skin and flesh are entirely consumed, leaving only a skeleton. As they are dragged onto the ground, they are revived as before by the winds of karma.
Such manifold sufferings are truly terrifying; those who fall into this hell are unable to escape them.
Furthermore, there is the vast Cold Frost Hell, where great masses of snow rise as high as mountains, and a fierce, bitter wind blows and pours down without ceasing.
There is a vast, deep abyss formed into a mortar, its appearance resembling that of crystal.
Various hell-wardens chase the sinners and force them all into it; tormented by the bitter cold, they utter cries of lamentation.

Furthermore, there are two pestles that strike one another from above and below to pound [the beings]; their bodies are crushed and destroyed like a mass of foam, yet the winds of karma blow them back to life just as before, no different from before. They suffer for a long time until their karma is exhausted, at which point they finally emerge.

All those sentient beings, due to the causes and conditions of defiled wisdom and perverse desire, become attached to the physical forms of others and refuse to let go; they crave a slight pleasure and undergo the retribution of much suffering.
Therefore, the World-Honored One, out of profound compassion and having given rise to a heart of great pity, spoke this sutra:
"O bhikṣus! All the various causes of suffering in the world have birth as their root."
If the conditions for birth are absent, cyclic existence ceases of its own accord; how much more so would the immeasurable suffering of future births cease?

Because there is birth, there is the aggregate of form; because of the aggregate of form, there is the aggregate of feeling; because of the aggregate of feeling, there is the aggregate of perception; because of the aggregate of perception, there is the aggregate of mental formations; and because of the aggregate of mental formations, there is the aggregate of consciousness.
Thus, arising in continuous succession, they increase the mass of suffering and revolve without end.
It is like a band of thieves entering a city, setting fires and plundering to harass and disturb the common people.
Thus, these five aggregates rely upon that city of consciousness, giving rise to various afflictions that damage the sense faculties.
Furthermore, old age, sickness, and death cause harm and distress to all that is pleasant in the world.

This is undesirable, like three kinds of enemies who constantly pursue one: first, those who always seek out one's faults; second, those who cause one to fall into peril and hardship; and third, those who wait for the opportunity to end one's life.
Therefore, bhikṣus!
You should constantly cultivate the right practice of the "Canopy of Merit," uphold the sūtras, and practice according to what is taught.
Even if you are surrounded by the many enemies of old age, sickness, and death, do not give rise to fear; thus you will be able to transcend the perilous and evil paths.
This great man brings benefit to two worlds; like a lotus born from fire, he is most rare and extraordinary, and thus dwells in tranquil and sublime bliss.
O bhikṣus!

The essential nature of that merit is correctly revealed as being delightful in both its own causes and its results; it even gives rise to untainted wholesome dharmas, such that the actions of body, speech, and mind all attain purity. Abiding in non-retrogression and receiving the prediction of enlightenment, it emits a magnificent radiance like the full autumn moon, whereby all the world receives benefit.
He delights in vast giving without limit or obstruction, bestowing gifts upon all who come to beg, causing the hearts of all sentient beings to be filled with joy.
Like a victorious general whose mind advances with fierce valor, he dwells in peace and security, like one relying on a virtuous king.

Like the great ocean that receives the flow of all rivers, and like Mount Meru that is firm and immovable, all sentient beings revere him as their father and mother; he receives offerings and respect from all the world, attains supreme and foremost auspiciousness, is praised by kinsmen and friends, fulfills all his aspirations, and ultimately transcends the bitter sea of saṃsāra.
The nature of merit elucidated here is like a golden vessel: firm, lovely, and the most excellent refuge for all sentient beings. The nature of non-merit is not to be cherished;
it is like an unbaked clay jar that is certain to break, causing sentient beings to wander through the evil realms.
Just as a worldly parasol, when held by a person, wards off all heat wherever one travels in the four directions, yet being a product of craftsmanship, it will soon decay;

so too, the parasol of merit, sustained by right practice, can dispel all the burning afflictions of birth and the like, as well as the scorching and boiling of the fires of hell, for it is composed of manifold virtues and is maintained without destruction.
"In Śrāvastī there was once the daughter of an elder who had become the wife of a man of noble family. Later, she gave birth to a son.
Because her expenditures were without measure, their resources gradually declined until they were in straits. She said to her husband:
'I shall go to a distant land and strive diligently to seek wealth.'"
"You should cherish and raise this child.
As many years passed, the husband still had not returned.
When the child grew up, he gradually became dissolute; he fell in love with a neighboring girl, who then untied the precious garland she was wearing and gave it to him.
Later, when the mother learned the cause of this, she instructed him with various kind words:
"My son, you ought not to take pleasure in such base matters; you must guard yourself with care so that I do not suffer for your sake."
Day after day, she increased her vigilance and restraint, not allowing him to wander about; at night, she placed his bed at the threshold of the sleeping quarters.

One night, tormented by sensual desire, he lay down for a moment but rose again before long, unable to remain still. He addressed his mother, requesting that she open the door so he might go to relieve himself.
The mother said to her son, "There are vessels here; you need not go out.
Because his mother had strictly forbidden him, his lustful mind increased all the more, and he eventually gave rise to an evil intent to harm her.
Having committed this sin, he was filled with deep terror and went to a monastery, saying:
"Venerable Sir!
I wish to leave the household life; I pray that you will graciously accept me."
At that time, the bhikṣus were unable to investigate or question him regarding his origins, so they shaved his hair.

Once he had become a bhikṣu, he fled to another country where he practiced with courageous diligence, strictly maintaining the pure precepts, cultivating meditative concentration, and delighting in the recitation of the sūtras.

There was a householder who, seeing that the bhikṣu possessed such virtues, conceived a mind of devotion and made offerings to him; he built a monastery for him and appointed him as its presiding master, whereupon the monastic community from the eight directions all came to rely upon him.

At that time, the bhikṣu expounded Mahāyāna sūtras for the assembly and further instructed them in the practice of corresponding dhyāna-vision, providing the four requisites so that they lacked for nothing.
At that time, the great assembly practiced with diligent and tireless effort, and gradually some attained the fruit of Arhatship.
Later, this bhikṣu was afflicted by the suffering of illness; although he took excellent medicines, his debility and wasting only increased.
He summoned the assembly of monks and skillfully offered an apology, saying:
"I have mistakenly assumed the role of leader and treated the virtues of the assembly with contempt; my disciples likewise caused them distress and confusion."
I only pray that you, out of your great compassion, grant me joy.
That which is eternal must come to an end; that which is high shall also fall; meeting inevitably leads to separation; and birth must necessarily return to extinction.
Having spoken these words, he suddenly passed away.
At that time, the great assembly and his disciples collectively performed meritorious deeds to provide for his posthumous welfare, and they deliberated among themselves, saying:
"Our teacher has entered parinirvāṇa; we do not yet know where his consciousness has been reborn."

Among his disciples, there was one who had realized the state of an Arhat; he entered meditative concentration and began his observation among the devas, then proceeded to the human realm, and even down to the spirits and animals, yet saw him nowhere. He then searched throughout all the hells and finally learned that his teacher had fallen into the Avīci Hell.
Upon seeing this, the disciples were filled with great doubt and confusion, thinking:

"When our Great Upādhyāya was in the world, he strictly maintained the pure precepts, possessed great learning and eloquence, and practiced with diligence without ever ceasing for even a moment; he gathered in and provided for the monastic community from the eight directions."
"For what reason has he received such a severe retribution?

At that time, the disciple again entered meditative concentration and observed: he saw that in a previous life, he had once harmed his own mother; because of this retribution, he had fallen into the Avīci Hell, where a blazing mass of fire burned his body, and he was being reviled in various ways by the hell-wardens:
"In your lifetime, you were base and ignorant, committing this heinous crime."
"Now, whom shall I dispatch?
The jailer immediately took an extremely hot iron hammer and crushed his head; blood flowed, and he fainted from the suffering, which was beyond description.

At that time, the disciple, a Great Arhat, having witnessed this event, exerted the power of his compassionate vows to extinguish the torment. Relying on the majestic virtue of the Dharma, he caused [the victim] to know his past lives and, through mindfulness of the Triple Gem, restored his roots of goodness.
Immediately his life was severed, and he was reborn in the Yāma Heaven.
It is the natural law for newly born devaputras who have taken up residence in that heaven to give rise to three kinds of thoughts:

first, to observe the clan from which they were born in their previous body; second, to observe the place where their body perished and their life ended; and third, to observe what merit they cultivated to obtain birth in the heavens.
At that time, having made this observation, the deva-son saw that he had previously committed a heinous crime, yet through the power of the Buddha’s grace, he had been reborn in this heaven.
He then thought: "Now, with a single mind free from any other thoughts, I seek only to see the Buddha, to draw near to him, and to make offerings, in order to repay his great kindness."
By the power of his heavenly merit, he was spontaneously adorned with various precious necklaces that graced his body.

During the first watch of the night, his body emitted a radiance that illuminated the entire Jeta Grove, making everything clearly visible; he then approached the Buddha’s dwelling and prostrated himself, touching his head to the Buddha’s feet.
He immediately scattered various celestial lotus flowers and māndārava flowers upon the Buddha until they reached a height exceeding his knees.
Having made this offering, he withdrew and sat to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts in the mind of that devaputra, immediately proclaimed for him the turning of the Wheel of Dharma of the Four Truths in its three phases.

Having heard it, he attained realization and insight; he saw the Truths without rising from his seat and realized the fruit of Stream-entry (*srotāpanna*). With the firm, stainless vajra-pestle of wisdom, he shattered the mountains of the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and false pride.
This Dharma of the Four Noble Truths cannot be proclaimed by any śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas, nor by parents or kinsmen.
Only the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has taken pity on me;

through oceans of shed tears and mountains of accumulated bones, he has closed the gates to the evil realms and opened the path to rebirth in the heavens. He has rescued those in the hells, the hungry ghosts, and the animals, causing them all to dwell securely in the wholesome fruits of human and celestial existence.
Then that deva spoke in verse:
"Due to the deep affliction of my defiled desires, I fell into the Avīci Hell;
By the power of the Buddha’s grace, I have been born in heaven, And am further enabled to realize the path to Nirvāṇa."
By relying upon the pure Dharma-eye, I am forever liberated from the various evil realms of saṃsāra,
as well as from the future flow of birth and death, and shall reach the shore of peaceful bodhi.
I have now beheld the Lord of Munis, whom it is difficult to encounter even in hundreds of thousands of lifetimes;
he has excellently transcended the causes of birth, old age, and sickness, and is worthy of receiving vast offerings from the world.
Holding precious necklaces as offerings, with palms joined and circumambulating to the right, my heart is filled with joy;
therefore, I prostrate to the Honored One of Two Feet, who can cause both gods and humans to awaken.
The Scripture on the Collection of the Right Practice of the Merit Canopy, Scroll Five.
