Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, the Court-Scattered Official and Acting Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial, the Great Master of Xuanfan, the Purple-Robed Śramaṇa Subject Rìchēng, and others, by imperial decree. At that time, after the Devaputra Transcending Evil Destinies had praised the Buddha with verses, his heart was filled with joy, like a merchant leader who has obtained great wealth and profit; like a farmer who has successfully harvested his crops; like a valiant general who has achieved victory on the battlefield; and like a long-suffering patient who suddenly attains complete recovery.
At that time, there was an Arhat in the assembly who, knowing the beginning and end of the circumstances regarding that devaputra, reflected:
"Although my own teacher passed away long ago, in which realm does he now dwell?"

At that time, there was a donor who was preparing a vegetarian feast at the monastery. A certain bhikṣu drew fresh, pure water and distributed it as an offering to the assembly of monks during the course of the meal.
That arhat received some of the water in a white-bronze bowl, intending to drink it; when his fingertips touched it, he found it to be extremely cool and refreshing. He then thought to himself:

"In the past, my teacher served as the abbot of this monastery and managed the affairs of the great assembly. Yet he was stingy with the community's property and greedily attached to material requisites."
I constantly pray that in my future lives I may again be born here.
Having committed such sins, if I were to fall into the hell of molten copper, how could I ever obtain this sweet spring?
Having formed this thought, he entered meditative absorption to observe; yet throughout the entire hell realm, as well as the realms of animals and hungry ghosts, he saw nothing at all.
He reflected further:
"Could it not be that my roots of goodness planted in the past have now reached maturity, such that I have taken rebirth in an exalted place?"
He then observed the various heavens in succession and saw that the teacher had been reborn in the Heaven of the Four Great Kings.
At that time, the Venerable One went to where he was, comforted him with greetings, and said to him:
"I have heard that this heaven can only be attained by those who cultivate various virtues and firmly maintain the pure precepts."
"Master, having accumulated transgressions over many lifetimes, how could you have reached this state?
At that time, the deva said to the Venerable One:
"In the past, I served as the abbot of a monastery; yet out of folly and evil conduct, I never confessed my faults."
When my life was about to end, with a mind of sincere and profound devotion, I took refuge solely in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha.
By virtue of these thoughts and through the power of the Three Jewels' grace, I have received this root of goodness and been reborn here.

When that venerable one heard these words, his heart was purified and leaped with joy at such an unprecedented occurrence; he then thrice exclaimed "How marvelous! amidst the great assembly of devas, humans, those still in training, and those beyond training, and related the aforementioned matter in detail.

The power and merit of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha are inconceivable; they can dissolve the immeasurable and extreme sufferings of the hells, increase the immeasurable roots of goodness in sentient beings, sever afflictions, and tear asunder the web of doubts, ultimately enabling one to reach the other shore of Bodhi.

All those who possess wisdom should exert themselves with diligence, purifying their body, speech, and mind, and cultivating generosity, ethical discipline, and meditative concentration; this is how one can repay the great kindness of the Buddha.

However, as the dispositions and desires of sentient beings vary, the World-Honored One employs skillful means to encourage them to cultivate these three types of practice gradually: for those who delight in enjoying the five sensory pleasures, he encourages them through skillful means to practice generosity;
for those who delight in being born in the heavens to experience superior and wondrous bliss, he encourages them through skillful means to maintain pure ethical discipline.
Some may delight in liberation and seek to transcend the limits of suffering; for them, the World-Honored One employs skillful means to lead them to practice meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
Therefore, the World-Honored One has taught these three practices, calling them the "Canopies of Merit" (*puṇyakaṭhika*); they should be fully and respectfully observed.

It was as if two spirits were contending over three objects—a chest, a pair of sandals, and a mallet—struggling with one another and crying out loudly, "There is a brahmin in such-and-such a place who is most upright; he may decide this matter."
The two spirits carried the object to that place and, with palms joined, said:
"Great Brahmin! You should divide this object equally for us."
The brāhmaṇa said:
"This is but a trivial matter.
Why must you compete over it, traveling such a distance to seek a resolution?"
The two spirits said:
"This is no small matter; it is most exceedingly difficult to obtain.
Behold this casket, for it possesses the power of transformation; whatever object one desires shall emerge from within it."
As for these twin sandals, if anyone steps upon them, they will be able to ascend to heaven and experience all manner of sublime delights.
Furthermore, as for that mallet, it can crush and subdue all enemies, causing them to retreat and disperse.
When the brahmin had heard these words, he immediately ordered the two spirits to step aside and said,
"I shall deliberate upon this for a long time to divide these three things so that each receives an equal share."
That brahmin hastily put on his sandals, took the mallet and the box, and departed through the air.
When the two spirits saw this, they regretted having revealed that these three items belonged to another.
In these metaphors, one should distinguish them well: giving is like a casket, for it fulfills one's wishes;
ethical discipline is like footwear, for it enables one to be born in the heavens;
meditative concentration is like a mallet, for it subdues all demons.

This is called the World-Honored One’s teaching on the correct practice of the "Canopy of Merit" (Puṇyāvatamsaka), which encompasses the skillful means of generosity, ethical discipline, and meditative concentration.

Within this, three types of unwholesome conduct are further clarified: namely, stinginess, violation of precepts, and mental distraction. These give rise to various afflictions and serve as the root of saṃsāra and the evil destinies; they are capable of destroying the merits of generosity, ethical discipline, and dhyāna-concentration.
Therefore, the World-Honored One has demonstrated in various ways the faults of stinginess: it is like filth and impurity that defiles sentient beings and brings about what is undesirable.
Thus, although such a miser may accumulate precious wealth, he is unable to practice generosity; he is like an owl or a vulture perched amidst a cluster of lotuses.

They fail to provide for their parents; they abandon and avoid their assembled kinsmen; they do not believe in virtuous words nor take pleasure in the teachings of the sūtras; relying on their own wealth, they cannot endure the prosperity of others. They are like intoxicated elephants, difficult to tame by nature, or like venomous serpents whom people do not wish to behold; when good people see them, they all distance themselves from them. They take no delight in rejoicing in superior meritorious deeds; when seeing others come to encourage or assist them, their hearts give rise to vexation, like one who seeks water in a dried-up well.

The sounds of the words they utter are not desired by others to hear; wherever they go, no one speaks with them; in the midst of a great assembly, they are like a fool; passing through a crossroads, they are like a rotting corpse.

Although that foolish person dwells in the world, they are unable to distance themselves from various faults and evils, unable to protect and maintain all wholesome merits, and unable to cause the seeds of all wholesome qualities to grow.
Thus, such a miser creates the causes for poverty; though wealthy in the present, he is unable to enjoy his riches, and when those with humble hearts come seeking, he cannot bestow even a small gift.
One should know that such a person is like a *śītavana* (cemetery), which no one in the world delights in relying upon.
The causes and conditions of this stinginess are as explained in the *Mahānāma-gṛhapati-sūtra*.
At that time, the World-Honored One was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, there was a great elder in that city named Mahānāman, who was immensely wealthy but childless;
he suddenly passed away. When King Prasenajit of Kośala heard of this matter, he hurried to his house, his body covered in dust and soil.
Having arrived, he took possession of all the treasuries and various wealth, entrusting them entirely to the officials.
When his business was concluded, he returned in his carriage to the place where the World-Honored One was, prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to sit to one side.
The Buddha said,
“Great King!
Why have you come here in such haste, with your body covered in dust?”
The king reported all these matters in detail to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said,
“Great King!
"How great is that great householder’s wealth?

The King replied, "His family is immensely wealthy, possessing vast amounts of property, gold, silver, and precious jewels; his storehouses contain countless hundreds of thousands of koṭis of various goods."

Though he was thus wealthy and without equal, he consumed only coarse and simple food; the clothes he wore were tattered and worn; when he went out, he rode in a dilapidated carriage with a canopy made of gathered leaves.
Whenever he wished to eat, he would first bolt his door; though he consumed food and drink daily, he never ate to full satisfaction.
Even when śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, beggars, travelers from afar, or performers of the arts came seeking food and drink, not a single person ever received even a small portion.
Then, King Jayasena again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I pray that you will explain to me the retribution brought about by the fault of stinginess committed by the householder Mahānāman.”
"May those who hear it all attain awakening.
The Buddha said,
"Great King!"

Although this householder was thus very wealthy, he did not honor his elders or kin, nor could he enjoy his own wealth; he took no pleasure in giving to the most excellent fields of merit, and his friends, relatives, servants, laborers, and all his subjects abandoned him entirely.

It should be known that although such a person dwells amidst wealth, because of their stinginess they are discordant with it; they are like a lotus flower growing from impurity, like a fierce tiger crouching in a beautiful garden, like exquisite food placed upon poison, like a mani-jewel produced from a precipitous cliff, like sweet ripe fruit planted on a high crag, like a pure ground smeared with filth, like one who takes poison in hopes of prolonging life, like one who claims to practice celibacy while living in a house of courtesans, or like one full of anger who desires love and respect, or like one with erroneous understanding who claims to be skilled in debate—their speech is like that of a foolish child, lacking any consistency, speaking what is not Dharma as Dharma and what is unwholesome as wholesome, thereby inviting all manner of worldly ridicule.

This is merely guarding wealth; it is falsely called "richness. Although one possesses rare treasures, they benefit no one; though one labors all day long, it is as if one has no wealth at all. When others see this, they all deem it inauspicious, and even close friends will not go to visit or inquire after them.
Such a miserly person is loathed by all, like a flock of geese that does not dwell in a cold forest.

Because of their wealth, they bind themselves; they do not realize that life is like a mountain torrent, nor do they reflect that the great terror of impermanence is about to arrive, for in a single kṣaṇa, one’s own life may be lost.
One should know that wealth and possessions likewise do not endure for long, being like the ears of an elephant that never rest even for a moment.

Such a person fails to pose humble questions to the Dharma teacher; hearing praise for the practice of giving, their heart lacks faith and joy; seeing one come to guide them, they hide away and flee to a distance; and even if they should encounter such a person, they respond instead with insults and abuse.

Thus, although such a fool possesses abundant wealth, it is no different from what one obtains in a dream; even to the point of being stingy and begrudging, burying it in the ground, he will not seek excellent medicine even when afflicted by the suffering of illness. Upon hearing that a physician has been summoned, his mind gives rise to vexation, and because of this chronic ailment, he meets his end.
When people heard of its destruction, there was none who did not express delight.
The entire body, now disintegrated and impossible to approach, was consumed by fierce flames; foul-smoking fumes billowed forth until it was suddenly reduced to ashes, carried away by the wind.
It should be known that such a person will certainly fall into the evil realms and undergo various sufferings within the hells.

Upon emerging from the hells, they will be reborn among the hungry ghosts (*preta*); their bodies will be massive, naked, black, and emaciated, constantly scorched by blazing fires until their limbs are withered and rotten.

His two eyes are like deep pits, his belly is exceedingly large, and his throat is like a needle; having gone through long kalpas without food or drink, his skin and bones stand joined together, unable to support themselves.

They constantly consume excrement and filth to sustain their lives, smearing it upon their lips and mouths without feeling any aversion; if they see saliva or mucus, they scramble for one another, and even if they obtain a small portion, they experience great terror.
Furthermore, they are born in remote, desolate wildernesses and parched seas where even the name of water is unheard of.

Their bodies are as tall and massive as mountain peaks; when buffeted by fierce winds, they sway and emit shrieks. Moreover, they serve as dwellings for soaring birds that come and go, pecking at them or seizing them, causing them to endure various forms of suffering.
From this, they obtain liberation from rebirth among other classes of hungry ghosts, namely: yakṣas, rākṣasas, piśācas, bhūtas, kūṣmāṇḍas, pūtanas, kaṭapūtanas, skandhas, and unmādas.
Should they happen to obtain a human form, their appearance will be exceedingly ugly; their skin will be black and coarse, as if scorched by smoke.
Their sensory faculties will be obstructed, and their eyes will lack clarity.
Destitute, hungry, and naked, he sustained himself by begging; he would constantly carry bricks and stones to strike his own chest.
When he obtained leftover, discarded food and drink, or even that which was infested with maggots, he considered it sufficient.
Constantly oppressed by wind, rain, cold, and heat, and bitten by mosquitoes, gadflies, and various insects, one forever loses happiness, renown, and auspiciousness.
Such evil retribution is truly terrifying.
This practice of stinginess is further explained in the *Venerable’s Question Sūtra*.
At that time, the World-Honored One was staying at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove in Rājagṛha.
At that time, there was a son of a householder in that city who frequently visited the Buddha’s dwelling, delighting in hearing the Dharma and aspiring with pure faith to leave the household life.
He spoke to his mother, saying:
“I pray that you, Mother, will permit me to leave the household life and practice the Way within the Buddha-dharma.”
The mother said:
"At present, you are my only son.
Once I have passed away, you may do as you please."
The son followed her instructions and diligently sought out wealth; he presented all the property he had acquired to his mother, saying:
"I pray that you, Mother, will take this and use it as you please, and if there is any remainder, cultivate various meritorious deeds."
Having obtained wealth, her mother was unwilling to practice charity; she accumulated vast amounts and buried them in the ground.
Whenever a śramaṇa came to beg for alms, she would raise her hand in reproach and scold him, saying, "A ghost has come!"
Upon hearing this, the son was displeased,
thinking, "Why does my mother, despite having so little food and drink, fail to give in charity?
He further urged her with persuasion, and she falsely claimed that she had already given it away.
Before long, his mother passed away.
At that time, the son of the elder performed extensive acts of giving as an offering for her, and subsequently renounced the household life.

Having entered the Dharma, he applied himself with diligent vigor, delighted in hearing the true Dharma, reflected according to principle, and perfected the faculties and powers. He mastered conditioned phenomena, awakened to the law of arising and ceasing, brought rest to all saṃsāra, transcended the five destinies, shattered the shell of ignorance, and became free from the craving of the three realms.

He regarded gold and jewels as mere rubble; though his body was smeared or cut, he gave rise to neither attachment nor aversion. His mind was equanimous like space, and having decisively and forever severed all afflictions, he manifested the realization of the fruit of Arhatship.
Mahābrahmā, Śakra, and all the devas together held him in high esteem, making offerings and praising him.

At that time, while the Venerable One was dwelling in a grass hut on the banks of the Ganges practicing meditative concentration, a ghost suddenly appeared standing before him. It was naked, hideously black like a charred stump, with disheveled hair, a large belly, and a thin neck; its limbs were ablaze as it wailed aloud.
The Venerable One asked,
"Who are you? The ghost replied to the Venerable One:
"I am your mother.
Since my life ended twenty-five years ago, I have fallen among the hungry ghosts (preta), suffering from extreme hunger and thirst, not even hearing the names of food, drink, or water."
If one sees a great river, it suddenly dries up;
looking from afar at a grove of fruit trees, upon reaching it, they are no longer there.
Thus, not even for a single moment is there the slightest happiness.
“I only pray that the Venerable One will rescue me; I wish to rely on this dwelling and beg for a little water to drink.
Having heard this, the Venerable One wept with compassion and sighed, saying:
“Having failed to cultivate merit while alive, one falls into the evil realms after death.”
"You should now give rise to sincere resolve and repent for your past transgressions.
The ghost said,
"My mind was shrouded by the defilement of stinginess, and I never gave even a small gift to any field of merit."
All the various kinds of wealth and property we possessed in the past were entirely buried as treasures in our own house.

Venerable One, please quickly retrieve those goods for me and hold a great assembly of giving, providing food for śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, bestowing gifts upon the poor, and making offerings to the Buddhas and the multitude of worthy sages.
"Recite my name, confess and repent, and vow that this body of mine may quickly be liberated from this suffering.
The Venerable One said,
"If you can thus reproach yourself and repent, your transgressions shall be extinguished."
The spirit said, "Because in my previous life I was devoid of shame and lacked a sense of propriety, I have been reborn with this naked form; I am unable to remain here.
The Venerable One said to him:
"If, after committing evil, one does not feel remorse, that karma is fixed;
if one can confess it, the transgression will not increase.
Since you have now resolved to do so, you may remain here."

At that time, the Venerable One summoned his relatives and returned to their former residence, where they excavated various items. As he had instructed, they organized a great assembly for giving, providing exquisite and delicious food as offerings to the Triple Gem, and ensuring that the brahmins and all beggars were fully satisfied.
At that time, the Venerable One’s mother stood to one side; beholding the vast assembly of countless people, she was ashamed of her own hideous appearance and wept aloud, crying out:
"I pray only that the World-Honored One will take pity on me and deliver me!"

Then that venerable one prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground, calling out his mother’s name in a loud voice and vowing that by virtue of this merit she might quickly attain liberation.
At that time, the World-Honored One, through the power of skillful means and the empowerment of his majestic spiritual authority, preached the Dharma for her.
At that time, hundreds of thousands of sentient beings in the assembly heard the Dharma, attained realization, and gained the vision of reality.
The hungry ghost was freed from suffering and immediately passed away.

The Venerable One then re-entered meditative concentration and observed that the ghost had been reborn among the wealthy ghosts; he went to that place and explained the karmic causes of his past life for him, causing him to resolve his mind toward awakening and exhorting him to practice acts of charity.
"Now you should cultivate merit and seek the essential way of liberation as soon as possible.
Having heard this transformation, the ghost reflected for a long while and said,
"Venerable One!..."
"I cannot give.
When the Venerable One heard this, he sighed in lamentation:
"You are utterly foolish; the habit of stinginess still persists within you, and you do not realize that dark karma surrounds you on all sides."
"The realm of ghosts is extremely wretched; why do you not feel weary of it and fear it?
Having rebuked him with various skillful means and urgent exhortations, he gradually guided and transformed him until two pieces of white cotton cloth were obtained.
After the Venerable One accepted them, he took them and offered them to the community of monks.
Before he had time to trade them, he ordered a bhikṣu to take exclusive charge of them.
Yet the ghost remained stingy and could not bring himself to give them up; that very night, he took them secretly and departed.
Having lost it, the bhikṣu went and informed the Venerable One.
The Venerable One reflected:
"This is no ordinary person."
"I shall go and fetch it.
Having arrived at the place where the ghost was, he indeed obtained the cotton cloth.
He stole it three times in this manner, and each time he took it, it was restored as before.
The bhikṣu who handled the cotton cloth also felt resentment in his heart, and he immediately tore it apart and distributed it among the assembly of monks.
After each had received their portion, some used it to patch their robes.
That ghost came again and stealthily stole the robes away.
The Buddha said:
“You should know that a stingy mind is a great fault, for by its fetters one falls forever into the evil realms.

Therefore, I now employ skillful means to reveal this, so that all sentient beings may sever the defilement of stinginess and joyfully cultivate the vast and pure karma of giving. This is called the correct practice of the canopy of merit consisting of the gathering of generosity.”
The Scripture on the Collection of the Right Practice of the Merit Canopy, Fascicle Six.
The Scripture on the Collection of the Right Practice of the Merit Canopy, Fascicle Seven.
Compiled by Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna.

Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, the Court Scattered Official, Acting Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial, Great Master of the Propagation of the Dharma, the Imperially Enfeoffed Purple-Robed Śramaṇa, Subject Rìchēng, and others, by imperial decree:

If there are sentient beings who, with various kinds of things, practice giving to other sentient beings—namely, food and drink, clothing, bedding, medicine, and even all manner of exquisite treasures and storehouses—and are able to bestow them all upon others, such a giver is called one who practices "vast giving."

Alternatively, there may be sentient beings whose minds delight in practicing generosity, yet who have not yet acquired the various aforementioned objects; they give according to what they themselves possess. Such giving is called "giving according to one's capacity."
The Buddha said:

"These two kinds of giving refer to the actions of body, speech, and mind, as well as the aggregates of feeling, perception, and so forth, which operate together with volition and are performed simultaneously; that which is given while manifest before one, and that which is cherished through continuity—this is called giving."
If one gives away whatever one possesses by generating a pure mind for even a single moment, this is also called giving.

Furthermore, two types are clarified: first, the impure, and second, the pure. A practitioner of wholesome giving should understand these, whereby they will be able to establish all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).

If a donor lacks ethical discipline, does not accord with correct principle, and is not endowed with right view—specifically, one who claims that giving yields no fruit—then such a donor will receive no karmic reward.

Alternatively, there may be a recipient who lacks precepts, does not understand the teachings, and is deeply attached to false views, asserting that giving yields no fruit and that for such a giver there is likewise no retribution.
This is called impure.
If the donor observes the precepts, understands the Dharma with right view, and knows that there is a fruit of giving, then such a donor will indeed receive its retribution.

Alternatively, when the recipient possesses the precepts, understands the Dharma, and holds right view, and they declare that there is a fruit of giving, then for that donor there will be its retribution.
This is called the state where both donor and recipient are pure and their right practice is perfected.
If the donor is pure and the recipient is impure, this is also said to be the accomplishment of the reward for giving.

Or, the donor may be impure—meaning that fool who clings stubbornly to his wealth, like a servant attending to his master, or one who gives only after being coerced by officials and messengers, or bound and tormented by distress;
or one who gives only after being threatened with plunder and harm by enemies and bandits, and having experienced various terrors.
Or, one gives only after someone has been tormented by the sufferings of old age, illness, or decay and is gradually approaching the gate of death; such instances as these are not called giving.
Or, one observes various performances such as singing and dancing, and gives only after having purchased one's own reputation for beauty;
or, seeing another person give wealth to someone else, one considers oneself wealthy and noble and gives even more.
If one develops feelings of love and attachment toward the beautiful form of another, desiring to bring them under one's own control,
and consequently pays them double the price, such giving is not called *dāna* (generosity). Why is this so?

Although they give wealth, their minds are constantly afflicted by feverish distress; they are accompanied by greed, hatred, delusion, and doubt, do not accord with correct principle, and are not associated with virtue. They proceed only toward saṃsāra and perform what is unbeneficial; how could they possibly bring about those supramundane roots of goodness, the marks and signs of a Tathāgata, or the mark of webbed fingers like finely painted lines?
This is called the impurity of the donor.
Furthermore, two types are taught: first, impurity after having given; second, purity through dedication after having given.

At that time, in the city of Rājagṛha, there were several donors who, having performed meritorious deeds, provided various musical performances for entertainment and recreation within the monastery gardens of the Saṃgha.
At that time, the park keeper came and informed the monastery superintendent.
The senior bhikṣu said to the donors,
"Why have you come here to indulge in such negligence?"
"Though it may please you for a time, it will later bring about bitter retribution.
The garden-keeper bhikṣu said to the elder:
"When a donor is present, one uses pleasant words to make them rejoice; [but when they are gone, one speaks otherwise]."
"Why do you reprimand him and cause him to suffer distress?
Then that elder rebuked the park keeper:
"In the past, before you had studied, you did not know the Vinaya."
You serve those in white robes merely for the sake of wealth and profit.

Behold this enjoyment of wealth and pleasure; it causes the minds of the multitude to become deranged and gives rise to improper mental attention, serving as a condition for the destruction of the Dharma.
Then that elder spoke these verses:
"If one indulges in play and sensual pleasures within the monastery gardens,
that foolish person, blinded by ignorance, destroys the Dharma and falls into the evil realms."
Within this very state, one should practice generosity and uphold the precepts;
these two as companions can lead one to the gateway of liberation.
It is like a pure pond in which lotuses grow.
"Once those flowers have fully blossomed, they will inevitably bear fruit.
How is it that giving is said to be pure through dedication?

It is because that donor upholds the pure precepts; their essential nature and intentionality are fundamentally pure, and regarding all things such as gold, silver, precious jewels, granaries, and treasuries, as well as elephants, horses, and carriages, they are able to give them all away without any sense of stinginess.

Knowing that there is retribution for giving and that there is a future life, they feel weary of the rapid cycling of saṃsāra; delighting in realizing the true and eternal which is free from all faults, they do not give rise to defiled attachment toward the pleasures of the five worldly desires and are able to renounce them all; their minds remain unmoved by either blame or praise.

Upon seeing a beggar approaching, one should greet them with gentle words and a serene, pleasant countenance, free from frowning; regarding them as a venerable relative, one should feel no weariness in heart and fulfill their wishes according to their desires. One should swiftly bestow gifts without giving rise to doubt or regret, remaining free from flattery and deception, washing away the stain of stinginess, and single-mindedly delighting in benefiting others by taking up the burden of all sentient beings. One should maintain dignified deportment and sever all disputes and litigation.

If there should come one who begs for a limb or member of my body, I shall cultivate patience well and give rise to no anger or affliction; with an undistracted mind, I shall delight in the supreme gift, thinking:

"Since he seeks from me through skillful means, I shall joyfully bestow it upon him, so that I may fulfill the perfections of pure ethical discipline, diligence, meditative concentration, and sublime wisdom, swiftly realize the unconditioned state of dwelling in happiness in the present life, and attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
Furthermore, there are sentient beings who, due to their wealth, physical beauty, strength, and vigor, become deeply attached to sensual pleasures.

In this world, they do not associate with virtuous friends nor take delight in the Buddha’s Dharma; being stubborn and difficult to transform, they eventually give rise to various kinds of painful illnesses—such as those caused by wind, bile, phlegm, or the combination of all three—and thus meet their end.

Furthermore, all those in the world—officials, farmers, merchants, artisans, and all other people—their minds are constantly in a state of haste, finding no moment of leisure; they pursue only dissipation and entertainment, falling into the perilous and deep pit of the five desires, revolving through saṃsāra without knowing the way of escape.

With a heart of great compassion, I shall provide instruction and guidance; for those shrouded in the darkness of ignorance, I shall kindle the light of wisdom; for those without protection, I shall uproot their suffering; and for those without refuge, I shall enable them to find a place of peace—even if I must personally undergo the sufferings of the hells and other realms—by bestowing upon all sentient beings the merit of the acts of generosity I have cultivated, so that they may all be freed from suffering.

By the karmic fruit obtained through my giving, I do not seek the pleasures of the five worldly desires, nor do I delight in honor, prestige, or wealth; I vow to transcend saṃsāra and attain ultimate liberation.
This is called the purity of dedication after giving.
The Buddha said:
"I shall now briefly explain the causes and conditions from the past regarding such pure acts of giving as have been performed."

In the distant past, immeasurable eons ago, there was a land named Suśravas. Its king was named Sujaya, who possessed wealth, sovereignty, and a vast retinue. The realm was densely populated and enjoyed peace, security, and abundance; its inhabitants loved and respected one another, were free from disputes and litigation, never heard harsh words, and suffered no epidemics.
The forests were lush and verdant, and the fruits and melons were sweet; the soil was exclusively fertile, free from thorns and brambles, and all the necessities of life were fully provided.

In that era of supreme governance, the people were by nature benevolent and virtuous. He regarded the common folk with impartiality as if they were his only son; he cherished and delighted in the True Dharma, never abandoning it for even a moment. Possessing resolute great compassion, he felt pity for all beings, felt weary of and detached from conditioned existence, and thoroughly realized non-self. He was praised by the assembly of great men; abiding in vast generosity, his mind was free from stinginess, and he was able to relinquish everything he possessed.

Every morning at dawn, he would enter the almsgiving hall and comfort all who came to beg with kind words. To those who required food or drink, he gave delicious delicacies; to those who sought clothing, he gave exquisite garments. Even gold, silver, lapis lazuli, musaragalva, agate, pearls, mani-jewels, and the contents of his storehouses—he bestowed upon them all according to their desires.

Having given in this manner, the king entered the inner palace and summoned his consorts, male and female attendants, and the high ministers and officials; he bestowed gifts upon each of them until they were all fully satisfied. He relinquished everything he possessed without exception, save for the garments he wore upon his body.
At that time, King Suprabha reflected thus:
"I have now provided for all the people within this city, and they have all attained abundance.
Only the various small insects have not yet received my bounty; I wonder what means there might be to provide for them."

Then the king went to a place where there were many mosquitoes and gadflies; he removed the garment he was wearing and allowed them to feed until they were fully satiated, his mind free from any sense of hardship or weariness.
At that time, Śakra descended to observe the world of humans, and having witnessed this event, he marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence:
"King Śaṃjaya has been able to give rise to such vast compassion, benefiting and bringing peace and happiness to all sentient beings."
"I shall go there myself to test his sincerity.
At that time, Śakra transformed himself into a vulture with dark, soot-colored plumage and sharp, piercing claws and beak; he flew before him, intending to peck out both his eyes.
The King, having accumulated compassion and patience, was not at all startled or terrified;
instead, he looked upon the vulture with eyes of affection and said, "Now let my own flesh be eaten by you as you please.
As the bird hurriedly lowered its body, it suddenly vanished.
At that time, Śakra again transformed his body into that of a brahmin and approached the king, attending upon him with reverence:
"I pray only that the Great King will grant me his two eyes."
The king then said to him:
"Great Brahmin! If you truly desire it, you should take it yourself."
"I have not the slightest stinginess regarding my own eyes.
At that time, Śakra, knowing that the king’s practice was true and not false, concealed the brahmin and manifested his own form. With a heart full of joy, he praised him, saying: "Excellent!
Great King, your great compassion is now firm and your power of aspiration is resolute; your mind remains unshakable as you benefit sentient beings."
"Wherever all sentient beings hear the name of this king, they shall attain great auspiciousness.
Before long, they shall realize supreme enlightenment.
Thus, for one who gives in this manner, both the giver and the gift—whether extensive or meager—are entirely pure.

This person shall attain the dharmas of the foundations of mindfulness, right efforts, bases of psychic power, faculties, and powers; they will no longer regress from the path to enlightenment and will thus become a pure and supreme field of merit, capable of increasing the roots of goodness in all sentient beings.

Such a great man serves as a place of refuge for his parents, relatives, and friends; like a fine dwelling that can shield one from wind, rain, cold, heat, and various insects, he enables them to dwell in peace and security.

He is able to skillfully expound upon discourses amidst vast assemblies of countless śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and others; with a countenance of serene joy and a mind and body of courageous vigor, he subdues all heterodox views through his definitive wisdom.

For example, it is like a powerful fragrant elephant of the Snowy Mountains that crushes its enemies without fear in its heart; it is like a master teacher who instructs his disciples and does not abandon them, just as a mother thinks of her child.
One should know that such a person is like a cool pond, capable of rescuing all who suffer from thirst and exhaustion;
they are like a wondrous flower, beloved by all people, providing adornment wherever it blooms.
Just as a physician skillfully treats all manner of illnesses, providing peace and happiness wherever he goes;
or just as a mantra-holder can eliminate the bite of a snake, so too does he skillfully extinguish the poisons of greed, hatred, and delusion.

Seeing that sentient beings are impoverished and lacking in merit and wisdom, submerged for long kalpas in the mire of birth and death, he causes them to cultivate the true, corresponding wholesome dharmas, gradually leading them to the mountain of precious merit.
Just as the fragrance of a sandalwood forest wafts afar on the breeze, bringing delight to all who perceive it, so too is this person’s excellent reputation;
in every place, they receive universal respect and veneration.
Just as a royal capital is peaceful and free from fear, with all its people dwelling there in reliance upon it;
so too this person, practicing generosity, is closely approached by all, like the full autumn moon whose radiance is pure and clear, gazed upon by the entire world.
One who delights in practicing giving is likewise so.
Like the Honored Muni, whose faculties are tranquil, he teaches the Dharma of liberation; with joy he practices giving, vast, perfect, continuous, and without weariness.
"This is called the purity of liberation through right mindfulness in giving.

Furthermore, when that donor sees someone coming to beg from him, he should rise to greet them with hospitality and inquire after their welfare with a friendly disposition. He should offer various fragrant waters to cleanse their hands, and thereafter provide various foods and drinks according to the Dharma, granting whatever they may seek.
Even regarding all objects of entertainment, they offer them with a heart free from stinginess and full of joy.

Having made such offerings, they are able to cast off all hindrances and burdens, and further able to gather all roots of goodness. After casting off this body, their intermediate state (*antarābhava*) will be clear and sharp, and they will certainly be reborn in the Heaven of Contentment (*Tuṣita*), a place of supreme bliss and tranquility.
At that time, in that celestial palace there was a kalpavṛkṣa tree, its verdant leaves lush and flourishing, emitting wondrous radiance. Precious flowers bloomed everywhere in profusion.
Furthermore, various kinds of exquisite celestial garments were produced, which the devas and humans could take at will.

Furthermore, there were vast and pure palaces formed of various jewels with gold interspersed; countless jeweled vases were arranged in rows all around, and exquisite silk banners swirled gracefully in the wind.

Furthermore, there were hundreds of thousands of celestial maidens, their forms exquisitely beautiful and peerlessly upright. Their garments were adorned with exquisite flower garlands, and their bodies were bound with girdles of various jewels. Bracelets on their arms, earrings, jade pendants, and necklaces produced a gentle, harmonious resonance as they walked with slow, graceful steps—truly a sight most delightful.
Thus, celestial maidens filled the place.

At that time, the most excellent and foremost of those celestial maidens, knowing that a son of heaven had been newly born there, accompanied by her retinue and performing various musical performances, went in person to the gate of the celestial city to welcome him.

At that time, among the assembly was a newly born deva-son whose majestic virtue was exceptionally sublime and whose physical form was uniquely extraordinary; his deep blue hair was soft, curled to the right, and lustrous, such that no dust or impurity could defile it.

His eyes were pure, long, and wide like the petals of a blue lotus; his lips were a beautiful crimson like the *bimba* fruit; his teeth were white, even, and closely set like white jade or snow; his body emitted a radiance that reflected upon his face; and his stature was perfectly proportioned, bringing joy to all who beheld him.
Then that most excellent and foremost goddess said to the son of heaven:
"In this celestial realm, there is no pleasure more exquisite than this.
I only pray that you, O Benevolent One, will become my husband and dwell here with me for a long time, enjoying ourselves together."
He immediately poured water from a golden pitcher to wash his hands, and offered a celestial jewel crown and various necklaces and ornaments for adorning the body.

Furthermore, a heavenly maiden holding a white fly-whisk led the way as they proceeded to the Jewel Flower Forest, where they performed various songs and dances and played all kinds of music; gazing at one another, they experienced exquisite sensual delights.
Ascending once more to the subtle and wondrous palatial towers within the heavens, he wanders through their pleasure grounds with unimpeded freedom.

Sometimes, in jeweled ponds, they sport together; there, the celestial maidens vie to gather lotus flowers, each presenting them to the newly born deva-son. Or they scatter flowers to carpet the ground, each giving rise to thoughts of desire as they all approach him in intimacy.
Furthermore, another deva came to offer congratulations and consolation, saying:

"In your former human life, you practiced yoga and destroyed the causal conditions of greed and impurity; now you have attained birth here to experience supreme and wondrous bliss, surrounded by the respectful attendance of celestial maidens."
Then that celestial being prostrated at his feet and, with joy and praise, spoke these verses:
“Excellent, O benevolent one, born in this heaven, You enjoy the supreme pleasures of the five senses;
Like the pure full moon beautifying the vast sky, You are as fragrant as a blooming blue lotus.”
In the past, you cultivated vast and noble deeds; from your body issued subtle and pure radiance.
You always gazed upon sentient beings with eyes of compassion; therefore, gods and humans alike revere you.
Furthermore, there is a pure sandalwood grove, Its branches and leaves spreading lushly, most lovely to behold;
Long climbing vines are spread everywhere, hanging down on all four sides, And wondrous flowers cover it entirely, all in full bloom.
There dwell celestial maidens within it, their complexions pure white and most elegant;
their limbs are supple and emit a wondrous fragrance, vying with one another in song and dance without weariness.
That I have now been able to attend upon you, O Benevolent One, brings such clarity to my eyes and joy to my heart as has never occurred before;
this aspiration of mine shall not be in vain, for it cannot be attained through minor causes and conditions.
Constantly surrounded by hundreds of thousands of celestial maidens, adorned by their prior meritorious deeds—
such inconceivable rewards for giving should cause one to forever sever all doubts.
Then that newly born deva-son replied in verse:
"If one wishes to increase the treasury of merit, One should practice vast and pure giving;
One will certainly obtain supreme and wondrous bliss, Which neither water, fire, nor non-humans can destroy."
The bliss within the heavens is most rare; whatever one desires to enjoy appears before one.
All those in the world who are wise and discerning should give rise to a pure mind and practice the giving of alms.

"All sentient beings should reflect well upon this: having given such gifts, they will receive superior celestial retribution; subsequently, being born among humans, they will be born into great clans of noble lineage, possessing great renown and great majesty, with physical forms that are upright and dignified, pleasing for all to behold, with a complete circle of kinsmen and immeasurable wealth, which no adverse conditions can destroy."
As it is said in the *Vaiśākharājamātṛ-nidāna-sūtra*:
At that time, the king’s daughter, together with her retinue, departed from the palace and went to the garden to stroll and look about.

Having finished his inspection and rested, he immediately untied the exquisite, supreme pearls and precious ornaments that adorned his body, placed them in a cloth bag, and entrusted it to his maidservant; he then proceeded once more to the Buddha’s location, desiring to listen to the Dharma.
Having heard this, she returned to the palace, where her maidservant suddenly forgot the object she was entrusted with.
The daughter, displeased at hearing this, informed her father the King.
Her mother said to the King:
"This must certainly exist; even if there were one who saw it, they would not be able to take it.
Throughout many lifetimes, up until this present body, I have never given rise to even the slightest craving for another's property."
If one should give rise to this thought:
"I desire to seize the bodies and wealth of all sentient beings," then one will be unable to see the Buddhas or cause all sentient beings to attain their desired fruits.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda, having seen these items, immediately collected them.
The following morning, he went to the palace and presented them to the King.
The King said:
"The items he left behind were fortunately seen by the Venerable One;
had anyone else found them, they surely would have been concealed.
The mother said to the king:
"Why do you not believe me?
I shall throw this object onto the crossroads to test its power of merit; who among you can take it?
Having said this, he cast it away. Those passing by each perceived it differently: some called it impure, while others said it was a venomous snake, and they all abandoned it and departed.
The king still harbored doubts; while his mother was fast asleep, he took her ring and threw it into the river.
When the mother woke up, she said, "Who has taken my ring?"
The king said,
"Protected by the power of merit, how could I dare to take it?
His mother said:
"Cease for now;
you shall surely obtain it later.
Suddenly, one day, he dispatched a messenger to the market to buy a fish. Upon returning home and cutting open its belly, they found a ring, to the great astonishment of all.
The king immediately praised her, saying:
"Excellent, my mother!
Your words are definitive, like the roar of a lion."
Later, Ānanda again visited the king, who developed even greater faith and said:
"The power of merit is truly such as this; I shall henceforth joyfully cultivate meritorious deeds to the very end."

Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, the Court Scattered Official and Acting Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial, the Great Master of Xuanfan, the Purple-Clad Śramaṇa and Subject Rìchēng, et al., by Imperial Decree. The Buddha said:
“Great King!

It should be known that for all sentient beings in the world, the meritorious rewards received through pure giving cannot be destroyed by enemies; even hundreds of thousands of people cannot seize them away. Wherever one goes, merit serves as a guide; this remains true even in future lives, following one constantly like a companion.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"By virtue of the vast accumulations of meritorious deeds gathered in previous lives,
He has now become a king of men, Endowed with auspiciousness and noble dignity."
A hundred thousand attendants stood before the king;
because they were sustained by the power of his merit, they gazed upon him with trembling awe.
One should know that those meritorious deeds are like one's eyes, belly, hands, and feet.
I have always cherished and sustained them, ensuring they continue without interruption.
In the past, when I practiced the perfection of giving, I was able to relinquish everything except for a single elephant,
which I kept so that I might ride it wherever I went at my pleasure.
Delighting in dwelling within the mountain forests, he practiced various meditative concentrations;
at that time, all the people came to follow him,
some holding white fly-whisks in their hands, others carrying parasols.
As well as various carpets and rugs, wherever they went, they spread out seats and couches.
Each of them addressed the King, saying: "We lack merit and wisdom;
we now pray that you will allow us all to draw near to you and together cultivate all virtuous deeds."
Merit is the most excellent wealth, always bringing true happiness;
merit is the foremost kinsman, leading one to a place of peace and security.
Merit is like a wish-fulfilling gem, held within the palm of one's own hand.
He brings about the highest auspiciousness, and all his aspirations are fulfilled.
Possessing exquisite physical marks and features, he enjoys the pleasures of the five senses;
his speech is delightful for others to hear, being skillful and most lucid.
"Life shall be long-lasting, Secure and free from sorrow;
All sentient beings, upon seeing them, Will regard them as dear friends.

If sentient beings, directed toward a supreme field of merit, apply themselves with focused devotion according to the correct principle and practice giving, they will certainly obtain in this very life the corresponding karmic reward of abundant wealth and prosperity.
For example, Lady Suvarṇamālā, upon hearing of the Buddha’s merits, gave rise to a heart of praise and reverence, and offered her own previously possessed exquisite golden garland to the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, the daughter of King Sudarśana provided excellent food and drink as an offering to the Venerable Subhūti.
Furthermore, the brahmin woman Sūci cut off her own hair and sold it to provide a meal for the Venerable Mahākātyāyana; yet her hair grew back as it was before.
Because these three women offered pure gifts, they were all reborn in their present bodies as queens of the kingdom.
Furthermore, the householder Puṇyavatī went in person to invite the Buddha and his arhats to his home for a meal, whereupon his storehouses overflowed once again;
he was like the cowherd girl who offered sandalwood incense.
Even a village girl who offered a stalk of barley to a Buddhist stūpa attained rebirth in heaven.
Such are the causes and conditions for receiving retribution in the present life, as described in the *Rājāvavādaka-sūtra*.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. At that time, Queen Mallikā, the consort of King Prasenajit, gave birth to a daughter who possessed eighteen kinds of extremely hideous features.

As she gradually grew up and it became time to seek a husband for her, the noble clansmen were unwilling to form an alliance with her, while the king would not permit a marriage with those of low caste.
At that time, there was a son of an elder from a foreign land who had long resided in this city; having exhausted all his wealth, he wandered about destitute, finding no companion.
A minister informed the king, and the king granted his request.
The King then summoned him for an audience and said to him:
"I have an eldest daughter whom I shall take as your bride.
If you will follow her, you shall enjoy wealth and honor forever."
"If you wish to return to your own country, you may go together with me.
At that time, the king's daughter immediately adorned her body with exquisite and rare miscellaneous jewels and gave them as a wife to him, along with countless varieties of wealth and goods.
Then the son of the elder took her as his wife, and before long they returned together to their native country.
Once they had arrived home, his kinsmen sought an audience with him to offer their greetings.
The elder’s son said, “My wife is a princess; it is not easy to see her.
If you must see her, we shall certainly choose an auspicious day.”
Later, when his relatives arrived at his house again, the son of the elder said:
"Seven days from now, let us meet in the garden outside the city."
The assembly further deliberated and said:
"These words are definitive.
If you do not go, we shall fine you five hundred thousand coins."

When the seventh day arrived, the son of the householder prepared various kinds of exquisite food and drink; he first took a portion and placed it inside his room, informed his wife of this, and firmly locked the door.
At that time, the son of the elder took his fine as well as various foods and drinks and went to that garden.
At that moment, the people in the garden saw from afar that the son of the elder was coming all alone, and they all said to one another, "This man is deceitful;
he does not abide by our prior agreement."
Having arrived at the park, he said to his kinsmen:
"Please do not be angry with me.
I wish to pay the fine."

The assembly said, "Your wife is held in such high esteem that she is concealed in a deep chamber; even the light of the sun and moon is not permitted to see her, so how could we possibly manage to behold her!"
At that time, the princess lamented to herself:
"Though I am young, my appearance is exceedingly ugly.
What evil karma has brought about such loathsomeness?"
He exclaimed in a stern voice,
"Alas, what suffering!
It causes her husband to endure great shame and constant humiliation, as he is made to speak falsehoods and suffer punishment."
"Living in such a state as this, though one remains alive, what is the point?
He then took a silk sash and hung it around his own neck.
At that moment, the guardian deity of the house, having witnessed this, said:
"I shall release this princess and preserve her life so that she does not meet an untimely death.
You should know that the World-Honored One’s great compassion is inexhaustible; he constantly delights in rescuing and delivering various sentient beings, and frequently reflects:
"To which sentient beings should I now preach the essentials of the Dharma so that they may give rise to faith and understanding?"
Toward which sentient beings should I now cause them to wash away the defilement of greed?
Toward which sentient beings should I now cause them to pacify and eliminate the affliction of anger?
Toward which sentient beings should I now act so that they may eliminate their ignorance, delusion, and dullness?
Toward which sentient beings should I now act so that they may increase all their roots of goodness?
Toward which sentient beings should I now act so that they may emerge from the mire of birth and death?
Toward which sentient beings should I now act so that they may transcend the ocean of suffering within saṃsāra?
"Among which sentient beings should I now act so that they may be liberated from the fetters of affliction?
Among which sentient beings should I now act so that they may have the poisonous arrows of evil wisdom extracted?"
"Among which sentient beings shall I now cut off the four torrents and cause them to reach the other shore?
Among which sentient beings shall I now cause them to escape the various kinds of bitter suffering of the three miserable realms?"
To which sentient beings should I now bestow the water of the Dharma to cause them to eliminate their thirst and craving?
To which sentient beings should I now cause them to feel weary of and loathe the abscesses of sensory objects?
"Among which sentient beings should I now cause them to break the eggshell of beginningless ignorance?
Among which sentient beings should I now cause them to shatter and subdue the high mountain of their own conceit?"
"Among which sentient beings should I now cause them to distance themselves from all evils and clothe themselves in the raiment of shame and remorse?
Among which sentient beings should I now cause them to fully cultivate the training in ethical discipline, meditative concentration, and wisdom?"
"Among which sentient beings should I now cause them to penetrate all phenomena so that their minds attain mastery?
Among which sentient beings should I now cause them to obtain the pure eye of wisdom?"
"To which sentient beings should I now cause them to transcend and enter the gate of great liberation?
To which sentient beings should I now cause them to give rise to the mind of great bodhicitta?"
"To which sentient beings should I now bind the garland of bodhi upon their heads?
I shall now cause the daughter of King Jayasena to transform her hideous form so that she may obtain her wish."

Thus, in every moment and every thought-instant, the World-Honored One observes all sentient beings—whether near or far, few or many, superior or inferior, and of high, middling, or low capacities—and is able to deliver them all.
With the eye of wisdom, he sees all things without exception. As a verse says:
"The Buddha does not abandon sentient beings; Whether far or near, he transforms and delivers them all."
When it has ripened, it naturally produces a sweet flavor.
Therefore, the Honored Muni regards enemies and kin with a single thought;
he brings benefit and happiness to all sentient beings, yet does not hope for any recompense.

At that time, the World-Honored One, in order first to gather and transform the naked ascetics, the Nirgranthas, manifested the marks of a Great Man as he sat upon a precious lotus flower, his body draped in crimson robes like the newly risen sun. His physical appearance was serene, and he dwelt in majestic deportment, like a mountain of gold radiating boundless light. Amidst the great assembly of countless humans and devas, he appeared like the full moon amidst the stars; like a precious Tāla tree in a celestial palace gently swaying in a mild breeze, providing a delightful refuge for all; like a coral trunk adorned with precious flowers; like a great torch burning within a golden basin; like a white fragrant elephant entering the Nairañjanā River, its body sprinkled with the pollen of golden lotus filaments; and like a Karṇikāra tree in springtime blooming with golden blossoms, a sight beloved by all.

He is skillfully able to discipline all sentient beings; entering the various evil realms, he never gives rise to weariness or aversion. Wandering and transforming within the good paths, he skillfully expounds all dharmas, causing all to give rise to the aspiration for enlightenment and attain peaceful happiness.

Since beginningless time, all sentient beings have continuously committed various evil deeds such as greed, hatred, and delusion toward those who are enemies, friends, or neither. [The Bodhisattva] regards them all with equal compassion as if they were his only child, causing them all to escape the perilous difficulties of saṃsāra, just as the sun dispels darkness until nothing remains.
At that time, the World-Honored One, with a voice of omniscience, briefly expounded the essential Dharma for those non-Buddhists:

"One should know that all phenomena in the world, whether conditioned or unconditioned, are realized through wisdom to be entirely empty and quiescent. Due to the deluded mind of falsehood, one is confused regarding the vision of reality; yet their intrinsic nature is nirvana, fundamentally pure."
Upon hearing this teaching, his mind attained awakening; he was then able to sever his stubborn and arrogant self-conceit, just as a lion’s roar naturally causes massive boulders to shatter.

At that time, that Tathāgata defeated those of divergent views; having prevailed in the debate on doctrine, he manifested great supernormal powers and ascended to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven. All sentient beings therein praised the Buddha’s merits, declaring that none in all the worlds could surpass him.

Furthermore, he manifested the supreme, stainless mark of the invisible crown; his *uṣṇīṣa* was curled to the right, deep blue, lustrous, and lovely, while from between his eyebrows he emitted the light of the white tuft-mark (*ūrṇā-kośa*), like the full moon of autumn.
This is the foremost merit of the Tathāgata; it is not produced by the minor virtues of Brahmā, but arises from the Buddha’s great compassion for the benefit of others.
Even if all sentient beings were to abide in right reflection like a mass of atoms, none would be able to fathom it.

The *uṣṇīṣa* is neither hard nor soft; it is neither formed nor destroyed; it is neither hurried nor leisurely; it is neither moving nor still; it is neither swift nor slow; it is neither strong nor weak; it is neither sunken nor agitated; it is neither level nor precipitous; it is neither contentious nor silent; it is neither joined nor dispersed; it is neither attached nor detached; it is neither diligent nor lax; it is neither deliberating nor crossing over; it is neither illness nor affliction. It is the supreme auspiciousness and foremost merit, shared equally by all sentient beings.
At that time, those non-Buddhists’ minds became pure and filled with faith and understanding, and they attained a state of peaceful dwelling within the Buddha’s Dharma.
Meanwhile, the king’s daughter remained in her chamber; touched by the light of the Buddha’s radiance, her mind became tranquil and composed, and she thought to herself:
“Now the Buddha dwells in the world for the benefit and happiness of sentient beings; all who face calamities and hardships receive his deliverance.”
"I only pray, World-Honored One!
Do not abandon your great compassion; out of pity, please protect me and manifest yourself before me.
Having spoken these words, he prostrated himself from afar, weeping with tears streaming down.
The Buddha, knowing his intention, caused that chamber to suddenly become adorned and pure.
At that moment, the Tathāgata emerged from the earth, his body the color of pure gold, with the marks and signs of excellence perfectly majestic.

At that time, the king’s daughter beheld the physical marks of the Buddha and marveled at such an unprecedented sight; she reverently offered exquisite flowers and incense, presented precious jewels and necklaces as gifts, and with palms joined in salutation, approached him with deep respect.
The Buddha’s shadow covered his body, and he suddenly attained a handsome appearance.
His heart was filled with great joy, and he leaped for boundless delight; standing before the Buddha, he praised him with these verses:
"O Supreme Lion of the Śākyas, Dwelling in the Kiḷa Rock Cave,"
Possessing few desires and contentment, he is free from the faults of the world.
With wisdom as his sharp fangs and shame and remorse as his mane and whiskers,
he subdues all demonic adversaries, like a lion seizing a deer.
Patience serves as sturdy armor, with the power of loving-kindness as the bow;
skillfully launching those arrows of wisdom, one forever slays the thieves of affliction.
The eight liberations serve as a pond, and right conduct forms its embankment.
The water of stainless diligence opens the lotuses of the awakened mind;
With valor, one leaves all faults behind and uproots the source of the three realms of existence.
Bestowing the medicine of the impartial Dharma, one heals the diseases of greed, hatred, and delusion.
Possessing blazing majesty and virtue, adorned with the marks and signs of excellence,
he increases the mind of merit and bears the burden of all living beings.
Firmly established in dignified deportment, his faculties are free from distraction.
Like the kovidāra flower, those who behold it conceive love and joy.
Fearless and free from defilement, with the most supreme tranquility of mind,
liberated from all bonds, they achieve omniscience.
The Muni, the Great Bull-King, has no equal in the world;
he is able to rescue all sentient beings from sickness or from sorrow and affliction.
Clad in a saffron-colored *saṃghāṭī*, he remains serene and unmoving.
With various similes, I praise you with a pure mind:
like a golden tāla tree, its trunk towering, tall, and straight;
or like a pillar of molten gold, its radiance most brilliantly shining.
Furthermore, just as a mass of gold Coated with sandalwood paste,
The physical marks of the Buddha’s body Cannot be known through such comparison.
Or it may be said that a mountain of exquisite gold, With a single peak rising most steeply, [is like his form].
Blown by a fierce wind, it stands here immovably.
Some say that during a battle between the Asuras and the Lord of Devas,
this golden palanquin fell from there and suddenly appeared here.
Some say it is the banner of Śakra, fashioned entirely of pure gold,
towering and brilliantly radiant, suddenly appearing here;
others say it is the subtle and wondrous jeweled pavilion of the god Viśvakarman.
Adorned with various jewels, it suddenly appears here.
Or the Mother of the Buddhas of the Earth, having disgorged a treasury of wondrous jewels,
emits manifold rays of light and suddenly appears here.
After the Buddha had bestowed his transformation, he suddenly vanished.
At that time, the king’s daughter sat cross-legged, focusing her mind with single-minded concentration as she contemplated the Buddha’s body.
Meanwhile, the son of the elder, who had previously been in the garden forced to drink by his relatives until he was intoxicated, was being discussed by the assembly as follows:
"You may take the door keys from his hand and go quickly to his house to open the door and look inside.
Upon seeing that his wife was like a celestial maiden, everyone was struck with amazement and involuntarily prostrated themselves in greeting.
When the son of the elder returned home, his wife saw that he was handsome; she informed her husband of what had occurred above, saying:
"The Buddha, the World-Honored One, is the supreme field of merit; I shall go once more to pay my respects and make offerings."
Having performed these deeds of Buddha-work, he then made this vow:
"If all the evil karma of this body of mine has brought about such an ugly retribution, may I never again experience it."
"Furthermore, all sentient beings in the world shall be freed from ugly bodies and attain physical perfection.
Then, before the Buddha, he spoke again in verse:
"The World-Honored One’s wondrous marks and features Are fully endowed with all adornments."
May all sentient beings, upon seeing me, have their wishes fulfilled.
By virtue of my slight merit now, may it extend universally to all sentient beings,
so that they may entirely eliminate the causes of ugliness and all obtain the retribution of physical excellence.
The Buddha said,
“Worthy woman!
I do not praise myself, I do not speak falsely, and I do not seek offerings.”
"According to the karmic retributions experienced by sentient beings, I give rise to great compassion to rescue and protect them.
He then spoke in verse:
"I am the Teacher who tames the world; I seek neither fame nor gain."
Skillfully able to topple the banners of the five desires, Causing the minds of all sentient beings to be tranquil;
Fully endowed with the three knowledges and two practices, You shall bring auspiciousness to humans and devas.
I have already subdued the host of Māra-enemies; In the end, none can surpass me.
Forever free from all the faults and afflictions of the three realms of existence, Without giving rise to feverish distress, their minds are liberated;
With even those habitual tendencies exhausted without remainder, They receive vast offerings from the world.
Should there be sentient beings who come to inflict harm upon me, may my mind remain unmoved like space;
I vow to bear the burden of those ordinary and ignorant ones, until I realize the perfect, luminous, and untainted wisdom.
If there are bhikṣus, the fourfold assembly, and others, who all come to me desiring to hear the Dharma,
I shall cause them all to be fully endowed with the various codes of discipline, so that they will certainly become wise ones.
I am the crown prince of King Śuddhodana; delighting in the cultivation of ascetic practices, I dwelt among the mountain valleys.
Having attained liberation from the source of suffering—birth, old age, and illness—I have thereby realized the Unsurpassed Way.
"Because that princess made a pure-hearted offering to the Buddha, the World-Honored One, she obtained a beautiful and dignified physical form in this very life.
If anyone seeks the highest happiness, they should make pure offerings to the Buddha; this is called the 'Correct Practice of the Canopy of Blessings' as taught by the Buddha."
"You, bhikṣus!
Constantly delight in receiving and upholding [the teachings], and you should diligently practice and study generosity, ethical discipline, and meditative concentration.
