Testamentary Proclamation by the Minister of State for Ceremonial Affairs: The Great Master of Dharma, the Imperially Ennobled Purple-Robed Śramaṇa, Subject Rìchēng, and others, respectfully translated by imperial decree: "If one single-mindedly cultivates the practice of giving toward the Buddha and other supreme fields of merit, one will certainly obtain its reward."

In this manner, he even beheld the sovereigns of the world, whose nobility and honor were peerless; upon their heads they wore jeweled crowns inlaid with various treasures, while their ears and arms were adorned with rings and bracelets of gold and lustrous jade. Their countenances were fair and radiant, possessed of dignified and majestic features, and their robes were embellished with pearl necklaces and precious floral wreaths.

The palace where he dwelt was lofty, vast, and magnificent; its multi-storied pavilions, doors, and windows were all crafted with every kind of ingenuity, and canopies of various colored silks were spread everywhere.
Auspicious beasts, lions, and *kukila* birds were kept in cages as objects of pleasure.
The city walls rise steeply, guarded by powerful warriors, while elephants, horses, and carriages pass to and fro in dense throngs.
The inhabitants dwelling therein live in peace, security, and abundance; they are free from disputes, litigation, robbery, theft, flight, and all manner of afflictions or fears.
Everywhere there were exquisite sāla trees, tamāla trees, campaka trees, and aśoka trees, their branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits lush and lovely.

Wherever the King desired to go, they cleared away dust, filth, tiles, rubble, thorns, and brambles from the crossroads; they sprinkled the ground with various fragrant waters, and hundreds of thousands of musicians—playing flutes, pipes, lutes, drums, and conchs—escorted him from front to back.

The King rode upon a majestic dragon-elephant, his sovereign majesty and virtue exceptionally honored, supreme and stainless. His body was anointed with gośīrṣa sandalwood paste, the fragrance of which wafted afar.
He was clad in crimson silk robes like the rising sun, and in his right hand he held an exquisite white fly-whisk with a handle made of vaidūrya gem.
He held up a wondrous parasol with a shaft of gold, resplendent and adorned with various precious objects.
At that time, all the people within the city rejoiced; with palms joined, they praised him in unison and scattered many famous flowers until they covered the ground.

There were members of the noble clans who, employing their refined ingenuity, composed songs and hymns to commemorate and extol his virtuous governance; upon hearing these, the King’s joy increased all the more.
Such superior rewards are obtained through the merit of giving.
This is called practicing the perfection of giving with single-minded devotion toward the supreme field of merit, thereby accomplishing the canopy of merit.
How does one practice giving so that all sentient beings may invariably obtain worldly wealth and happiness, and enjoy the exquisite objects of the five sensory desires?
One should understand that such acts of giving do not merely bring about vast wealth and happiness, but can also accomplish the causes for unsurpassed wisdom.
Know that this giving is a firm treasury, indestructible by water, fire, or thieves.
One should know that this giving is the most excellent friend, serving as a constant companion in both this life and future lives.
One should know that this giving is like a fine seed, yielding fruits according to one's wishes at all times.
One should know that this giving is like a sublime staircase, by which one may ascend to the heavens to experience all manner of bliss.

One should know that this giving is like the light of a lamp, capable of dispelling the darkness of stinginess among the hungry ghosts; it can provide rescue within the evil realms and offer protection in places of peril and hardship; it enables one to cross the ocean of birth and death and reach the further shore.

If sentient beings, having understood this, repeatedly give rise to pure mental attention and diligently practice giving in an uninterrupted succession, their minds being free from stinginess regarding all they possess and not wasting anything in vain, they will develop a profound realization that these things are all insubstantial and will ultimately delight in cultivating the practice of pure giving.

For this reason, his excellent reputation spreads far and wide, and all who see him rejoice in admiration. He is always able to dwell in reliance with virtuous people, and when in the midst of a great assembly, his mind is free from timidity. He abides well in dignified deportment and praises the merit of giving, which can summon abundance, cause one to escape the evil realms, lead to rebirth in the heavens, and bring one toward the city of liberation; it inspires others with faith and understanding, causing them to abandon the defilement of stinginess.

You should know that this person is a great bodhisattva, a spiritual friend, and a true man of virtue; he is able to increase the genuine roots of goodness in sentient beings. All living beings should approach him, attend upon and make offerings to him, joyfully listen to the sublime Dharma, practice according to the principle, and seek the path of liberation.
As explained above, if one single-mindedly cultivates the practice of giving toward the Buddha and others, one will certainly obtain its reward.
Even if one does not encounter a single Buddha or Bodhisattva, if one can maintain such a mind of giving, the reward it evokes will be no different from what was previously described.
Therefore, the World-Honored One employs skillful means to manifest the path, enabling all sentient beings to practice and train in successive stages.
At that time, the World-Honored One was dwelling at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove in the city of Rājagṛha, traveling there to teach and transform others.
At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana thought to himself:
"Now that the World-Honored One and his great assembly of śrāvaka disciples are dwelling in this forest, it is necessary to establish a pure monastic residence."
Having formed this thought, he went to where Śakra was and said:
"Lord of Devas!

I venture to request that you, O Benevolent One, construct a vihāra for the Buddha, the World-Honored One, in the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove at Rājagṛha, so that he and his disciples, the great arhats, may dwell there together in retreat."
When Śakra, Lord of the Devas, heard these words, his heart was filled with great joy, and he accepted the instruction with the words, "So be it.

He immediately fashioned double gates, colonnades, windows, palaces, and towers out of countless gold, silver, precious gems, sapphire *indranīla* jewels, lapis lazuli (*vaiḍūrya*), and other such materials.
Coral served as its pillars, adorned and embellished with various kinds of precious substances.
Furthermore, various rare birds were carved from manifold jewels and suspended in mid-air, appearing as if they were soaring upward.
Countless precious mirrors were suspended all around, transparent and stainless, as brilliant as the stars and the moon.
Various celestial garments, radiant, pure, soft, and supple, were spread upon them, supported by golden frames.
It was adorned with rows of alternating vajra-jewel garlands and pearl flower garlands;
various famous incenses were burned, their fragrant smoke wafting everywhere, and diverse lamps were lit, shining brightly day and night.
Such an offering as this was unprecedented in the world.

Within that garden, everywhere were planted *nāgavṛkṣa* flowers, *campaka* flowers, *kurumba* flowers, *koṭapūga* flowers, and *aśoka* tree flowers; they bloomed all around, most lovely and delightful to behold.
Within the flower grove stands a coral pavilion; its gates, portals, windows, and railings are carved with extraordinary ingenuity and adorned with a profusion of various jewels.
When a gentle breeze blows through the flowers, their fragrance is perceived both near and far.

There dwell celestial maidens who move about within it, adorned with exquisite and rare jewels for necklaces; their ornaments are like beads held in the mouths of beasts, chiming with a *shanshan* sound.
Within the grove there are also yakṣī women, their forms upright and dignified, vying with one another to run and gaze, their topknots scattering precious flowers as they laugh and play together.
Furthermore, there are vast and pure lotus ponds composed of various jewels, filled with fragrant water.

Within these ponds are great jewel-lotuses with leaves of white silver and stalks of gold; therein dwell and stand many exquisite celestial maidens, moving their features and playing music as they perform wondrous songs and dances.
Furthermore, there were countless golden lotuses, *utpala* flowers, *kumuda* flowers, and *kahlāra* flowers, brilliantly radiant, in full bloom, and suffused with a pervasive fragrance.
There were various water birds—cormorants, ducks, and geese—soaring and alighting among the flower groves, preening their feathers and wings.
There were also sporting fish, swimming back and forth; as they brushed against the flowers and tossed up waves, they startled the gulls and ducks.

The surrounding steps were all made of gold, silver, crystal, and various precious gems; furthermore, along the banks of the pond stood forests of kalpavṛkṣa trees, their long branches brushing the water and their dense leaves providing interlacing shade, while various exquisite flowers bloomed in alternating succession.
Countless hundreds of thousands of noble families and commoners, adorned with wealth and joy, performed various musical entertainments, coming and going to view the sights without any hindrance.

At that time, the Lord of Devas constructed a vihāra for the Buddha, the World-Honored One, completing it after one full month; he provided all necessary provisions so that nothing was lacking, and all manner of storehouses were filled to overflowing.
He approached the Buddha and spoke these words:
"This ground is auspicious, vast, and magnificently pure; it is exactly equal to the Nandana Grove.
I pray that the Tathāgata will come to this place to dwell during the summer retreat."
Out of compassion for him, the Buddha accepted it.

Furthermore, he offered hundreds of thousands of most excellent dragon-elephants to the Tathāgata, and hundreds of thousands of exquisite celestial maidens who held parasols and fly-whisks and fanned them with cool breezes, to serve the great disciples.
Furthermore, hundreds of thousands of gandharvas performed exquisite music as an offering.

At that time, there was an elder in the city of Rājagṛha whose family was immensely wealthy with immeasurable treasures and riches; he was considered even more distinguished than the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa.
However, that householder was deeply attached to false views and had placed his faith in the teachings of the non-Buddhist Nirgrantha.
Upon seeing this situation, he felt doubt and uncertainty in his mind.

At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, knowing that the man’s faculties were ripe for conversion, went to guide him, preaching the essentials of the Dharma and extolling the merits of the Buddha.
Having heard the Dharma, his mind attained awakening and understanding, and he addressed the Venerable One, saying:
"I now resolve my mind to take refuge in the Tathāgata; I wish to go and draw near to him, to pay him respect, and to make offerings."
He then went together with the Venerable One to the place where the Buddha was, prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, and stood to one side.
The Venerable One addressed the Buddha:
“This great householder has abandoned what is false and returned to what is correct; having first given rise to faith, he now wishes to make offerings to the Buddha and the assembly of monks.”
"I only pray that, out of great compassion, you will accept his earnest invitation.
Knowing this, the Buddha silently granted his consent.
At that time, the elder, realizing that the Buddha had accepted his invitation, was filled with great joy and returned crawling on his hands and knees.

He immediately adorned his residence with countless varieties of rare jewels and exquisite silks; he ensured that the gate-towers, halls, and pavilions were all newly cleaned and purified, and prepared a hundred kinds of refined and exquisite foods and drinks.
When the preparations were completed, he immediately dispatched a messenger to inform the World-Honored One:
"The time for the meal is approaching; we only hope that, out of great compassion, you will accept our humble offering.

At that time, the World-Honored One emerged from the monastery, his majestic virtue sovereign and his marks and signs perfectly dignified. His body radiated light as brilliant as the blazing sun, and accompanied by his disciples—the great Arhats whose faculties were tranquil, whose minds had attained mastery, and whose deportment was refined and graceful—he proceeded to the house.
Furthermore, there were hundreds of thousands of devas and devīs, their bodies and minds serene and free from all distraction, their persons anointed with sandalwood, reverently surrounding him.
When the people saw this, they marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence and came to inform the elder.

Furthermore, there were hundreds of thousands of laymen and laywomen who, their hearts filled with joy and celebration, snapped their fingers in prostration. Each offered the finest, most solid black sandalwood as incense for worship; the fragrance they burned exceeded a hundred thousand *hu*.
Furthermore, they played immeasurable and most sublime music, its pure, elegant, and resonant sounds shaking the earth.

At that time, the elder arranged various banners and canopies in succession, spreading out curtains and adorning them with strings of pearls; he burned great precious incense and went in person to welcome and honor him.
The elder’s internal and external relatives each brought handfuls of famous flowers and scattered them.

When the Buddha, the World-Honored One, had arrived at that residence, a seat was prepared for the Buddha in the center of the hall; it was spread with layers of exquisite silk and cotton, soft and supple, while carpets of various colors were laid across the floor.

Rows of jeweled banners were draped with nets of pearls hanging down on all four sides; exquisite pennants of various colors were suspended in a brilliant array, and hundreds of thousands of precious bells were inlaid upon them, their sounds harmonious as they were stirred by a gentle breeze; strings of pearl flower-garlands hung everywhere from the jeweled canopies.

Having prepared the scented ointments, powdered incense, and pure water in the ritual pitcher, he invited the Buddha to ascend the seat; he then took a piece of new, high-quality, exquisite white cotton cloth, cut it to make a robe, and knelt to offer it to the Buddha.

Thereupon, the foremost great arhats and those newly ordained bhikṣus entered the hall and sat down in order. They offered the finest flavors among all the various foods to the Buddha and the Saṃgha; everyone was fully satisfied. Having finished eating, each person withdrew their bowl and washed their hands.
Then that elder joined his ten fingers in palms-together salutation and, gazing up at the Honored One’s countenance, praised him in verse:
“The Tathāgata is endowed with the most excellent marks; The subtle secondary characteristics adorn his entire body.
His hair is long, fine, and not disheveled; Lustrous and deep blue, like the king of bees.”
The Tathāgata’s brow is broad and perfectly level, Neither deficient nor diminished, yet most firm and solid;
Between his brows, the white tuft of hair always curls to the right, Radiating light like the full moon in autumn.
The Tathāgata’s two eyes are utterly pure; his eyelashes are like those of a bull king, never blinking.
Cultivated, broad, and exquisitely beautiful, they constantly radiate light, as lovely as the *kuṇḍalaka* flower.
The Tathāgata possesses forty teeth, pure white and closely set like jade or snow;
his mark of the broad and long tongue is wondrous and inconceivable, comparable to the red hue of the palāśa flower.
The Tathāgata further possesses the merit of the nose: it is lofty, prominent, and straight, with the nostrils not visible;
the lips are neither drawn back nor drooping, being fresh and lustrous like the *bimba* fruit.
Thus the Great Seer’s face is perfectly round, And his earlobes are supple and well-proportioned;
Like a blooming, exquisite lotus flower, Free from all defilement, one never tires of beholding him.
The physical form of the Tathāgata is like a mass of gold, firm, solid, and peerless;
his complexion is like the campaka flower, neither emaciated nor showing the network of veins.
His two arms are plump, round, and exceedingly lustrous;

The lines upon his palms manifest myriad forms and images, Fully endowed with the marks of the wheel, complete with hub, spokes, and rim, As well as the jeweled banner, the precious vase, the fish, and so forth.
The breadth of his chest is like the breast of a lion; the auspicious mark of the "joyful swirl" is clearly delineated.
His abdomen is level and full, proportionate to his body; his navel is deep, spiraling to the right, and perfectly round and pure.
His twin calves are like those of the king of celestial deer; as he walks, his body turns without looking back.
His right foot is raised first, displaying the marks of the seal; he moves with steady grace and fearlessness, like a lion.
The Tathāgata appears in the world, Like the sun ascending into the sky, illuminating all with its light;
He is able to bring auspiciousness to sentient beings, And both devas and asuras alike offer him faith and worship.
Thereupon, having praised the Buddha with these verses, the householder’s heart was filled with great joy and his power of faith became firm; amidst the great assembly, he spoke again in verse:
“The Muni, honored for his ten powers, Is able to shatter the nets of all Māras.
Forever free from the defilement of afflictions, His faculties are eternally tranquil.”
Of the most supreme and noble lineage, The kinsman of the sun, born of the Ikṣvāku clan,
Valiant and of great diligence, He has awakened from all faults.
The fearless Lion of the Śākyas, Endowed with every merit—
Having accomplished the subtle and wondrous Dharma, he reveals it for the sake of sentient beings.
Within the ocean of suffering of the three realms and amidst the various perils of saṃsāra,
taking precepts as the foundation, one will ultimately be able to transcend them all.
By upholding pure precepts, you have tamed your own mind;
having skillfully subdued all demonic adversaries, you are worthy of receiving sublime offerings.
Possessing great wisdom and great compassion, you do not abandon your original vow.
Out of compassion for all sentient beings, you cause them all to be free from sorrow and suffering.
Most excellent Teacher and Tamer, without peer in the three realms,
you skillfully extract the arrows of poison and sever the fetters of the three realms of existence.
Manifesting great supernormal powers, he is able to subdue all heterodox views;
revealing the Eightfold Noble Path, he causes others to cultivate the various holy conducts.
He is called the Great Caravan Leader, capable of performing great assemblies of giving.
These are called the ones of great wisdom; they act as the eyes of the world.
They are called great beings who can swiftly distance themselves from all evils, cut off the torrential flood of birth and death, and reach the place of peace and security.
The World-Honored One, the Great Guide, of the victorious Gautama clan, possesses a body of golden hue with the [thirty-two] marks; those who behold him can never tire of doing so.
He tames all sentient beings and leads them to enter and understand the True Teaching.
Forever free from all that is unwholesome, with a pure mind untainted by defilement;
like clouds dwelling in the void, they pour down the nectar-like flavor of the Dharma,
causing all sentient beings to nourish the seeds of their roots of virtue.
The Tathāgata, the Great Holy Honored One, together with the assembly of bhikṣus,
abides in the most supreme peace and security, and is able to reach the other shore.

Furthermore, they are able to encourage the cultivation of the Eightfold Noble Path and elucidate and proclaim the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths, causing those who hear them to attain realization and understanding in their minds.

They praise the various merits of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, as well as their immeasurable wisdom, their intrinsically pure nature, and their vast, majestic power that none can surpass; they are able to uproot [beings] from the cycle of birth and death.
To those suffering from the affliction of death, he employs skillful means to entice them into entering the city of liberation;
he causes them to gradually cultivate all dharmas of merit, to guard the pure precepts, and to practice *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.

Through the four fearlessnesses, the four bases of psychic power, the four right efforts, and so forth, he remedies all forms of indolence, and through the four foundations of mindfulness, he brings clarity.
Maintaining mindfulness so as not to forget, they cultivate the four immeasurable minds with equanimity; relying on the power of the five faculties, they sever the obstacles of the five destinies;
they realize that the characteristics of the five aggregates are equal for both self and others; they fully perfect the six pāramitās;
and with the seven noble riches, they bestow gifts universally upon all.

Cultivating the feet of pure precepts, they tread upon the flowers of the seven factors of enlightenment; with single-minded concentration, they dwell securely in the contemplations of the seven expedient means, analyze and expound the eight branches of the noble path, skillfully practice the nine successive meditative attainments, and are endowed with the ten powers. Their fame reaches the ten directions, they obtain the ten masteries, and eventually achieve buddhahood.
At that time, the World-Honored One, seeing that the elder had made this vow amidst the great assembly, praised him, saying:

“Excellent! You are now truly a great dragon among men, a lion among men, the most supreme and most eminent, a great seer among men. Like a white lotus, you are free from all defilement; you are capable of ferrying all sentient beings across and capable of bearing the burden of unsurpassed bodhi.”

At that time, the World-Honored One extended his golden hand like a blooming lotus; the webbing between his fingers was exquisitely patterned. As a father caresses his son, he placed his hand upon the elder’s head and, with a Brahma-voice resonating like spring thunder, spoke these words:

“In a future age, you shall attain Buddhahood, and your name shall be Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān, named ‘The One Who Fulfills the Aspirations of Sentient Beings.’”
"Endowed with the ten powers, he shall destroy all hosts of Māras; his land will be pure, vast, wealthy, and blissful.
At that time, there were sons of the gods in the void who rained down exquisite fragrant flowers as an offering.
All sentient beings throughout all Buddha-worlds conceived faith and delighted in cultivating meritorious deeds.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"In future ages, you shall accumulate supreme merit."
Within the ocean of birth and death, you rescue all who are drowning.
After the passing of countless kalpas, you shall attain the Way of the Buddha;
with a pure and stainless eye of wisdom, you will directly realize all phenomena.
Possessing the marks and emitting radiance, like the bright sun in the world,
you cause all sentient beings to eliminate the darkness of the three poisons.
Among the great assembly of devas and humans, you are the most supreme and unsurpassed.
Skillfully taming sentient beings, causing them all to practice the holy life;
as the foremost guide, endowed with all-knowledge,
you have attained supreme enlightenment like a lotus emerging from the water.

At that time, after the World-Honored One had bestowed the prophecy of Buddhahood upon that elder in the midst of the great assembly, the people within the kingdom of King Bimbisāra all conceived faith and marveled at this unprecedented occurrence.

Because the Buddhas and others have exclusively cultivated the practice of giving, they are constantly the sovereigns among humans and devas, possessing great majestic power; through their constant benefit and peace for all sentient beings with great compassion, they will certainly attain unsurpassed bodhi.
For this reason, the Buddha commanded the bhikṣus and others that they should always receive, uphold, and proclaim this sūtra for others.
I have explained its practice extensively; fearing it would become too prolix, I shall now cease.
The merit of observing the precepts shall now be revealed.
Why is it that, immediately following the discussion of giving, one speaks of observing the precepts?
This follows the sequence established in various sūtras.

Furthermore, when sentient beings are heedless and attached to pleasure, it is mostly due to their own internal wrong reflections that they act accordingly and even manifest such conduct, leading eventually to the violation and destruction of the precepts through body and speech.
In order to cause sentient beings to give rise to the antidotes, the characteristics of maintaining ethical discipline are explained after the discussion of generosity.
If a disciple of the Buddha or any layperson strictly maintains those prohibitive precepts without transgression, this is called pure maintenance of ethical discipline.

If sentient beings give rise to wrong thoughts and engage in physical, verbal, and mental karma, committing numerous transgressions—killing sentient beings and severing their life-faculties; taking what belongs to others without it being given; being addicted to sensual desires without ceasing for even a moment; engaging in false speech, frivolous talk, harsh words, and double-tongued speech; giving rise to great wrong views that deny cause and effect; killing one’s father, harming one’s mother, killing an Arhat, shedding the blood of a Buddha with a malicious mind, or causing a schism in the Saṃgha; destroying stupas and monasteries; stealing the property of the Saṃgha; defiling bhikṣuṇīs of pure conduct; delighting in reviling and insulting virtuous people; constantly enjoying gathering in groups to speak meaningless words; and showing contempt for the Dharma and its teachings while greedily attending to worldly affairs.

They maintain themselves through wrong livelihoods and commit various evil deeds: acting as executioners or jailers, slaughtering animals, fishing, breaking into homes, and robbing; they even plunder the meager possessions of the poor.
They administer poisons to others to harm sentient beings; they take pleasure in castrating elephants, horses, oxen, and the like.
They destroy villages and clear away forests.
Their speech is cruel and venomous, and they revile and mock the virtuous.
Feigning dignified deportment while their minds are crooked and deceitful, they speak well of what is not good; they give to those who do not deserve it.
Having committed manifold transgressions, at the time of death, all manner of signs of suffering manifest before them.
Once consciousness has ceased and passed away, evil karma follows them as they fall into hell to undergo extreme suffering.
There are four hells: first, the Pit of Hot Ashes;
second, the Swamp of Corpses and Excrement; third, the Forest of Swords; and fourth, the River of Ashes. These four hells are known as the "neighboring" hells.
Furthermore, there are eight fundamental hot hells:

first, Saṃjīva (Reviving); second, Kālasūtra (Black Thread); third, Saṃghāta (Crushing); fourth, Raurava (Screaming); fifth, Mahāraurava (Great Screaming); sixth, Tapana (Heating); seventh, Pratāpana (Great Heating); and eighth, Avīci (Uninterrupted).

At that time, there were various wardens within that hell, their appearances hideous and most terrifying; some had the heads of oxen, donkeys, elephants, and the like. Their forms were tall and large, stout and possessed of great strength;

their skin was black and rough, and their hair and body fur were yellowish-red. With knitted brows and angry eyes, upturned noses and drooping lips, their two arms were rigid and hard. In their hands they held iron clubs, or sharp axes, spears, halberds, mallets, saws, swords, wheels, and nooses—various instruments of torture from which all emitted fierce flames.

These various hell-wardens are fierce, treacherous, and violent; they harbor not the slightest heart of compassion for those sinners. Whether by burning, boiling, hacking, or sawing, the sinners die instantly, only to be restored to life in a mere moment.

Alternatively, they may be driven into the hells of Hot Ashes (Kukūla) and Corpse Excrement (Kuṇapa), where their feet are scorched and rotted when set down, yet return to their former state when lifted.
Seeing a forest in the distance, they go there to escape; once arrived, the branches and leaves all become sharp blades, which fall from above and hack and sever their bodies.

There are various predatory beasts—tigers, rhinoceroses, lions, makaras, and the like—who open their mouths and spit fire, with fangs and teeth so sharp and keen that they chew and devour sentient beings who have committed evil.
There is a great iron tree named Sālamalī, upon which are hundreds of thousands of sharp iron thorns, each thorn sixteen finger-widths long.
At that time, the hell-wardens drive the sinners toward it, piercing them with the thorns as they move up and down the tree.
Various evil birds flock together upon them, with sharp beaks and hard talons, either pecking or clawing.

The hell-wardens sometimes take large, scorching iron balls and pry open their mouths with tongs, forcing them to swallow; or they pour molten copper into their mouths, which burns through from the throat down to the bowels, leaving everything completely charred and rotten.
Some have their tongues pinned with iron nails, and are then made to be plowed over by oxen with iron plows.
Others are cast into large iron mortars and pounded to pieces with pestles.
Or they may have their bodies clamped between iron chests, so that blood flows from their ears, noses, and mouths, and all their limbs are destroyed without remainder.
There is a great pit of burning charcoal, extremely deep and fiercely blazing; they cast those sinners into its midst, and in an instant, they are transformed into a mass of fire.
At that time, the various hell-wardens all rebuked him together:
"In former times, you committed many evils and lacked compassionate conduct, violating and breaking the prohibitive precepts.
Now you receive this retribution; you should know it for yourself."
"In this state, there is extreme suffering that is difficult to endure and impossible to bear; one undergoes punishment for a long duration until one's karma is exhausted before finally emerging.

For this reason, the Buddha commands you, bhikṣus: constantly receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra, and explain it to others, so that they may cultivate giving and precepts and thereby achieve the canopies of merit."

The Buddha said: "Those who break the precepts do so because of their evil wisdom; through mental construction within the mind, they fail to give rise to antidotes, and being oppressed by burning afflictions, they commit various transgressions."
It is just as when a blazing fire is placed within the hollow of a withered tree; it will surely burn it to ashes.
Like a rotten seed, though planted in fertile soil, it can ultimately never sprout;
likewise, for one who has broken the precepts, no seeds of goodness can grow within the field of the Buddha’s Dharma.
Furthermore, just as when the roots of a forest of trees are all cut down, the trunks, branches, and leaves no longer flourish;
so too it is with a person who violates the precepts—they sever their roots of goodness and destroy their dharmas of merit.
It is like a dried-up well: those who are parched with thirst and seek its water can never obtain it;
likewise, when virtuous people seek the Dharma from such a person of broken precepts, they likewise shall not obtain it.
Just as a caṇḍāla is unfit to be a king and all the people are unwilling to trust or submit to him,
so too a precept-breaker is unfit to preach the Dharma, and all sentient beings are unable to listen to or receive it.
It is like a person who seeks the flavor from a rotten sugarcane; it can never be obtained.
Likewise, if one seeks merit from a person who has violated the precepts, there is ultimately none to be found.

Furthermore, when laypeople see that those śramaṇas are solitary, free from entanglements, and dwell in tranquility and bliss, they abandon their homes to take up the life of a śramaṇa out of a desire for such pleasure; yet they lack the correct cause, their minds are not resolute, and they are foolish and dull-witted.
Having become a śramaṇa, he again delighted in managing worldly affairs and became addicted to sensual desires, thereby violating the precepts.
At that time, there were elders among the assembly who rebuked him, speaking these verses for him:
"You wear the three robes of the Buddha, Yet you delight in performing unrighteous acts."
They bring disgrace upon that pure assembly, no different from outcaste Caṇḍālas.
With evil thoughts in their inner minds regarding the various realms of the five desires,
they are like a young calf who constantly longs for water and grass.
Delighting in worldly affairs, trading various rare and precious things,
manipulating their prices up or down, and speaking without sincerity—
such a person is like a leaking cup; their mind is never satisfied.
Seeking but meager wealth and profit, one fabricates matters of falsehood and deception.
Like a bee gathering nectar from flowers, one ought to rely upon a grove of lotuses;
yet returning instead to a thicket of thorns, one needlessly endures all manner of hardship.
In the great ocean of my Buddha-dharma, I shall never tolerate such a corpse;
just as seeds will not sprout again within salty, barren soil, so too,
when one is entangled by leprosy, there is no means by which it can be cured.
"You have committed various evil deeds; why do you not feel alarm and fear?
You are like a leaking boat—how can you possibly ferry yourself or others across?
The Buddha said:
A person who has broken the precepts is incapable of fulfilling any purpose.

Because of excessive desire, their mind seeks much; they violate the physical forms of others, constantly harbor fear and apprehension, lose their reputation, and become separated from virtuous friends.
One should know that such people are like those who are miserly; they ultimately possess not even a slight merit of giving.
Those who break the precepts are like the poor who have no hands; though they may reach a mountain of jewels, they obtain nothing.

Like an impure vessel that is full and overflowing; like a pitfall that people see from afar and avoid; like a snake in a room that causes constant fear; like a fierce tiger crouching in a beautiful grove; like a perilous and evil road that people do not wish to travel; like a broken cart that cannot carry a load; like a wicked person whom the multitude all cast out; like a venomous serpent whose very sight one does not wish to behold; like a śītavana cemetery that most people loathe; like a mad elephant brought under control by a skilled trainer; and like a thief who is dreaded by the wealthy.
It is just like a painted *campaka* flower that lacks the fragrance of its scent; such is the case for one who possesses no precepts.
It is like a sandalwood forest containing a *tila* tree; because their odors are mixed, it should be cut down immediately.
Even if one possessed a hundred thousand tongues within a single mouth, one could not fully describe the faults of breaking the precepts; their number would be boundless.
Because of breaking the precepts, one cannot increase the impartial wholesome dharmas for all sentient beings.
As it is said in a sutra:
A certain man said to his son-in-law,
"Drive the carriage now and enter the forest to cut firewood."
Because he was felling firewood, he lost his oxen;
because he was searching for the oxen, he left someone to guard the cart.
Before the oxen were recovered, the cart was lost as well.
This man, filled with panic, searched everywhere.
Upon reaching a pond, he saw a flying bird; he immediately seized his axe and hurled it from afar.
He missed the bird, and the axe fell into the pond.
Leaving his clothes on the bank, he entered the pool to seek his axe; however, the axe could not be found, and his clothes had been stolen by someone.
Returning home naked, it was already dark; having reached the entrance of his house, he peered secretly through the window.
The members of that household all thought a thief had arrived and struck him with a staff, wounding one eye so that blood flowed from it and he fell to the ground in a swoon.
At that time, a malevolent insect descended from above; smelling the scent of blood, it further devoured his other eye.
At dawn, the father-in-law came out from his house; recognizing him as his son-in-law, he questioned him in astonishment.
[The son-in-law] recounted the aforementioned events in full.
Thereupon, acting for the sake of his son-in-law, he spoke this verse:
“Having lost one’s robes and impaired one’s sight, what can a human being do?
Since they are incapable of performing service, they are therefore cast far away.
It is just as for a disciple of the Buddha: it would be better to abandon one’s extensive learning,”
One should guard and uphold the precepts; one who breaks the precepts is like one without eyes.
Know that such a destroyer of the precepts is a śramaṇa only in name;
he should not receive offerings, for he has lost all virtuous merits.

Furthermore, it is said therein: For example, suppose there is an elder who has many sons; he constantly instructs and admonishes them to be free from negligence, and then entrusts to them his various treasures, wealth, slaves, and servants. In this way, they will be able to long preserve their happiness.

Among his sons, there were some who were extravagant and addicted to the pleasures of women; upon hearing this, the elder immediately assembled his kinsmen and sternly rebuked them, sending them out of the house with a small amount of wealth, and further admonished them, saying:
"Be careful not to be dissolute and squander your riches, lest you later suffer poverty and be cast aside by others."

This son of a householder did not follow their instructions; before long, his wealth was entirely exhausted. His appearance became haggard, and he had to sustain himself by begging, becoming an object of contempt and disdain to his own kinsmen.
When the father, the elder, saw this, he was filled with grief and distress; his heart abandoned all hope, and before the assembly he cried out in a loud voice:
"This is not my son! This is not my son!"
Upon hearing this, they were filled with deep shame and remorse.
The Buddha said,
"I am also like this."

If any disciples violate the prohibitions and precepts, lacking shame and remorse, they shall immediately be expelled from within the Buddha-dharma, and neither the factors of enlightenment nor the various meritorious dharmas and manifold noble riches shall be entrusted to them.
Then, amidst the great assembly of devas, humans, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas, he cried out in a loud voice:
"This breaker of the precepts is not my disciple."
"Having caused them to hear this,
they shall feel shame for their transgressions and offenses.

Furthermore, once those laypeople have gone forth, they should dwell in accordance with the purity of the śramaṇas, wearing the saffron robes, carrying the alms bowl, donning the lamp of diligence, and cultivating extensive learning.
Relying instead on worldly ways to lead an improper livelihood— riding elephants and horses, donning armor, and entering the midst of battle formations with bows and arrows slung over their backs—
such as these individuals, who within my Dharma destroy the code of discipline, I do not wish to even look upon with my eyes.
For example, just as many painted lanterns in the world cannot dispel darkness,
so too it is with those foolish people who are unable to give rise to the untainted noble wisdom that illuminates the world.
Just as an actor, though wearing exquisite robes and a crown and proclaiming himself a king before a multitude, possesses no actual supreme enjoyment;
so too, a person who has broken the precepts, though wearing the kashaya and assuming the appearance of a śramaṇa, lacks the pure, supramundane, sublime bliss.

Furthermore, it is like a poor man who falsely claims to be wealthy and noble; amidst a great assembly, he raises his voice and declares, "I am a householder," yet in reality, he possesses no autonomy or mastery.
Those who break the precepts and merely bear the name of śramaṇa cannot attain the wondrous fruit of liberation.

The Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna compiled this;

translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, Chao San Dafu, Acting Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial, Great Master of Xuanfan, the Imperially Enfeoffed Purple-Robed Śramaṇa, the Subject Rìchēng, and others, in accordance with the Imperial Decree. Furthermore, it is stated herein that those who violate the precepts are unable to accomplish any of the various meritorious dharmas belonging to the Tathāgatas.
For example, it is like a king’s daughter who marries a poor man; having arrived at his home, she says to her husband:
"I am a king’s daughter, and my every desire shall be as I wish.
You must provide me with the finest incense, flowers, garlands, and various precious ornaments for adorning the body; all such items from the treasury must be fully prepared."
"If it be so, I shall remain here.
The poor man replied,
"The aforementioned items do not exist within my home."
Having heard this, the princess rebuked him, saying:
"If you are so impoverished, I shall depart.
The Buddha said:

“Those who break the precepts are likewise in this regard: they cannot achieve the maiden of supreme, pure liberation; they cannot obtain the incense of the ‘heat,’ ‘summit,’ and ‘patience’ stages; they cannot obtain the flowers produced by the Prātimokṣa vows; they cannot obtain the garlands produced by dhyāna-concentration and liberation; they cannot obtain the various treasuries of the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma); they cannot obtain the king of wisdom produced by hearing, reflection, and cultivation; they cannot obtain the most supreme and excellent perfect enlightenment (samyaksambodhi); and they cannot obtain pratyekabuddhas and śrāvakas as their retinue.”

This person who breaks the precepts, due to a lack of wholesome karma, possesses no merit in their present life; all virtuous people take no pleasure in dwelling with them, and whatever they say is not trusted by others; thus, they shall forever lose all the Dharma-treasures of the Tathāgata’s supramundane qualities.
At that time, Venerable Ānanda rose from his seat, approached the Buddha, and addressed him, saying:
“World-Honored One, why is it that among your disciples, those who have violated the precepts are not taught the profound essentials of the Dharma, and are no longer accepted but instead cast out?”
Everyone says that the Tathāgata is not one of great compassion.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“I regard all sentient beings in the world with equal pity and mercy; regarding the Dharma I teach, my mind has no stinginess or regret.”
Because they are not suitable vessels and lack the capacity to receive it, he does not teach them.

This is not like the way worldly wise men preach the Dharma, who perceive signs of opposition or compliance among sentient beings; if there is opposition, they do not proclaim the teaching, as if clutching an object in their fist and withholding it.
Suppose there is a king who holds a great assembly for giving alms, inviting śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and others, providing them with whatever they require.
A certain brāhmaṇa comes from another region and stands before the king, begging for many things.
Having heard these words, the king gave nothing to them at all.
At that time, a close minister urged the king to bestow gifts upon the brahmins according to his own inclination. The king then replied:
"It is not that I am being stingy."
"This man has no merit; therefore, I do not give it to him.
The Buddha said, "Ānanda!
I am also like this.
Because they have broken the precepts and are not vessels for the Dharma, I do not preach to them.
Even if I were to preach to them, they would be unable to receive it.
Just as a vessel with a hole is unfit for holding water, so that even if one diligently draws and pours it in day and night, it leaks away again;
likewise, one who has broken the precepts is unable to contain the water of the Dharma of merit.

If one should violate even a small portion of the prohibitive precepts, that person will likewise be unable to accomplish the various treasures of the Dharma, such as the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*).
It should be known that the pure morality maintained by such a person is not called "perfect" and no longer increases.
Because such ethical conduct does not increase, one’s progress toward the dharma of liberation also does not increase.
Because one does not progress in the dharma of liberation, that which they have attained is not the path of tranquility; it is merely called a semblance of liberation.

If one firmly upholds the precepts and does not transgress them, that person will then understand and penetrate each of the various treasures of the Dharma, such as the factors of enlightenment, and through correct reflection, attain dwelling in peace and security.
"O you bhikṣus!
Constantly delight in receiving, upholding, and expounding this sūtra for others; through the merit of such giving and precept-keeping, you shall achieve the canopy of blessings.

If bhikṣus abide in right reflection, draw near to virtuous friends, and delight in hearing the true Dharma, they can eliminate the world’s sorrows, fears, and burning afflictions, and repel unwholesome dharmas so that they do not arise, just as one extinguishes a blazing fire until nothing remains.
If bhikṣus dwell in wrong reflection, it will give rise to negligence and cause the mind to become distracted; they will then grasp only at the causes and conditions of the five desires.

Such sentient beings are born into a place where afflictions arise, and they will certainly lose and ruin all dharmas of merit. Like untimely hail that destroys the crops, they can bring about various calamities in the world; they constantly harbor flattery and crookedness, lack shame and remorse, and are reviled, disparaged, and treated with contempt by laypeople.

These are not persons of the Dharma; their aspirations are inferior, and they do not yearn for the pure and wholesome fruits of those śramaṇas. Consequently, they are unable to drink the nectar-like water of the Dharma of all Tathāgatas.

Delighting in the commission of various evils and seeking to enter perilous paths, they embrace the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals, taking those places of extreme suffering as their refuge.

If one does not believe or accept the Buddha’s words in one's heart, even a minor transgression of the precepts will result in severe retribution; how much more so for the immeasurable suffering brought about by the extensive commission of evil karma?
As it is told in the *Elapattra-nāgarāja-kāraṇa-sūtra*:
Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying at Vārāṇasī, in the Deer Park at Ṛṣipatana, proclaiming the essential points of the Dharma to a great assembly.

At that time, the Naga King Elapatra, knowing that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, was preaching the Dharma there, gave rise to a pure mind and desired to go to the Buddha’s presence to attend upon and make offerings to him. He then thought to himself:
"I am of the naga class and have many enemies; should we happen to encounter one another, they will surely cause me harm."

He then transformed his own body into that of a Wheel-Turning King (cakravartin), with a countenance of exquisite dignity and sovereign majesty; his body was adorned with various precious necklaces and ornaments, and he held a wondrous parasol while riding upon a jeweled palanquin, attended by a retinue of seven treasures and a thousand sons, both internal and external.
Furthermore, he was surrounded in front and behind by an army of ninety *koṭis*, and followed by hundreds of thousands of non-Buddhist practitioners, brahmins, ascetics, and beggars.
With majestic spiritual power acting as his protection, like Śakra, Lord of the Devas, he immediately hastened to the assembly of the Tathāgata.
At that time, the World-Honored One was surrounded by the fourfold assembly, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, and others, who paid him reverent homage as he preached the Dharma for them.
At that time, having witnessed this event, the assembly was filled with wonder and doubt; they came forward and addressed the World-Honored One:
"Who is this king whose majestic power is such as this?"
The Buddha said to the great assembly:
"This is not a king of men.
Wait but a moment, and you shall know it for yourselves."
When that dragon king had arrived at the Buddha’s dwelling, he prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to sit to one side.
The Buddha said:
“Dragon King!”
"In the past you were deluded, and now you receive this retribution.
For what further reason have you come to this state?
You ought to quickly arise and leave this place; cast off these manifested forms and assume your original shape, so that you may return here once more to appear before this assembly."
Then that dragon king addressed [the Buddha], saying:
“World-Honored One!
We who possess the bodies of dragons have many enemies; were we to suddenly encounter one another, we would surely cause disaster.”
"It is for this reason that he has manifested these transformations.

When the Buddha, the World-Honored One, had heard these words, he commanded the Great Yakṣa Vajrapāṇi to follow and protect the dragon king, leading him to another place where he would restore his original form.
His body was massive, coarse, rough, parched, and cracked, a physical frame formed by the accumulation of various evil characteristics.

Due to his past karma, he possessed seven heads, each topped with an *elā* tree; because of those trees, he suffered from constant trembling and agony, with pus and blood flowing together in extreme stench and filth, while they were infested and devoured by countless maggots.
Having returned to his original form, he went back to where the Buddha was.
The head of that nāga was in the city of Vārāṇasī, while its tail reached the country of Takṣaśilā.
At that time, those in the great assembly who had long been free from greed were struck with terror upon seeing this horrific sight, and they all thought to themselves:
"What kind of sentient being could have such a retribution as this, and yet come here?"
The Buddha addressed the great assembly:
"This was none other than a Cakravartin King who had temporarily transformed himself to come to my presence; I have now sent him away so that he may manifest his true form.
When the śramaṇas heard the Buddha’s words, they sighed with grief and remained silent in deep distress.
At that time, having assumed the form of a nāga, the Nāga King Elapatra wept and addressed the Buddha:
"I only pray that the World-Honored One, out of great compassion and pity, will prophesy when I shall be liberated from this evil realm."
The Buddha said:
"Dragon King!
I shall now speak for you; you should give rise to true faith."

In the future, when the lifespan of sentient beings reaches eighty thousand years, a Buddha named Maitreya will appear in the world; that Buddha will prophesy that you shall be released from this dragon body after the passage of this period of time.
At that time, having heard the Buddha’s teaching, the Dragon King raised his voice and wailed, his tears flowing like a river.
The Buddha, with great kindness and compassionate words, instructed him:
"You should blame yourself; to increase your sorrow and suffering in vain is futile."
"I cannot remain long in this assembly now.
At that time, the dragon king deeply reproached himself:
"My evil karma is such that there is nothing comparable to it; I pray that by the power of the Buddha, I may soon be freed from this suffering."
He then made this vow:
"From this day forward until the end of the future age, my mind shall not harbor perverse thoughts nor give rise to negligence; I shall not even harbor the intent to kill or harm so much as an ant."
Having spoken these words, he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and suddenly vanished from the assembly.
Then Ānanda rose from his seat, joined his palms with single-minded devotion, and asked the Tathāgata:
“What transgression did this Dragon King commit in the past that caused him to fall into the realm of dragons?”
Furthermore, by what karma did we come to have seven heads, with an *erāvaṇa* tree upon each head, which sway and cause us agony while pus and blood flow together?
We only pray that the Tathāgata will explain the causes and conditions for our sake, so that we may know our transgressions.
At that time, the World-Honored One said to Ānanda:

"In the past, during the Bhadrakalpa, when the lifespan of sentient beings was twenty thousand years, a Buddha appeared in the world named Kāśyapa Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān."

At that time, that dragon king went forth in the Buddha-dharma to practice the path, becoming a bhikṣu learned in the Tripitaka. Loathing and fearing the afflictions, he practiced the conduct of seclusion and cultivated śamatha in a quiet and solitary place.

Having emerged from meditative concentration, the sun had already passed its zenith; he entered that village to beg for food, receiving either something or nothing, and was rebuked by people, whereby various afflictions arose within him.
He departed from that village and went to an araṇya, where he wandered back and forth beneath an īra tree.
Then, with both hands, he took its leaves; having plucked them thus four times, he continued to pluck them again and again until they were crushed and cast away.
At that time, the Buddha, having understood this, rebuked the bhikṣu and explained the characteristics of the precepts to him, intending for him to repent and apologize.
He refused to accept it with faith and spoke these words:
"This is an insentient object; what fault could there be in it?"
"Due to these two causes and conditions, he undergoes this retribution of suffering.
Because he begged for food at the improper time, he was born among the nāgas.
Because of his lack of faith, he was born from the airāvaṇa tree."
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"That Nāga King Elāpattra, having created a small cause of evil, now undergoes much suffering.

He himself created the cause and he himself receives the fruit; it was not the external elements of earth, water, fire, or wind that could bring this about, but all was produced by the workings of his own inner mind."
"If there are sentient beings who ultimately delight in performing unrighteous black karma, they will certainly experience the retribution of suffering within the evil realms.
If there are sentient beings who ultimately delight in performing pure white karma, they will certainly experience the retribution of happiness among humans and devas."
If sentient beings perform actions that are a mixture of good and evil, they will experience their retribution in a mixed manner.
Therefore, monks, you must never commit black karma under any circumstances, and you must resolutely cultivate white karma.
The retribution of karmic results arrives suddenly, like a torrential flood; the influence of wholesome and unwholesome deeds is unfailing. As a verse says:
"Even if it passes through immeasurable eons, that karma cannot be destroyed."
"When the retribution ripens, sentient beings will inevitably experience it.
The Buddha said: "O bhikṣus!..."
One should rely on the Buddha’s words and contemplate them according to reason; one must not transgress even slightly against any of the prohibitive precepts.

Therefore, I shall now explain in detail the faults and calamities of violating the precepts, so that sentient beings may develop a deep sense of dread, forever sever all evils, and diligently practice all forms of goodness.
"O bhikṣus! If you expound this sūtra for others, you will achieve the canopy of merit.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda in the assembly addressed [the Buddha], saying:
“World-Honored One!
How is this mark of upholding the precepts to be fully understood?
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"If one wishes to enter the Buddha-dharma, one must first uphold the five precepts: namely, refraining from taking life, abstaining from taking what is not given, avoiding sexual misconduct, abandoning false speech, and abstaining from intoxicants that lead to heedlessness."
One should understand each of these modes of practice individually. Ānanda!

In every city and village, wherever there are virtuous people—laymen and laywomen of pure faith—who rely upon the wholesome Dharma, delight in upholding the pure precepts, and give rise to a pure mind, they are able to receive and maintain these five precepts for as long as their lives last.
As stated in the *Puṇyakriyāvastu-sūtra*:
"How does one maintain the precepts so as to accomplish meritorious deeds?
If a person refrains from killing any sentient being, that person is said to maintain the precept of non-killing."

Regarding the taking of life: from the initial arising of the thought determining that one shall kill a particular living being, or by commanding another to kill, when one gives rise to the mind of application (*prayoga*) and actually severs that life—whether by cutting, slicing, or consuming—it is said that this person incurs the offense of killing.
If a person, regarding the property belonging to others, refrains from taking what is not given, that person is said to uphold the precept against stealing.
Stealing refers to taking another's property without it being given, whether by means of robbery, or by concealing and withholding what another has forgotten.
From the very beginning, when one initiates the preparatory mind and steals another's property, that person is said to have committed the offense of theft.
If a person can remain free from all defiled desires, or does not give rise to the intent to violate another’s form, that person is said to uphold the precept against sexual misconduct.
Regarding sexual misconduct: one must not go to the homes of those who are not kinsmen, to brothels or public streets, or to places where carnal desire arises.
Nor should one employ clever means to leave behind pearls or necklaces for the constant guardians of another's kin, nor should one use force against others who are in distress.
One who gives rise to such thoughts and carries them out through their actions is said to have incurred the offense of improper desire.

If a person can distance themselves from false speech, speaking with sincerity and truthfulness so that mind and mouth do not contradict one another, this person is said to uphold the precept against lying.
Regarding false speech: it refers to saying one has not seen what was seen, or saying what is unreal is real, as explained in the Vinaya.
For example, there may be a bhikṣu who has come from afar, and someone asks him:
"If you have seen such-and-such a person?
Although he has indeed seen them, he replies, "I have not seen him.
In cases such as these, one incurs the offense of lying.

If a person, having cautioned themselves against it, does not drink alcohol—even if its fragrance wafts by on the wind—and has no desire even to smell it, this person is said to uphold the precept of abstaining from intoxicants.
There are three kinds of alcohol:
the first is called *sura*, which is produced by mixing fermented rice with yeast.
The second is called *madya*, which is produced solely from the juice extracted from roots, fruits, flowers, or leaves.

These two types of liquor possess color, fragrance, and flavor; when their scent wafts on the wind, all who smell it desire to drink. Once drunk, they become intoxicated and give rise to heedlessness.
The third is *maireya* (hereafter abbreviated as *mèi*).
These three types of liquor—if one takes pleasure in drinking them, that person is said to have committed the offense of drinking alcohol.
Furthermore, as stated in the *Nandika Sūtra*, regarding fermented grain liquor (*maireya*), one should not produce it.

Once a bhikṣu has drunk it, it gives rise to negligence, causes the depletion of wealth, and results in insufficient sustenance; it increases anger, or leads to mutual physical assault and the exchange of harsh words, resulting in much litigation and dispute.

Having already reached the point of losing their robes and being naked without shame, their ill repute spreads abroad; virtuous people distance themselves from them, they neglect the recitation and study of Mahāyāna sūtras, their wisdom diminishes while ignorance increases, and they show no reverence for the Three Jewels, their parents, or their kinsmen, nor are they held in high esteem within their clan.
In this way, such violations of the precepts arise from drinking the three kinds of intoxicants mentioned above, thereby giving rise to various faults.
Therefore, one should know that one must no longer commit acts such as killing, but should always remain far removed from them.
