Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, the Court Scattered Official and Acting Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial, the Great Master of Xuanfan, the Imperially Enfeoffed Purple-Robed Śramaṇa, the Subject Rìchēng, and others, by imperial decree. Herein is briefly elucidated the characteristic of upholding the precepts.

Beginning with the diligent maintenance and secret protection of the sense faculties, moderation in food and drink, the reduction of sleep, and the constant delight in honoring the cultivation of all holy practices (*brahmacarya*); not rejoicing in or dwelling upon memories of past pleasures; and further being able to manifest the virtues of a śramaṇa and the faults of cyclic existence and the miserable realms.

Associating with virtuous friends, attending to things according to principle, delighting in hearing the true Dharma, and entering into an understanding of its meaning; eliminating greed, anger, and delusion, severing all afflictions, dispelling false and delusive thoughts, and increasing clear wisdom; they focus exclusively on seeking liberation without ever becoming weary.
Should they commit even the slightest transgression or stain, they are able to confess and reveal it all without concealment.
Regarding all wealth and possessions, their minds are free from stinginess, and they always delight in bestowing gifts upon suffering beings.

Fully understanding that the five desires harbor many faults and afflictions, he conceived a sense of detachment toward the bonds of affection for his own kin, regarding them as if they were deep-seated enemies.
Dwelling alone in forests and wilds, he abandoned all clamor and bustle; he did not accumulate surplus possessions, thus distinguishing himself from greedy men.
When there are those who come seeking the Dharma, they do not give rise to stinginess or envy, but immediately proclaim it for them, causing them to gain faith and understanding.

They are able to use the sword of wisdom to eliminate the thieves of affliction, earning the respect and praise of all virtuous people, and becoming worthy of receiving the offerings of the world’s finest clothing, bedding, food, and drink.
One abandons all thoughts of the flavors of meat and, regarding worldly fame and profit, has no desire to acquire them.
Regarding the two types of karmic paths—wholesome and unwholesome—one possesses decisive faith and understanding in both their performance and their cessation.

Having attained personal realization, he eliminated his conceit and, with a mind intent on benefiting others, expounded the Dharma for them; he transformed non-Buddhist followers such as the Nirgranthas, causing them also to give rise to faith and understanding and to dwell securely in the Buddha-dharma.
Whatever possessions one has beyond the three robes, one should give them away with a pure mind.
Such a person dwells within the lineage of the noble ones; their body and mind are cool and refreshing, free from all feverish afflictions.

One should understand that the six sense bases lack any true reality; they are like a festering abscess covered by a membrane, constantly being bitten and fed upon by the mosquitoes and gadflies of the afflictions.
Those who possess wisdom diligently seek skillful means, using the fragrant smoke of the sublime dharmas—the foundations of mindfulness and the Eightfold Noble Path—to fumigate and drive them away.
One should understand that the five aggregates are like a plantain tree; if a mind of craving arises, one should conceive the thought of their lack of solidity.
Because of that craving, one loses and destroys the right path; therefore, one must first restrain the sense faculties so they do not become distracted.
Gradually causing them to practice and abide in samādhi,

one brings about the realization that the intrinsic nature of objects is nothing but suffering— like a dense thicket of thorns difficult to traverse, or like sentient beings defiled by dust and grime, which are then washed clean with the water of the True Dharma.
Observing those aggregates, sense bases, and elements in this way, one sees that they give rise to various afflictions and are not to be relished.
This clarifies that there are two kinds of upholding the precepts: first, impure upholding of the precepts; second, pure upholding of the precepts.
As stated in the Vinaya, there were two bhikṣus who were diligent in upholding the precepts; each resided in a different region, and their good reputations spread far and wide.
At that time, all the people looked up to their virtue and went together to those places to attend upon and make offerings to them.
At that time, there was a king named Kaniṣka who, having heard that two bhikṣus were upholding the pure precepts, went to their dwelling accompanied by his ministers and attendants.
Seeing those elders, whose dignified deportment was solemn and who were practicing meditative concentration, he conceived a heart of reverence and first offered them greetings with a welcoming mind.
The king said:
"Virtuous One!
Maintaining the precepts in such a manner, what do you seek to attain?"
The bhikṣu replied, "In my mind,
I aspire to become a king in a future life.
Upon hearing these words, the king felt no joy.
"How can one who upholds the precepts yet lacks the discernment of wisdom instead turn toward the cycle of saṃsāra and its entanglements?
You have deceived and deluded the devas and the people.
I shall not offer you sustenance here."
"Maintaining the precepts in such a manner is called impure.
He then went to where a newly ordained bhikṣu was staying, and the king asked him:
"Regarding the precepts you now maintain, what do you wish to aspire for?"
The bhikṣu replied:
“I have received Your Majesty’s inquiry.
That which I seek is to attain bodhi, for the benefit and happiness of all beings.”
Upon hearing these words, the king was filled with great joy and said:
"To uphold the precepts in this manner is indeed not erroneous; to be free from all defilements is what is called purity."
"I must now perform the supreme offering.
Thinking thus, the śramaṇa gave rise to a vast and expansive mind, and Śakra and all the devas should offer him worship.
When the people heard the king’s praise, they all joined their palms together and prostrated at the feet of the bhikṣu.
The king then looked toward his various attendants and said,
"Each of you should take what is most precious to you and offer it as a gift.
This is what is called the pure observance of the precepts.
As the Blessed One has taught, there are ten conditions that constitute impure observance of the precepts:

first, the pursuit of harm; second, deep attachment to defiled desires; third, not seeking liberation; fourth, constant indolence; fifth, pervasive conceptualization and craving; sixth, falling away from right practice; seventh, maintaining oneself through wrong livelihood; eighth, losing peaceful happiness; ninth, meager learning and lack of study; and tenth, neglecting and forgetting what has been recited and practiced.
What is meant by "embracing harm"?
It refers to fearing the power and authority of kings, princes, and ministers, and thus constantly remaining far removed from them, as well as from all manner of evil disciplinary codes.

Even if a bhikṣu is pressed by thirst, he should not seek water from them to drink; for one who has not severed the afflictions, has not attained the divine feet, and cannot discipline himself, will give rise to much fear and alarm.
What is meant by being deeply attached to and defiled by desire?
It refers to the continuous flow of improper thoughts regarding the five sensory objects, characterized by an inherently dissolute nature that neglects the practice of wholesome deeds.
What is meant by not seeking liberation?
They abandon what is excellent and pursue what is improper; furthermore, they disparage what is excellent and praise the pleasures of the five desires.
What is meant by being constantly prone to indolence?

It refers to repeatedly dwelling upon past actions that were not beneficial, engaging in mutual disputes, and relying on one's own means of livelihood to indulge as one pleases, thereby giving rise to arrogance. Such persons fail to pay respect to those who are elderly and virtuous, making excuses for their failure to rise in greeting.
What is meant by "pervasive calculation and longing"?
It refers to mutual flattery and praise toward learned companions in the holy life (sabrahmacārin) for the sake of seeking gain and offerings.
What is meant by "falling away from right practice"?
Delighting in the commission of various evils and transgressing the precepts, they lack skillful means to give rise to the path of remediation.
What is meant by "wrong livelihood"?
It is fearing that one is difficult to sustain oneself, and thus the mind knows no contentment.

As stated in the Vinaya, a bhikṣu of wrong livelihood engages in conduct contrary to the discipline, falsely manifesting extraordinary appearances and boasting of his own virtues amidst the great assembly; he speaks much and is shameless, like a mad dog.

Whether relying on their lineage, extensive learning, or debating skills, or preaching the Dharma to others at inappropriate times, they may possess some slight virtue; yet, because of their greed for profit, those who hear the Dharma mostly do not believe or accept it.
Hearing someone say,
"In such-and-such a place, there is a great family of brahmins and elders who are bestowing various garments and sundry requisites," he went immediately to that location and said to the elders:
"I am an elder of venerable virtue; it is my wish that you first grant me the most supreme and marvelous things.
At that time, the householder, fearing the arising of clamor and contention, did not oppose his intent and gave them to him.
When the servants and officials saw him, they all treated him with contempt and disdain; they refused his offerings, expelled him, and sent him away.
At that time, the bhikṣu felt sorrow and distress in his heart and spoke these words before the elder:
"Previously, I did not wish to go to one of inferior lineage to seek my necessities."
"Now that he has gained nothing, he remains without shame; though he is of low birth, he can still practice joyful relinquishment.
Thus the bhikṣu speaks with crafty words and deceit; because of his excessive seeking, his mind is constantly tormented by feverish distress.
What is meant by "losing the bliss of peace"?

Those who uphold the precepts should abide in the practice of the Middle Way, which is neither painful nor pleasant; they should not, like the non-Buddhist Nirgranthas and others, sit or lie upon thorns or subject their bodies to the five heats, undergoing toil and suffering in vain without any fruit or benefit.
If one is attached to pleasure, there is likewise nothing realized; it only increases negligence, which later brings about the retribution of suffering.
What is meant by "having heard little and not studying"?
Though one may externally restrain evil, internally one lacks clear wisdom; being consistently and exclusively ignorant, one is unable to inquire or seek instruction.
What is meant by "neglecting and forgetting one's recitations"?
It refers to those who think only of eating their fill and fail to advance in their practice; they merely satiate their bowels, while impurities overflow.
They are not truly śramaṇas, yet they claim to follow the brahmacarya; they are like sounding conch shells that produce nothing but empty noise.
If any one of these ten conditions is present, this is called impure observance of the precepts;
practitioners should understand this clearly.

If a person possesses deep-seated, resolute faith and understanding, such that they feel great dread even toward minor transgressions, one should know that this person abides well in pure ethical discipline.

As it is said in the Vinaya: there was once an elder who purchased a servant; the man was young and poor, having sold his own body to support himself, yet in his inner heart he maintained the Buddha’s precepts.
Suddenly, the elder ordered me to take life, whereupon I immediately said:
"The elder is a man of integrity; why would he send someone to commit the act of killing?
One must distinguish between what is wholesome and what is unwholesome; as one who upholds the Buddha's precepts, I dare not obey such a command."
The elder was moved to realization and thus desisted from the killing.
Furthermore, there was a king named Kīlaka who constantly governed the world with severe punishments;
if among the common people there were any transgressions, all those subject to the officials were to be executed.
At that time, there was a man who was about to be executed. That caṇḍāla prostrated before the king and said:
"I have now resolved my mind and have just received the Buddha's precepts; I vow not to kill any criminals, nor will I harm even an ant."
The king said,
"You observe the Buddha's precepts and defy the royal decree.
Since you have no further use, what benefit is there in maintaining you?"
Then the caṇḍāla spoke again to the king, saying:
"I am now determined not to violate my pure precepts.
May Your Majesty observe for yourself: even Śakra and the various devas do not dare to transgress the Buddha's regulations, much less those such as myself."
The king said,
"It is indeed so.
You shall first have your head severed by severe punishment."

The caṇḍāla said: "Although this present body of mine is subject to the King, I shall have other bodies in future lives. By means of the merit and roots of goodness from observing these precepts, I shall attain the most sublime happiness in the world, even reaching the heavens to go there at will according to my wishes. In future lives, I shall joyfully seek the wholesome Dharma, increasing the powers of faith, diligence, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom. With the water of merit, I shall wash away the defilements of the three poisons, such as greed, until they are purified without remainder. I shall certainly attain the fruits of stream-entry and so forth, up to the Tathāgata’s pure and wondrous Dharma-body."
Having made this vow, he cried out in a loud voice before the great assembly:
"This body of mine is born of causes and conditions and shall surely come to an end in a single kṣaṇa; yet, to protect the Buddha's precepts, my mind is free from sorrow and fear."
Upon hearing these words, the king’s wrath increased all the more, and he immediately commanded his messengers to drive the caṇḍāla away and take his life in the Śītavana cemetery.
At that time, the people were all filled with astonishment and said to one another:
"This great man is truly rare; for the sake of protecting the Buddha's precepts, he has sacrificed his own life."

Therefore, you should know that among all sentient beings, regardless of whether they are small or great, high or low in caste, if they can possess a profound mind of shame and remorse, maintain firm faith and understanding, and do not transgress, they may be called those who purely uphold the precepts.
In this context, the lack of purity in observing the precepts is further clarified.
As stated in the Vinaya, there was a bhikṣu who practiced the life of seclusion, dwelling among mountain crags and valleys.
Suddenly, during the night, he took some parched grain for food; due to his haste, he broke his vessel.
When the assembly heard this, they rebuked that bhikṣu, saying: "Though you dwell among the mountains, you eat at improper times;
this is called 'impure observance of the precepts.

Furthermore, there was another bhikṣu who was originally a brāhmaṇa and later left the household life to practice the Way in reliance on the Buddha-dharma, delighting in dwelling alone in the wilderness.
Due to habit, he would constantly fold up his *kāṣāya* robe at night and sit in a squatting posture (*utkuṭukāsana*).
Once, when a former disciple came unexpectedly to visit him, he said to him:
"If there is no one here, you may enter that *āmra* grove, gather some fruit, and bring it back."
The disciple, having received these instructions, immediately went to that place and was seized and bound by the master.
This is also called "impure observance of the precepts."
Furthermore, there was a bhikṣu dwelling in an araṇya who practiced the conduct of tranquility. While entering a village for alms, he happened to pass by a brothel.
A woman there asked him:
"For what reason has a precept-observing bhikṣu come here to this place that is not conducive to liberation?"
"If you delight in socializing, you shall enter a pit of fire.
Thus, although this bhikṣu dwells in a secluded place, he fails to observe carefully and is thereby censured by others.
This is also called impure observance of the precepts.
There were two bhikṣus dwelling in an araṇya who, though actually devoid of virtue, claimed to possess it.

Following a group of merchants, they entered the great ocean; there, violent and malevolent black winds arose out of season, and the waves surged with such turbulence that all were struck with terror. Various aquatic creatures and beasts, including makaras, moved back and forth in a chaotic manner, striking and wrecking the ship.
The multitude of people was in a state of turmoil and lamentation; some managed to float to safety, while others were submerged and drowned.
When the old bhikṣu had fallen into the water, seeing that he was frail and decrepit and could not save his own life, he immediately untied the life-preserver and gave it to his companion.
Having obtained them, he took many precious jewels, mani-gems, and the like, and consequently lost his life.
This is called impure observance of the precepts.
Next, the pure observance of the precepts will be explained.
There was a bhikṣu traveling along a distant road who was completely stripped of his robes by a band of thieves.
Among them was one man who had previously been a śramaṇa; knowing that the bhikṣu guarded his precepts, he said to his companions, "Bind him with grass and leave him there."

The bhikṣu focused his mind exclusively on the precepts established by the Buddha; he would not pluck or break even a single blade of grass or leaf, remaining prostrate by the roadside and not daring to move in the slightest.
When the king encountered him while out hunting, he saw him from afar and, suspecting him to be a naked heretic who had failed to rise out of pride, went straight to interrogate him.
Knowing that this bhikṣu was guarding his pure precepts so as not to harm even a blade of grass or a leaf, the king marveled at such rarity;
he then ordered him to be released, provided him with food and drink, and further bestowed robes upon him.
This is what is called the pure upholding of the precepts.
There were two bhikṣus coming from afar who wished to go and make offerings to the Tathāgata’s relics; as they traveled along the road with great hardship, they sought water to drink.
The first bhikṣu, driven by thirst, had no time to examine it and drank the water immediately.
Although the second bhikṣu was also parched with thirst, he observed that there were insects in the water and said to his companion:
"It would be better for me to die of thirst than to harm the lives of other beings."
"One must not transgress the precepts of the World-Honored One.
Sitting upright beneath a tree, he endured his thirst until death.
By virtue of these causes and conditions, he was reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; there he beheld the Buddha, heard the Dharma, and realized the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpanna).
This is what is called pure observance of the precepts.
There was an upāsaka who had long practiced the holy life; suddenly his house was consumed by fire, and he cautioned his sons:
"Be careful not to extinguish the fire with water containing living beings."
Why is this? Because I protect the minute insects within the water at the expense of my wealth; how could I fall into the evil realms for the sake of a small profit?
This is what is called maintaining pure precepts.
Therefore, the wise should abide in pure ethical discipline and remain forever far removed from impure ethical discipline.

One should know that when a Tathāgata appears in the world, he constantly delights in benefiting all sentient beings; he closes the gates to the evil realms and reveals the path to rebirth in the heavens; he burns the fuel of afflictions and uproots the source of craving; he transforms all living beings to cause them to renounce their homes and abandon their fetters, leading them all to attain auspicious peace and happiness; and ultimately, he causes them to transcend the torrential stream of birth and death, to board the vessel of wisdom and reach the other shore, gradually and completely realizing Bodhi and Nirvāṇa.

They raise the great banner of the Dharma, crushing the various non-Buddhists' arrogance and all unwholesome practices; they cause them all to resolve upon courageous and diligent effort, washing away their parching thirst with the water of the True Dharma.

Having heard the Dharma, he practiced and studied according to the teachings; he accumulated the treasure-trove of the jewels of Dharma-wealth and merit, dwelt securely in supernormal powers, transcended the three realms of existence, realized the ultimate truth, and abided in the state of liberation.

Maintaining the precepts in this manner is praised by all Buddhas; one should know that such a person is the eye of the world, capable of guiding sentient beings to a place of peace and security. They are like a bright lamp that can dispel the darkness of ignorance, like pure water that can wash away the defilement of sins, like a wondrous and excellent medicine that cures the disease of afflictions, like a great king of physicians who skillfully extracts the arrows of desire, like a fertile field in this world that produces the sprouts of merit, and who is well able to instruct indolent sentient beings, causing them to give rise to a joyful heart and delight in upholding the pure precepts.
If a person delights in performing unwholesome courses of action, they will inevitably suffer harm, just as one who dwells with an enemy.
Likewise, if one seeks liberation by relying on the non-Buddhist Brahmanical teachings, it will instead bring about calamity and misfortune.

One should rely upon the teachings of the Buddhas of antiquity, seeking liberation through the distinctive marks of the *kāṣāya*; thus one can extinguish all unwholesome roots and cause the armies of Māra to give rise to great anxiety and fear.
By the power of wisdom, they sever the afflictions, attain great renown, and remain free from all decline and suffering, ultimately accomplishing the path to sublime Bodhi.

As it is said of the wise Aśvaghoṣa: he firmly maintained the pure precepts and skillfully expounded the essential points of the Dharma; in his present life he obtained fame and benefit, and upon rebirth in the heavens he received superior karmic rewards, increasing his luminous wisdom and manifold virtues.
One should know that those who are well able to maintain pure precepts are like a poor man who has obtained a vessel of excellence; whatever they seek, they obtain according to their wishes.
Those who maintain pure precepts should always be diligent and reverently guard them, serving them with no thought of weariness as if attending upon a venerable teacher.

It is likewise so. As the World-Honored One has said, one who maintains pure precepts shall obtain ten kinds of efficacy. First, because of maintaining the precepts, whatever one undertakes is free from error;

afflictions do not arise and the mind is constantly joyful. Because of this joy, one takes deep delight in the Dharma with the heart; because of delighting in the Dharma, the body attains pliancy (*praśrabdhi*); because of pliancy, one experiences sublime bliss; because of sublime bliss, one induces meditative concentration (*samādhi*); because of attaining concentration, one realizes the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*); because of realizing the limit of reality, one dwells securely in Bodhi, turns away from hindrances and defilements, and abides in the wisdom of non-self (*anātman*). Thus, one is able to eternally sever subtle afflictions, such that one knows: "Birth has been exhausted, the holy life (*brahmacarya*) has been established, there is no further existence to be received, and I am heading toward the realm of Nirvāṇa."

Second, by virtue of upholding the precepts, one commits no further sins through the three types of action, remains far removed from the evil realms, and experiences no fear at the time of death. As the merit and wholesome deeds performed manifest before one, one is reborn according to one's wish in a superior realm to enjoy happiness.
Third, by virtue of maintaining ethical discipline, one's excellent reputation spreads abroad, and those who hear it offer praise.
Fourth, by virtue of maintaining ethical discipline, one sleeps in peace and awakens in peace, with neither body nor mind afflicted by distress.
Fifth, by virtue of upholding the precepts, one is always cherished and protected by the devas.
Sixth, by virtue of upholding the precepts, one remains free from timidity when amidst the great assembly.
Seventh, by virtue of upholding the precepts, non-human beings will not seek out one's faults.
Eighth, by virtue of upholding the precepts, one will be regarded by all wicked people as a kinsman.
Ninth, by virtue of maintaining ethical discipline, one lacks for nothing in their needs and need not strive for them; they constantly receive the respect and offerings of virtuous people.
Tenth, by virtue of maintaining ethical discipline, all that one aspires to is accomplished according to one's wishes.

If one desires to seek birth in a most noble lineage, as a wealthy householder or a brahmin family; or if one seeks birth among the various devas of the six heavens of desire, up to the heavens of the form realm and the formless realm; or if one seeks the tranquil liberation of the fruit of arhatship free from desire—in all such cases, one shall attain their wishes as they intend.

The merit obtained from maintaining the precepts in this way is like the great ocean—profound, vast, and boundless; were I to explain it in full detail and sequence, I could not exhaust it even until the end of the future.
Regarding the power of upholding the precepts as explained above, who has ever attained such sublime retribution?
It is the Buddha, the Great Sage, who has accomplished it all.

From the initial generation of the mind of enlightenment and the cultivation of pure precepts, until the attainment of the three knowledges (*traividya*), the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), the powers (*bala*), the fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), and so forth—the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor characteristics are exquisite and distinct, perfect and without deficiency. His dark hair curls to the right, black and glossy like a bee; the halo around his neck is like the full moon; his countenance is dignified and beautiful like a blooming lotus; his physical form is exceptionally prominent like a mountain of refined gold; his two feet are level and well-set; and his limbs are perfectly rounded like a *nyagrodha* tree.

He always regards all sentient beings with eyes of love; all who see the Buddha receive benefit, as he employs skillful means to rescue and deliver them from the evil realms. Because he is without equal in all the worlds, he is called the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, the One Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, the Sugata, the Knower of the World, the Unsurpassed One, the Tamer of Men, the Teacher of Gods and Humans, the Buddha, and the World-Honored One.

If sentient beings uphold the pure precepts, they will be able to attain the aforementioned merits, becoming no different from all Tathāgatas, and will be well able to bring benefit and happiness to all sentient beings; therefore, after explaining generosity, the upholding of those precepts is clarified.
The sequential characteristics have already been explained as before. You bhikṣus!
You should always, with a single mind, delight in practicing giving and precepts, and manifest them for others; thus you will fully accomplish the canopy of merit.
